name: Aaron Ciechanover
summary: Aaron Ciechanover is an Israeli biochemist and Nobel laureate recognized for his groundbreaking work on ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation. Along with Avram Hershko and Irwin Rose, he characterized the Ubiquitin-Proteasome System (UPS), a fundamental cellular process that identifies and breaks down unwanted or damaged proteins. This discovery has profoundly impacted our understanding of cellular regulation, disease mechanisms, and the development of new therapeutics.
contributions: Co-discovered ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation (the Ubiquitin-Proteasome System or UPS)
Elucidated the mechanism by which cells label proteins with ubiquitin for targeted degradation
Revealed the critical roles of the UPS in essential cellular processes like cell division, DNA repair, and immune defense
His research led to the development of anti-cancer drugs, including proteasome inhibitors like Velcade®
Established connections between UPS dysregulation and the pathogenesis of malignancies and neurodegenerative disorders
quotes: "Ubiquitin is everywhere, and it's not only for degradation."

"If I would have been asked a few years ago, 'What's ubiquitin?' I would have said it's a degradation signal. Now if somebody will ask me what ubiquitin is I say it's a passport…. It's dynamic and it's very flexible. You can use the same molecule to send different signals to different molecules to fulfil different functions."
"Every experiment, regardless of the outcome, contributes to the advancement of science."

name: Ada Lovelace
summary: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician who worked with Charles Babbage on his proposed Analytical Engine. She is regarded as the first computer programmer for recognizing that such a machine could go beyond pure calculation.
contributions: Wrote the first published algorithm intended for a machine
Foresaw that computers could manipulate symbols, not just numbers
Bridged mathematics and imagination, laying conceptual groundwork for computer science

name: Ada Yonath
summary: Ada Yonath is an Israeli protein crystallographer who was awarded the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her pioneering work on the atomic structure and function of ribosomes. Her research significantly advanced structural biology, revealing how ribosomes synthesize proteins and providing insights crucial for developing new antibiotics. She is also credited with pioneering the cryocrystallography technique.
contributions: Pioneering the study of the atomic structure and function of ribosomes
Determining the three-dimensional atomic arrangement of a large ribosomal subunit
Developing cryocrystallography, a technique that overcomes radiation damage to protein crystals
Identifying tunnel-like structures within ribosomes through which newly synthesized polypeptide chains pass
Mapping the structure of ribosomal subunits using X-ray crystallography
Elucidating the modes of action of antibiotics by targeting ribosomal structures
quotes: "You can always try another approach; even change your subject when a scientific strategy or experiment fails."
"I don't walk into the lab in the morning thinking, 'I am a woman, and I will carry out an experiment that will conquer the world.' I am a scientist, not male or female. A scientist."
"If one has curiosity, then one stands the chance of attain a high level of scientific inquiry."

name: Adam Riess
summary: Adam Riess is an American astrophysicist and Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins University and the Space Telescope Science Institute. He is best known for leading the 1998 discovery that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, a phenomenon attributed to "dark energy." For this groundbreaking work, which revolutionized cosmology, he shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. His research continues to focus on measuring the universe's expansion rate and understanding dark energy.
contributions: Led the High-z Supernova Search Team in the 1998 discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe.
Shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for providing evidence of the accelerating expansion of the universe.
Conducted extensive research using Type Ia supernovae as precise cosmological probes to measure cosmic distances and expansion rates.
Developed new methods and led efforts using the Hubble Space Telescope to increase the precision of dark energy findings and measure the Hubble constant.
Provided evidence for an early phase of decelerating expansion of the Universe, further supporting the dark energy-dark matter model.
quotes: “My involvement in the discovery of the accelerating universe and its implications for the presence of dark energy has been an incredibly exciting adventure. I have also been fortunate to work with tremendous colleagues and powerful facilities. I am deeply honored that this work has been recognized.”
“Dark energy is incredibly strange, but actually it makes sense to me that it went unnoticed, because dark energy has no effect on daily life, or even inside our solar system.”
“We believe that everywhere that you have space, empty space, that you cannot avoid having some of this dark energy.”

name: Akira Yoshino
summary: Akira Yoshino is a Japanese chemist and Nobel laureate, recognized for his pivotal role in developing the first safe and commercially viable lithium-ion battery (LIB). His innovations enabled the portable electronic revolution and are crucial for electric vehicles and renewable energy storage. He currently serves as an honorary fellow at Asahi Kasei Corporation and a professor at Meijo University.
contributions: Invented the first safe, production-viable lithium-ion battery (LIB).
Developed a carbonaceous anode, utilizing petroleum coke, to replace metallic lithium, which enhanced battery safety and lifespan.
Introduced the aluminum foil current collector, functional separator membrane, and a positive temperature coefficient (PTC) device to improve battery safety and performance.
Conceived the coil-wound structure for lithium-ion batteries, enabling high current discharge despite low electrolyte conductivity.
Secured the basic patent for the LIB in 1985, which paved the way for its commercialization in 1991.
quotes: "It is very important to think every day."
"There are many fields that haven't yet been discovered and I want (younger researchers) to challenge the unknown and pave new ways, without following the paths of others."

name: Alain Aspect
summary: Alain Aspect is a French physicist recognized for his pivotal experimental work on quantum entanglement. His experiments, particularly those testing Bell's inequalities, definitively showed that quantum mechanics violates local realism, thus profoundly impacting our understanding of quantum reality. This work, for which he shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics, has been fundamental in establishing the field of quantum information science and technology.
contributions: Experimental verification of Bell's inequalities using entangled photons
Pioneering quantum information science
Demonstrating wave-particle duality for single photons
Contributions to laser cooling of atoms, including cooling below the one-photon recoil limit
First direct observation of Anderson localization with ultra-cold atoms
quotes: Entanglement cannot be understood as usual correlations, whose interpretation relies on the existence of common properties.
The main ingredient of the first quantum revolution, wave-particle duality, has led to inventions such as the transistor and the laser that are at the root of the information society.

Certainly we do not need quantum mechanics for macroscopic objects, which are well described by classical physics – this is the reason why quantum mechanics seems so foreign to our everyday existence.

name: Alan Turing
summary: Alan Turing was a British mathematician and logician widely considered the father of theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence. His wartime codebreaking at Bletchley Park helped turn the tide of World War II.
contributions: Formalized computation with the concept of the Turing machine
Proposed the Turing test as a benchmark for machine intelligence
Led codebreaking efforts that cracked the German Enigma cipher

name: Albert Einstein
summary: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose theory of relativity transformed our understanding of space, time, gravity, and energy. His work laid much of the foundation of modern physics and made him a global symbol of scientific genius.
contributions: Developed the special and general theories of relativity
Explained the photoelectric effect, foundational to quantum theory (1921 Nobel Prize in Physics)
Derived the mass–energy equivalence, E = mc²

name: Aleksey Yekimov
summary: Aleksey Yekimov is a Russian solid state physicist renowned for his pioneering work in nanomaterials. In 1981, he discovered semiconductor nanocrystals, known as quantum dots, demonstrating how their optical properties are dependent on their size. This foundational research, which unveiled size-dependent quantum effects in colored glass, led to him sharing the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. His discoveries have profoundly impacted fields like electronics and medicine by enabling new technological applications.
contributions: Discovery of semiconductor nanocrystals (quantum dots) in 1981.
Demonstrated size-dependent quantum effects in copper chloride nanocrystals in glass.
Developed the theory of quantum confinement with Alexander Efros.
Co-recipient of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots.
His work enabled advancements in QLED displays, solar cells, and biomedical imaging.
quotes: "It's the middle of the night here!"
"I woke up,"
"I still remember that picture,"

name: Alexander Wissner-Gross
summary: Dr. Alexander Wissner-Gross is a computer scientist, inventor, and investor. He is best known for proposing the theory of causal entropic forces, which frames intelligent behavior as a drive to maximize future freedom of action.
contributions: Proposed the theory of causal entropic forces linking intelligence to future option-keeping
Holds multiple patents and has published across physics, AI, and complex systems
Co-host of the Moonshots with Peter Diamandis podcast

name: Andrea Ghez
summary: Andrea Ghez is an American astrophysicist renowned for her groundbreaking research on the center of the Milky Way galaxy. She shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for the co-discovery of a supermassive compact object, now recognized as a black hole, at the galactic center. Her work utilizes advanced high spatial resolution imaging techniques to study stellar dynamics, providing crucial evidence for the existence and role of supermassive black holes in galaxy evolution.
contributions: Co-discovered the supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.
Pioneered the use of high-resolution imaging techniques, including infrared speckle imaging and adaptive optics, for astronomical observations.
Leads the UCLA Galactic Center Group, focusing on understanding the physics of gravity near black holes and their role in galaxy formation.
Provided pivotal evidence for the existence of supermassive black holes and their influence on galactic evolution.
quotes: Gravity wins over all other known forces.

Black holes are very exotic objects. Technically, a black hole puts a huge amount of mass inside of zero volume. So our understanding of the center of black holes doesn't make sense, which is a big clue to physicists that we don't have our physics quite right.

I feel more passionate about the teaching side of my job than I have ever been, because it's so important to convince the younger generation that their ability to question and think is crucial to the future of the world.

name: Andrew Fire
summary: Andrew Fire is an American biologist and professor of pathology and genetics at Stanford University School of Medicine. He is best known for his co-discovery of RNA interference (RNAi) with Craig C. Mello, a fundamental mechanism of gene regulation where double-stranded RNA silences specific genes. This breakthrough earned them the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2006, revolutionizing the understanding of gene expression and opening new avenues for therapeutic development.
contributions: Co-discovered RNA interference (RNAi) with Craig C. Mello.
Demonstrated that double-stranded RNA molecules can selectively suppress the activity of matching target genes.
Showed that RNAi regulates gene expression in various organisms, including plants, animals, and humans.
Identified RNAi's role in defending against RNA virus infections and maintaining genome stability.
Conducted pioneering research on gene regulation mechanisms in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.

name: Andrew Wiles
summary: Andrew Wiles is a distinguished English mathematician specializing in number theory, globally recognized for his groundbreaking proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. His extensive research has unified disparate mathematical ideas and advanced the understanding of elliptic curves and modular forms. He has held significant academic positions at Princeton University and the University of Oxford.
contributions: Proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
Proof of the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture for semistable elliptic curves
Proof of the main conjecture of Iwasawa theory
Significant contributions to the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
Development of new mathematical tools unifying number theory, elliptic curves, and modular forms
quotes: Perhaps I could best describe my experience of doing mathematics in terms of entering a dark mansion. You go into the first room and it's dark, completely dark. You stumble around, bumping into the furniture. Gradually, you learn where each piece of furniture is. And finally, after six months or so, you find the light switch and turn it on. Suddenly, it's all illuminated and you can see exactly where you were. Then you enter the next dark room.
Always try the problem that matters most to you.

name: Anne L'Huillier
summary: Anne L'Huillier is a French-Swedish physicist renowned for her work in attosecond physics and laser science. She is a professor of atomic physics at Lund University and a recipient of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics. Her groundbreaking research involves using intense laser light to generate attosecond pulses, allowing scientists to observe the ultrafast movements of electrons in atoms and molecules. This has opened new frontiers in understanding electron dynamics and led to the field of attochemistry.
contributions: Discovered high harmonic generation in gases
Pioneered the field of attosecond physics
Developed experimental methods to generate attosecond pulses of light
Enabled the observation of electron dynamics in matter on attosecond timescales
Set a world record for the shortest laser pulse (170 attoseconds) in 2003
quotes: "Even now, 30 years afterwards, we are still learning new things."
"When you fail, it's about being obstinate and to continue. This is a quality that you need to have if you want to do research, to be obstinate and to never give up. That's essential."
"Yes, we are mostly empty space — I love that concept."

name: Anton Zeilinger
summary: Anton Zeilinger is an Austrian quantum physicist and Nobel laureate in Physics. He is renowned for his pioneering experimental research on quantum entanglement and quantum information science. His work has significantly advanced our understanding of the fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics and laid the groundwork for future quantum technologies, including quantum communication and computation.
contributions: Pioneering experimental work on quantum entanglement phenomena.
First experimental demonstration of quantum teleportation.
Development of multi-particle entangled states, known as GHZ states.
First experimental realization of entanglement swapping.
Pioneering long-distance quantum communication and cryptography, including satellite-based experiments.
Contributions to matter-wave interferometry, including with large molecules like fullerenes.
quotes: We have to give up the idea of realism to a far greater extent than most physicists believe today.
Entanglement is the feature of the quantum world that forces us to say farewell to all our cherished views of how the world is built up.

name: Ardem Patapoutian
summary: Ardem Patapoutian is a Lebanese-American molecular biologist and neuroscientist, recognized for his groundbreaking work on the molecular mechanisms of touch and temperature sensation. He co-received the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries of ion channels, including PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, which detect mechanical stimuli, and TRPM8, a cold-sensing receptor. His research has significantly advanced our understanding of how mechanical forces and temperature are translated into nerve signals.
contributions: Discovery and characterization of the PIEZO1 ion channel for sensing mechanical stimuli.
Discovery and characterization of the PIEZO2 ion channel for touch, proprioception, and interoception.
Identification of TRPM8, an ion channel that detects cold temperatures and menthol.
Elucidation of how mechanical forces and temperature are converted into electrical impulses in the nervous system.
Pioneering research in mechanotransduction, the cellular process of sensing mechanical stimuli.

name: Arieh Warshel
summary: Arieh Warshel is an Israeli-American biochemist and biophysicist, a pioneer in computational studies of biological molecules. He shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Martin Karplus and Michael Levitt for the development of multiscale models that combine classical and quantum mechanics to simulate complex chemical systems. His groundbreaking work has significantly advanced the understanding of enzyme catalysis and the design of new pharmaceuticals.
contributions: Developed multiscale models for complex chemical systems, combining classical and quantum mechanics.
Pioneered computer simulations of the functions of biological molecules.
Co-developed the Quantum Chemistry/Molecular Mechanics (QM/MM) method for simulating enzymatic reactions.
Introduced molecular dynamics simulations in biology, including the first simulation of a biological process.
Pioneered microscopic modeling of electrostatic effects in macromolecules and simulations of protein folding.
Co-developed computer programs for molecular simulations, widely used in drug design.
quotes: "This is the best tool to see how molecules are working."
"If we find a way to fight this problem, it's going to help human health."

name: Arthur Ashkin
summary: Arthur Ashkin is an American physicist and Nobel laureate known for inventing optical tweezers, a groundbreaking tool that uses laser beams to trap and manipulate microscopic particles, atoms, viruses, and living cells. His work on radiation pressure of light revolutionized the ability to study delicate biological materials without physical contact. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2018 for this invention, which has significant applications in biology, medicine, quantum optics, and nanoengineering.
contributions: Invented optical tweezers for manipulating microscopic objects with laser light
Pioneered the optical trapping and manipulation of neutral particles using radiation pressure
Applied optical tweezers to biological systems, including living cells, viruses, bacteria, and DNA
Co-discovered the photorefractive effect in piezoelectric crystals
Conducted early research in nonlinear optics, optical fibers, and parametric oscillators
quotes: "When I described catching living things with light people said, 'Don't exaggerate, Ashkin'!"
"I was interested in science since I was a kid, so I tell my wife that's the only thing that I'm really good at."
"I'm making cheap electricity."

name: Arthur McDonald
summary: Arthur McDonald is a Canadian astrophysicist and Nobel laureate, recognized for his leadership of the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) experiment. His work conclusively demonstrated that neutrinos change "flavor" (oscillate) and possess mass, a discovery that fundamentally revised the Standard Model of particle physics. This breakthrough also provided a deeper understanding of the sun's processes and the evolution of the universe.
contributions: Led the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) Collaboration as its director
Discovered neutrino oscillations, showing that neutrinos change identities or "flavours"
Demonstrated that neutrinos have a non-zero mass, necessitating revisions to the Standard Model of Particle Physics
Solved the long-standing solar neutrino problem
Co-recipient of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of neutrino oscillations
quotes: "It's fun, once you get there."
"I am fascinated by it, I am still fascinated by the fact that you can do calculations that actually show how the universe works in great detail from the most microscopic to the largest scales."

name: Avi Loeb
summary: Avi Loeb is an Israeli-American theoretical physicist and the Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science at Harvard University, specializing in astrophysics and cosmology. He is recognized for his research on black holes, the first stars and galaxies, and his controversial yet influential work on the search for extraterrestrial life, notably his hypothesis that 'Oumuamua might be an alien artifact. Loeb founded the Black Hole Initiative and currently leads the Galileo Project, dedicated to systematically searching for extraterrestrial technological artifacts.
contributions: Chaired Harvard's Department of Astronomy (2011-2020)
Founded and directed the Black Hole Initiative at Harvard University (2016-2021)
Directs the Institute for Theory and Computation within the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics
Proposed the hypothesis that the interstellar object 'Oumuamua could be an extraterrestrial technological artifact
Established the Galileo Project for the systematic scientific search for evidence of extraterrestrial technological artifacts
Made contributions to the understanding of the first stars and galaxies, and gravitational microlensing
quotes: "One of the most difficult lessons to impart to young scientists is that the search for the truth can run counter to the search for consensus."
"It would be arrogant to think we are alone."
"The existence of intelligent life on Earth is more than sufficient justification to approach seriously the scientific, as opposed to fictional, search for life elsewhere in the universe."

name: Avi Wigderson
summary: Avi Wigderson is an Israeli-American mathematician and computer scientist renowned for his foundational contributions to theoretical computer science, particularly in computational complexity theory. He has significantly advanced the understanding of algorithms, randomness, and their applications in computation and cryptography. His work has forged deep connections between mathematics and computer science, earning him prestigious accolades like the Abel Prize and the Turing Award.
contributions: Significantly contributed to and deepened the field of computational complexity.
Made fundamental contributions to zero-knowledge proofs, which are now integral to blockchain technology.
Investigated the role of randomness in computation and revealed deep connections between computational hardness and randomness.
Co-developed the "zig-zag graph product," linking group theory, graph theory, and complexity theory.
Made key contributions to the theoretical basis for internet security and cryptography.
quotes: “I consider myself unbelievably lucky to live in this age.”

"[Computational complexity] is a young field. It is a very democratic field. It is a very friendly field, it is a field that is very collaborative, that suits my nature. And definitely, it is bursting with intellectual problems and challenges.”
“It's good to have hard problems.”

name: Avram Hershko
summary: Avram Hershko is a Hungarian-born Israeli biochemist who, along with Aaron Ciechanover and Irwin Rose, was awarded the 2004 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation. His groundbreaking work elucidated how cells regulate essential processes by selectively removing unwanted proteins, influencing understanding of cell division, DNA repair, and the molecular basis of diseases. He remains an active researcher and Distinguished Professor at the Technion–Israel Institute of Technology.
contributions: Discovered the ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation system.
Elucidated the mechanism by which cells remove unwanted proteins.
Demonstrated the role of ubiquitin in controlling vital cellular processes like cell division, DNA repair, and gene transcription.
Established the molecular basis for diseases such as certain types of cancer and cystic fibrosis.
His research provided the foundation for the development of drugs, including Velcade, used in cancer treatment.
Identified the three types of enzymes (E1, E2, E3) involved in ubiquitin-protein ligation.
quotes: "The boundaries between chemistry, biology, physics and medicine are rapidly disappearing. Only a comprehensive understanding of the chemical and physical processes in our cells and organ systems will yield the insights needed to develop rational approaches to the prevention and treatment of disease."
"Try to find a unique problem which is important, but which is not yet in the center of the attention of biology or of chemistry."

name: Barbara Liskov
summary: Barbara Liskov is a distinguished American computer scientist renowned for her foundational work in programming languages and distributed computing. She pioneered abstract data types, developed the influential Liskov Substitution Principle, and designed programming languages such as CLU and Argus. Her contributions have significantly advanced modern software design, enabling the creation of more reliable and maintainable systems. Liskov is an Institute Professor at MIT and a recipient of the Turing Award, the highest honor in computer science.
contributions: Introduced abstract data types and the principle of data abstraction
Developed the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) for object-oriented programming
Designed and implemented the CLU programming language, influencing modern languages like Java and C++
Created Argus, the first high-level language to support the implementation of distributed programs
Led the development of the Venus operating system
Made pioneering contributions to distributed computing and fault tolerance, including Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT)
quotes: "The key to building reliable software is to understand that complexity is the enemy."
"You never need optimal performance, you need good-enough performance. [...] Programmers are far too hung up with performance."
"It's really just common sense."

name: Barry Barish
summary: Barry Barish is an American experimental physicist and Nobel Laureate, primarily recognized for his pivotal role in the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO). His leadership at LIGO led to the first direct observation of gravitational waves, confirming a major prediction of Einstein's Theory of Relativity and opening a new era in astronomy. He also made significant contributions to high-energy particle physics, including experiments that revealed the quark substructure of nucleons.
contributions: Led the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) to the first direct detection of gravitational waves.
Awarded the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.
Conducted pioneering experiments in high-energy neutrino physics, revealing the quark substructure of nucleons.
Provided crucial evidence for the existence of weak neutral currents.
Directed the MACRO experiment, contributing evidence for neutrino mass and oscillations.
quotes: I didn't know if I would succeed. I was afraid I would fail, but because I tried, I had a breakthrough.
The actual size of the signal was about one thousandth the size of a proton!
I have somewhat ambivalent feelings about the recognition of individuals when so much of this was a team effort.

name: Ben Feringa
summary: Ben Feringa is a Dutch synthetic organic chemist renowned for his pioneering work in molecular nanotechnology, specifically the design and synthesis of molecular machines. He was a co-recipient of the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his development of the first light-driven molecular rotary motors. His research aims to create artificial molecular systems with dynamic functions for applications in fields like materials science and targeted drug delivery.
contributions: Discovery of the first light-driven molecular rotary motor in 1999.
Development of molecular cars (nanocars).
Pioneering work in molecular nanotechnology and molecular machines.
Significant contributions to asymmetric catalysis and stereochemistry.
Research in photopharmacology for light-controlled bioactive molecules and targeted drug delivery.
Development of chiroptical molecular switches based on chiral overcrowded alkenes.
quotes: "These molecular machines might have a dramatic effect on how we make materials and on what kind of smart functions we can do in the future."
"We want to have the antibiotic switched on exactly on the spot where the infection is."
"We ask questions. We have the freedom to be critical. We have the freedom to explore."

name: Benjamin List
summary: German chemist Benjamin List, born in 1968, is a director at the Max Planck Institute for Coal Research and a professor of organic chemistry. He was awarded the 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry jointly with David MacMillan for their independent development of asymmetric organocatalysis, a groundbreaking method that uses small organic molecules to drive chemical reactions more efficiently and sustainably. His work has significantly impacted pharmaceutical research and made chemical processes greener.
contributions: Co-development of asymmetric organocatalysis, a new type of catalysis utilizing small organic molecules.
Discovery of the amino acid proline as an efficient chiral catalyst for intermolecular aldol and Mannich reactions.
Pioneering methods for the synthesis of important molecules without the intensive use of environmentally damaging heavy metals.
Development of Asymmetric Counteranion Directed Catalysis (ACDC).
Development of textile-organic catalysis, which can involve sequestering soluble organic catalysts to textile materials for applications such as water treatment.
quotes: "We discovered that there is a third way to make chemical reactions faster, cheaper and more sustainable."
"One of the best things with being a scientist, according to Nobel Laureate Benjamin List, is that you discover things that nobody else has seen before."
"Communicating science accurately is vital – otherwise we will never achieve trust in science."

name: Bert Vogelstein
summary: Bert Vogelstein is a renowned American oncologist and cancer researcher credited with pioneering the field of cancer genetics. His seminal work revealed that cancers arise from the progressive accumulation of genetic mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, establishing a foundational paradigm for modern cancer research. He has significantly advanced understanding of cancer pathogenesis, leading to improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, including the development of liquid biopsies for early detection.
contributions: Proposed the sequential accumulation model of genetic mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes as the cause of cancer.
Discovered the critical role of the p53 tumor suppressor gene in human cancers.
Identified other key tumor suppressor genes, including DCC and APC, and mismatch repair (MMR) genes.
Pioneered the concept and development of "liquid biopsies" for early cancer detection.
Published some of the first genome-wide sequencing studies of cancer.
quotes: "I thought, if we're ever going be able to help patients like this man's daughter, we're going to have to figure out what the cause of this disease is. Without knowing the cause of the disease, it's seemed impossible to figure out a way to prevent it or cure it."

"It took us about 2 months to realize we had discovered a cancer gene [p53] that was likely involved in most cancers in the world, and that was going to start a revolution in cancer research, which it did."

"Our end goal is not really publishing papers and making discoveries that turn out to be important. Our end goal is emptying the cancer center across the street in the hospital. To us, the papers are just way stations to the end."

name: Beth Shapiro
summary: Beth Shapiro is an American evolutionary molecular biologist renowned for her pioneering work in ancient DNA and paleogenomics. She specializes in analyzing genetic material from extinct and endangered species to understand their evolutionary history and inform conservation efforts. As Chief Science Officer at Colossal Biosciences, she leads groundbreaking research in de-extinction and species preservation.
contributions: Pioneering the field of ancient DNA analysis and paleogenomics.
Generated the first DNA data from a dodo, determining its evolutionary relationship to pigeons.
Developed experimental and computational tools for population-scale questions using ancient DNA.
Leading de-extinction efforts for species like the woolly mammoth, dodo, and dire wolf at Colossal Biosciences.
Applying genetic engineering tools to bolster genetic diversity and protect endangered species.
Authored influential books such as "How to Clone a Mammoth: The Science of De-Extinction" and "Life As We Made It."
quotes: Conservation isn't just about saving species, but about maintaining the ecological conditions that protect human health.

Vascularized organoids develop into complex structures that are physiologically relevant models for studying diseases. Because they can be grown from a particular individual, [they can be used for] testing personalized treatments for cancers and other diseases.
It's thrilling to see the research we've been doing in the labs not only seeing the light of day, but being applied to science that will positively impact the planet.

name: Bonnie Bassler
summary: Bonnie Bassler is an American molecular biologist renowned for her groundbreaking research on quorum sensing, a process by which bacteria communicate using chemical signals. Her work has fundamentally changed the scientific understanding of bacterial behavior, revealing them as social organisms that coordinate group activities. Bassler's discoveries have significant implications for developing new strategies to combat bacterial infections and understand microbiomes.
contributions: Discovered the universal mechanism of quorum sensing, demonstrating how bacteria engage in cell-to-cell communication.
Identified autoinducers (AI-1 and AI-2) as key chemical signaling molecules for both intra-species and inter-species bacterial communication.
Elucidated how small regulatory RNAs control quorum sensing and virulence in pathogenic bacteria like *Vibrio cholerae*.
Pioneered the concept of interfering with quorum sensing as a novel approach to develop anti-microbial therapies, distinct from traditional antibiotics.
Revealed that bacterial viruses (phages) can eavesdrop on bacterial communication to decide when to attack their hosts.
quotes: "I think being open-minded about what Nature is trying to tell you is the key to being creative and successful."
"You think of yourselves as human beings, but I think of you as 99 percent bacterial."
"[Bacteria] have an incredibly complicated chemical lexicon that ... allows bacteria to be multicellular."

name: Brian Greene
summary: Brian Greene is an American theoretical physicist and professor of physics and mathematics at Columbia University. He is renowned for his groundbreaking discoveries in superstring theory and for his exceptional ability to popularize complex scientific concepts for general audiences through bestselling books and television programs. Greene also co-founded the World Science Festival, an annual event dedicated to promoting science literacy.
contributions: Groundbreaking discoveries in superstring theory.
Co-discovery of mirror symmetry.
Discovery of spatial topology change, including flop and conifold transitions.
Authored best-selling popular science books such as "The Elegant Universe" and "The Fabric of the Cosmos", explaining complex physics concepts.
Co-founded the World Science Festival in 2008 to engage the public with science.
quotes: “When kids look up to great scientists the way they do to great musicians and actors, civilization will jump to the next level.”
“Science is the process that takes us from confusion to understanding...”
“Physicists have come to realize that mathematics, when used with sufficient care, is a proven pathway to truth.”

name: Brian Kobilka
summary: Brian Kobilka is an American physician and molecular biologist who was awarded the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. His groundbreaking research focuses on G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), elucidating their structure and mechanism of activation. His work has profoundly advanced the understanding of cellular signaling and significantly impacted drug discovery and development.
contributions: Identified and cloned the gene for the beta-adrenergic receptor in the 1980s.
Demonstrated the structural similarity between the beta-adrenergic receptor and rhodopsin, revealing a large family of G-protein-coupled receptors.
Achieved the first high-resolution crystal structures of the beta2-adrenergic receptor, a key G-protein-coupled receptor.
Elucidated the molecular mechanisms underlying GPCR activation and transmembrane signaling.
Paved the way for developing more effective drugs by providing detailed insights into GPCR function.
Co-recipient of the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his discoveries concerning G-protein-coupled receptors.
quotes: "It was so exciting to see this three-dimensional structure and finally know how these trans-membrane regions interact during signaling. I hope my discovery leads to better and less-expensive drugs for patients."

name: Brian Schmidt
summary: Brian Schmidt is an American-Australian astrophysicist and Nobel laureate, best known for his pivotal role in discovering the accelerating expansion of the universe. As the leader of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, his research provided compelling evidence for this phenomenon, leading to the concept of dark energy. His work has fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the cosmos and its evolution.
contributions: Co-discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe
Provided evidence for the existence of dark energy
Formed and led the High-Z Supernova Search Team
Pioneered the use of Type Ia supernovae as cosmological probes
quotes: "Even if I stumble on to the absolute truth of any aspect of the universe, I will not realise my luck and instead will spend my life trying to find flaws in this understanding - such is the role of a scientist."
"I am an astronomer, and my job is to look to the heavens to better understand the universe and our place in it."
"There can be theory but, you know, the problem is you've got to be able to test it. So theories are one thing, testing is another."

name: Bruce Beutler
summary: Bruce Beutler is an American immunologist and geneticist who received a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He is recognized for his discoveries concerning the activation of innate immunity, particularly identifying the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) receptor, Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). His research has significantly advanced the understanding of how the immune system detects infections and has led to therapies for inflammatory diseases.
contributions: Discovery of the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) as the mammalian receptor for bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
Elucidation of the role of Toll-like receptors in sensing microbial invaders and activating innate immunity.
Isolation of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and characterization of its inflammation-promoting effects.
Development of TNF inhibitors, which are used as therapies for inflammatory diseases like rheumatoid arthritis.
Pioneering the use of random germline mutagenesis and forward genetics in mice to identify key components of the immune system and other biological processes.
quotes: "That's been a great help to millions of people, and I'm proud of that."

"I was often told by people, including by my father, that I was putting all of my eggs in one basket. But I must say in retrospect, if we hadn't been focused and committed to one problem, we probably wouldn't have got there. It was risky but I would counsel people to undertake high-risk projects and do them serially, rather than to work in parallel with a number of low-risk projects."
"Getting the Prize was never the goal. You should go into science to explore and discover something and because you feel understanding nature to be deeply rewarding, not to get the Nobel Prize."

name: Carl June
summary: Carl June is an American immunologist and oncologist renowned for his pioneering work in developing CAR T-cell therapy, a revolutionary cancer treatment. He serves as a professor in Immunotherapy at the University of Pennsylvania, where his research focuses on genetically engineering T cells for cancer and HIV cell-based therapies. His groundbreaking contributions have led to the first FDA-approved gene therapy for cancer, profoundly impacting the field of immunotherapy.
contributions: Pioneered the development of Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for cancer treatment
Led the development of tisagenlecleucel (CTL019), the first FDA-approved cell therapy and gene therapy for cancer
Discovered the CD28 pathway, identified as a major control switch for T cells
Developed robust T-cell culture systems that permit the growth of central memory T cells
Applied cell-based approaches for immunotherapy of HIV infection
quotes: "Cure is a big word and that's been the goal from the beginning for cell and gene therapy. It wasn't to hit lay-ups in basketball terms, it was to hit three-pointers."
"I really fell in love with research, and I found I could have more impact in the clinic this way."

"Oddly enough, it was when we were doing trials with CAR T cells in HIV patients, and we found that genetically modified T cells could persist for years in the patients. I had always thought that the cells would die or be rejected."

name: Carl Wieman
summary: Carl Wieman is an American physicist and educationist, recognized for his groundbreaking work in quantum physics and his significant contributions to science education. He shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2001 for creating the first true Bose-Einstein condensate. Wieman has also championed evidence-based teaching methods and developed innovative tools to improve STEM education.
contributions: Co-created the first true Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) in 1995 with Eric Allin Cornell.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2001 for fundamental studies of the Bose-Einstein condensate.
Pioneered the use of experimental techniques to evaluate the effectiveness of teaching strategies in physics and other sciences.
Founded the PhET Interactive Simulations project, offering free, research-based online tools for science learning.
Advocated for and implemented active learning and research-based teaching methods in STEM education.
Served as Associate Director for Science in the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
quotes: Education is about learning to make better decisions.
Brains are like muscles -- if you want to beef them up, you have to exert them strenuously for a long time.
I always think that one of the most important aspects for being a good scientist is the capacity to have a large threshold for frustration.

name: Carol Greider
summary: Carol Greider is an American molecular biologist and Nobel laureate known for her foundational work on telomeres and the enzyme telomerase. Her co-discovery of telomerase revolutionized the understanding of how chromosomes are maintained and has had profound implications for research into cellular aging, cancer, and age-related degenerative diseases. She is currently a Distinguished Professor of Molecular, Cell, and Developmental Biology at the University of California, Santa Cruz.
contributions: Co-discovered the enzyme telomerase in 1984, which is responsible for maintaining the ends of chromosomes (telomeres).
Pioneered research on the structure and function of telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes.
Provided early evidence that telomere length is related to cellular aging and senescence.
Demonstrated that telomerase activity is often activated in cancer cells, allowing them to bypass normal cellular aging and proliferate indefinitely.
Awarded the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discoveries concerning how telomeres and the enzyme telomerase protect chromosomes.
quotes: "I thought of myself as 'stupid' because I needed remedial help."

"I believe that learning to develop my compensatory skills also played a role in my success as a scientist because one has to intuit many different things that are going on at the same time and apply those to a particular problem."
"We didn't know at the time that there were any particular disease implications [in our research]. We were just interested in the fundamental questions of cell biology."

name: Carolyn Bertozzi
summary: Carolyn Bertozzi is an American chemist renowned for pioneering bioorthogonal chemistry, a field that allows chemical reactions to occur within living systems without interfering with their natural processes. Her groundbreaking work has significantly advanced the study of glycans (cell surface sugars) and their roles in diseases. She was a co-recipient of the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her contributions to click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry, which have opened new avenues for drug development and targeted therapies, especially in cancer treatment.
contributions: Coined the term and founded the field of bioorthogonal chemistry, enabling chemical reactions within living organisms.
Developed click reactions that function inside living cells to map molecules and cellular functions.
Advanced the understanding of cell surface sugars (glycans) and their involvement in diseases like cancer, inflammation, and viral infections.
Invented targeted enzyme therapeutics for immuno-oncology.
Developed Lysosome Targeting Chimeras (LYTACs) for extracellular targeted protein degradation.
Pioneered site-specific bioconjugation methods for synthesizing next-generation antibody-drug conjugates.
quotes: "Your purpose as a scientist is not to achieve fame or money. The main goal is to make discoveries and gift them to humanity."
"When the world is in trouble, chemistry comes to the rescue."
"If you learned something from it, it's not a failure."

name: Carolyn Porco
summary: Carolyn Porco is an American planetary scientist renowned for her work exploring the outer Solar System through spacecraft imaging. She led the imaging science team for the Cassini mission to Saturn and was a key member of the Voyager imaging team. Her research has significantly advanced our understanding of planetary rings and moons like Enceladus and Titan. Porco is also recognized for her efforts in public science communication.
contributions: Led the imaging science team for the Cassini mission to Saturn from 2004 to 2017.
Contributed to discoveries about Saturn's rings and moons, including lakes and seas on Titan and geysers on Enceladus.
Served as a member of the Voyager Imaging Team, contributing to imaging work during encounters with Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune in the 1980s.
Collaborated with Carl Sagan in planning the iconic 1990 "Pale Blue Dot" image taken by Voyager 1.
Recognized as an expert on planetary rings and the Saturnian moon, Enceladus.
Founded "The Day the Earth Smiled" event.
quotes: “All the atoms of our bodies will be blown into space in the disintegration of the solar system, to live on forever as mass or energy. That's what we should be teaching our children, not fairy tales about angels and seeing grandma in Heaven.”
“We humans, though troubled and warlike, are also the dreams, thinkers, and explorers inhabiting one achingly beautiful planet, yearning for the sublime, and capable of the magnificent.”

name: Charles Darwin
summary: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection became the unifying foundation of the biological sciences. His observations aboard HMS Beagle reshaped how humanity understands life on Earth.
contributions: Formulated the theory of evolution by natural selection
Authored "On the Origin of Species," one of the most influential works in science
Established common descent as a unifying principle of the life sciences

name: Charles M. Rice
summary: Charles M. Rice is an American virologist and Nobel Prize laureate known for his seminal research on the hepatitis C virus (HCV). His work was instrumental in proving that HCV alone could cause hepatitis, leading to the development of an infectious molecular clone of the virus. This breakthrough enabled the creation of cell culture systems and animal models, which were critical for the development of highly effective antiviral drugs that cure chronic HCV infection. He is currently the Maurice R. and Corinne P. Greenberg Professor in Virology at The Rockefeller University.
contributions: Co-discovered the Hepatitis C virus, for which he was awarded the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Produced the first infectious molecular clone of the Hepatitis C virus, an essential tool for studying its replication and developing treatments.
Established flaviviruses, a group including yellow fever and dengue viruses, as a distinct family of viruses.
Developed cell culture systems and animal models to study HCV replication and evaluate antiviral efficacy.
Identified host proteins, such as claudin-1, required for Hepatitis C virus entry into liver cells.
Paved the way for the development of highly effective, curative drugs for chronic Hepatitis C virus infection.

name: Chi-Huey Wong
summary: Chi-Huey Wong is a Taiwanese-American chemist renowned for his pioneering contributions to glycoscience and chemical biology. He developed innovative chemo-enzymatic and programmable methods for synthesizing complex carbohydrates and glycoproteins, significantly advancing the understanding of their biological roles. His research has led to the development of carbohydrate-based medicines and vaccines with broad applications in human health. He currently serves as a Scripps Family Chair Professor at The Scripps Research Institute.
contributions: Developed chemo-enzymatic methods for the practical synthesis of oligosaccharides and glycoproteins.
Introduced hierarchical and programmable one-pot synthesis methods for the rapid preparation of complex oligosaccharides.
Pioneered the use of enzymes as catalysts in organic synthesis.
Developed carbohydrate-based vaccines for various diseases, including cancer, influenza, HIV, and SARS-CoV-2.
Created glycan microarrays and glycosylation probes for the analysis of glycan-protein interactions.
quotes: "When I was working on my doctorate at MIT, there was a lot of discussion about environmentally friendly chemistry and how to make chemicals at room temperature, which wouldn't require so much energy. I thought using enzymes, which are very efficient and catalyze a wide range of biological reactions, would be the best way to accomplish this."
"We know glycosylation plays a central role in a wide array of cellular communication and function, but we still know very little about what exactly is happening."

name: Cornelia Bargmann
summary: Cornelia Bargmann is an American neurobiologist renowned for her groundbreaking research on the genetic and neural circuit mechanisms underlying behavior, primarily utilizing the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*. Her work has significantly advanced the understanding of how genes influence neuronal development, function, and behavior, particularly in the context of olfaction. She has also played a key role in broader scientific initiatives, including serving as the Head of Science for the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative.
contributions: Elucidated genetic and molecular mechanisms of olfaction and their influence on complex behaviors in *C. elegans* [1, 2, 5, 7, 9]
Uncovered key signaling pathways that direct the proper wiring of neurons in *C. elegans* [1, 5]
Identified the odr-10 gene as a specific odorant receptor for diacetyl in *C. elegans* [1, 5, 9]
Helped identify the mutation activating Ras in human bladder cancer and cloned the oncogene HER2, relevant to breast cancer [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
Discovered the SYG-1 protein, crucial for directing neurons to form connections during development [2, 5]
Developed various tools for observing and manipulating neuronal function, including microfluidics devices and a split protein (GRASP) for labeling synapses [9]
quotes: "I always loved science more than anything else because of the `blue collar' aspect of it—the fact that you actually do it" [1]
"When you have a really complex problem, and you have no idea how a system works, genetics is a good way to get a foothold" [9]
"The strength of C. elegans is that you would be able to link together what molecules were important, what cells they were acting in, and what they were doing there." [9]

name: Craig Mello
summary: Craig Mello is an American biologist and professor recognized for co-discovering RNA interference (RNAi) with Andrew Z. Fire, a breakthrough for which they received the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. His work revealed a fundamental mechanism of gene regulation, transforming molecular biology and opening new avenues for therapeutic development. Mello continues to research the roles of small RNAs in biology and disease.
contributions: Co-discovery of RNA interference (RNAi) with Andrew Z. Fire in 1998.
Elucidating mechanisms of gene regulation by short double-stranded RNAs (siRNA).
Developing gene knockout techniques utilizing RNAi.
Pioneering research into the fundamental roles of small RNAs in biology and disease.
Studies on embryogenesis and gene silencing using the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans as a model system.

name: Craig Venter
summary: J. Craig Venter is an American biologist and entrepreneur renowned for his pivotal contributions to genomics and synthetic biology. He led the private-sector effort to sequence the first draft of the human genome and pioneered the whole-genome shotgun sequencing method. Venter also achieved the groundbreaking feat of creating the first self-replicating bacterial cell with a synthetic genome.
contributions: Led one of the first draft sequences of the human genome.
Developed the expressed sequence tags (ESTs) method for rapid gene discovery.
Pioneered the whole-genome shotgun sequencing technique.
Created the first self-replicating bacterial cell with a synthetic genome.
Sequenced the genome of the first free-living organism, Haemophilus influenzae.
Co-founded The Institute for Genomic Research (TIGR), Celera Genomics, and J. Craig Venter Institute (JCVI).
quotes: I think from my experience in war and life and science, it all has made me believe that we have one life on this planet. We have one chance to live it and to contribute to the future of society and the future of life. The only 'afterlife' is what other people remember of you.
Moving forward in science is as much unwinding the distorted thinking of the past as it is putting a clearer idea on the table.

It is my belief that the basic knowledge that we're providing to the world will have a profound impact on the human condition and the treatments for disease and our view of our place on the biological continuum.

name: Cumrun Vafa
summary: Cumrun Vafa is an Iranian-American theoretical physicist and Hollis Professor at Harvard University, renowned for his foundational contributions to string theory and quantum gravity. His work, including the development of F-theory and the "swampland" program, aims to unify fundamental forces and explore the nature of the universe's deepest laws.
contributions: Co-discovery with Strominger that black hole entropy can be accounted for by solitonic states of superstring theory.
Developed F-theory, a 12-dimensional theory that compactifies to 10-D Type IIB superstring theory, connecting string theory to particle physics.
Initiated the "swampland" program, which explores apparently consistent but ultimately inconsistent theories of quantum gravity, helping to constrain the vast string landscape.
Elucidated the relation between geometry and quantum field theories through string dualities, known as "geometric engineering of quantum field theories".
Made contributions to topological string theories and the understanding of mirror symmetry.
quotes: "For me, the most beautiful aspects of physics are not the complicated math equations or even the ability of predicting how things will happen. What attracts me to physics is what it teaches us about the bigger picture. The general philosophical lessons that are embedded in physical laws are what excite me."
"String theory is revealing the deepest understanding of the Universe we have ever had."

name: Daniel Nocera
summary: Daniel Nocera is an American chemist and professor at Harvard University, recognized for his groundbreaking work in renewable energy and artificial photosynthesis. He invented the "Artificial Leaf" and "Bionic Leaf" systems, which efficiently use sunlight to split water into hydrogen and oxygen, and to produce biomass, liquid fuels, and fertilizer from air and water. His research aims to develop distributed, carbon-neutral energy solutions for global energy needs.
contributions: Invented the Artificial Leaf, a silicon-based catalyst for solar water splitting to produce hydrogen and oxygen.
Developed the Bionic Leaf (Bionic Leaf-C and Bionic Leaf-N) for highly efficient production of biomass, liquid fuels, and biofertilizer from sunlight, air, and water.
Pioneered the field of Proton Coupled Electron Transfer (PCET), establishing its mechanistic understanding and theoretical framework.
Co-founded Sun Catalytix, a company focused on energy storage technologies, and Kula Bio, which commercializes the Bionic Leaf-N as a living biofertilizer.

name: Dave Blundin
summary: Dave Blundin is an AI entrepreneur and investor who founded Link Ventures. Trained in MIT's AI Lab, he programmed some of the largest-scale neural networks of his era and has spent three decades building at the intersection of artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship.
contributions: Founder and managing partner of Link Ventures
Pioneered early large-scale neural networks and neural network quantization
Co-host of the Moonshots with Peter Diamandis podcast

name: David Charbonneau
summary: David Charbonneau is a pioneering astronomer and professor at Harvard University, renowned for his work on exoplanets. He is best known for making the first detection of an exoplanet transiting its star and for developing methods to characterize exoplanet atmospheres. His research significantly contributes to the search for habitable worlds beyond our solar system.
contributions: Made the first detection of an exoplanet eclipsing (transiting) its parent star in 1999, providing the first constraint on its composition.
Pioneered the use of space-based observatories (Hubble and Spitzer Space Telescopes) for studying exoplanet atmospheres and making the first direct detection of light emitted by an exoplanet.
Co-founded the Trans-Atlantic Exoplanet Survey (TrES), which used a network of telescopes to discover exoplanets.
Leads the MEarth project, an array of robotic telescopes dedicated to finding temperate, terrestrial exoplanets orbiting small stars.
Serves as a co-investigator in the NASA TESS Mission, searching for nearby transiting exoplanets.
Contributed to the discovery of rocky planets within the habitable zones of nearby small stars.
quotes: For generations, humans have looked up at the stars and wondered if there existed inhabited worlds other than our own. We are the first generation in human history with the technological ability to answer that question.

name: David Gross
summary: David Gross is an American theoretical physicist who was awarded the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with H. David Politzer and Frank Wilczek, for the discovery of asymptotic freedom. This discovery led to the formulation of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), which describes the strong nuclear force and completed the Standard Model of particle physics. He has also made seminal contributions to superstring theory, including the formulation of heterotic string theory.
contributions: Co-discovery of asymptotic freedom in the theory of the strong interaction.
Formulation of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD).
Contributions to the completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.
Formulation of heterotic string theory.
quotes: "From the age of 13, I was attracted to physics and mathematics."
"At the fundamental level nature, for whatever reason, prefers beauty and is marvelously inventive in inventing new forms of beauty."
"As we explore physics at higher and higher energy, revealing its structure at shorter and shorter distances, we discover more and more symmetry."

name: David Julius
summary: David Julius is an American physiologist and Nobel Prize laureate recognized for his groundbreaking research into the molecular mechanisms of pain and temperature sensation. His work, including the identification of the TRPV1 and TRPM8 receptors, revealed how the nervous system detects heat, cold, and painful stimuli. These discoveries have fundamentally transformed sensory biology and opened new avenues for developing treatments for chronic pain.
contributions: Identified and characterized the TRPV1 receptor, which detects capsaicin (the active compound in chili peppers) and noxious heat.
Contributed to the discovery and characterization of the TRPM8 receptor, responsible for sensing cold and menthol.
Elucidated how transient receptor potential (TRP) channels convert temperature into electrical signals in the nervous system.
Made pioneering contributions to the discovery of purinergic receptors, including P2Y and P2X classes.
Cloned and characterized serotonin receptors, such as the serotonin 1c and 5HT3 receptors.
quotes: "My research was born out of a fascination with, and desire to comprehend, how the body reacts to stimuli from ordinary foods, like chili peppers."
"We need to be making decisions based on data and not opinions."
"Exploiting these channels to develop non-opioid analgesics remains an important translational goal that has not yet come to fruition, but about which I remain optimistic."

name: David MacMillan
summary: David W.C. MacMillan is a Scottish-American organic chemist and the James S. McDonnell Distinguished University Professor of Chemistry at Princeton University. He shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his co-development of asymmetric organocatalysis, a method using small organic molecules as catalysts to build molecules. His work has significantly advanced greener chemical synthesis, pharmaceutical research, and the development of tools for chemical biology.
contributions: Co-developed asymmetric organocatalysis, a method for precise molecular construction using small organic molecules as catalysts.
Pioneered photoredox catalysis, which utilizes visible light to drive chemical reactions and enable new transformations in organic synthesis.
Invented µMap, a photocatalytic "proximity labeling" technology used in chemical biology to map protein interactions and study cancer cells.
Developed chiral imidazolidinone catalysts, often referred to as MacMillan catalysts, for various asymmetric syntheses.
Co-founded and served as the first editor-in-chief of the journal Chemical Science.
quotes: "what I love about doing research is um that yes we do science but it's also so creative."

name: David Wineland
summary: David Wineland is an American physicist who was awarded the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work in devising experimental methods to measure and manipulate individual quantum systems. His research has been instrumental in the development of laser cooling of trapped ions, the foundation of quantum computing operations, and the creation of ultra-precise atomic clocks.
contributions: Devised methods for laser cooling of trapped ions to very low temperatures.
Pioneered the use of individual ions for quantum-computing operations, including the first single-atom quantum logic gate.
Developed ultra-precise atomic clocks using laser-cooled ions, achieving world-record accuracy.
Experimentally demonstrated quantum mechanical phenomena like superposition and entanglement in individual ions.
Showcased quantum teleportation of information among massive particles.
quotes: I always liked to do things with my hands, work on mechanical things. It was an easy choice to go towards experimental physics.
I think in everything we've done—we never felt it was unattainable; we've just got to do it.
The quest for better navigation never goes away.

name: Dean Kamen
summary: Dean Kamen is an American inventor and entrepreneur with hundreds of patents. He created early wearable medical devices and the Segway personal transporter, and founded FIRST to inspire young people in science and engineering.
contributions: Invented the first wearable insulin pump and a portable dialysis machine
Created the Segway personal transporter and the iBot stair-climbing wheelchair
Founded FIRST (For Inspiration and Recognition of Science and Technology)

patents.title: Riderless stabilization of a balancing transporter (Segway)

name: Demis Hassabis
summary: Sir Demis Hassabis is a British AI researcher and co-founder of DeepMind. Under his leadership, DeepMind built AlphaFold, which solved the decades-old problem of predicting protein structures — earning him the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
contributions: Co-founded DeepMind, a world-leading artificial intelligence lab
Led development of AlphaFold, predicting the 3D structure of nearly all known proteins
Awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for computational protein design

name: Didier Queloz
summary: Didier Queloz is a Swiss astronomer and professor of physics, best known for co-discovering the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, in 1995 with Michel Mayor. This groundbreaking discovery earned them a share of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics and revolutionized the field of exoplanet research. His ongoing work focuses on detecting Earth-like planets and exploring the origin of life in the universe.
contributions: Co-discovery of 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star (1995).
Shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of an exoplanet orbiting a solar-type star.
Pioneered and developed the radial velocity method for detecting exoplanets.
Developed new astronomical equipment, observational approaches, and detection algorithms for exoplanet research.
Advanced research into Earth-like exoplanets, their habitability, and the origin and prevalence of life in the universe.
quotes: "We have so many planets that the question of life is obvious, that's the next step. I'm absolutely convinced there must be life somewhere else because I can't believe life is unique in the universe. There's too many stars, too many planets; that's pretty clear."
"The beauty of science is you never realise what you're doing when you're doing it. It's years after that you say 'oh my God!'"

name: Donald Knuth
summary: Donald Knuth is an American computer scientist and mathematician, and professor emeritus at Stanford University. He is widely recognized as the "father of the analysis of algorithms" for his fundamental contributions to theoretical computer science. Knuth is the author of the multi-volume work "The Art of Computer Programming" and the creator of the TeX typesetting system.
contributions: Authored the multi-volume series "The Art of Computer Programming"
Developed the rigorous analysis of the computational complexity of algorithms and popularized asymptotic notation
Created the TeX computer typesetting system, METAFONT font definition language, and Computer Modern typefaces
Introduced the concept of literate programming with the WEB and CWEB systems
Contributed to the development of string searching algorithms (e.g., Knuth-Morris-Pratt) and LR(k) grammars
quotes: Premature optimization is the root of all evil.
Science is what we understand well enough to explain to a computer. Art is everything else we do.
Computer programming is an art, because it applies accumulated knowledge to the world, because it requires skill and ingenuity, and especially because it produces objects of beauty.

name: Donna Strickland
summary: Donna Strickland is a Canadian optical physicist and a pioneer in the field of pulsed lasers. She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2018, along with her Ph.D. supervisor Gérard Mourou, for their co-invention of chirped pulse amplification. Her groundbreaking work has led to the development of the most intense laser pulses ever created, with wide-ranging applications in medicine and industry.
contributions: Co-invented chirped pulse amplification (CPA) with Gérard Mourou
Developed a method for generating high-intensity, ultra-short optical pulses
Paved the way for applications in laser eye surgery (LASIK)
Enabled precise laser micromachining for small glass parts, such as those used in cell phones
Authored more than 90 publications in laser technology
quotes: "We wondered if it was a prank. But then I knew it was the right day, and it would have been a cruel prank."
"I see myself as a scientist, not a woman in science."
"I think everybody in the world should be told that do what you love and what you think you are good at."

name: Doris Tsao
summary: Doris Tsao is a prominent American neuroscientist known for her groundbreaking work on visual perception, particularly how the brain processes and recognizes faces. She pioneered the use of fMRI with single-unit electrophysiological recordings to identify and characterize the "face patch system" in the macaque brain, a network of regions specialized for face processing. Her research clarifies the neural coding principles underlying object and face identity, contributing significantly to our understanding of how the brain constructs our visual reality.
contributions: Pioneering the use of fMRI combined with single-unit electrophysiological recordings in primate visual processing.
Discovery and elucidation of the macaque "face patch system," specialized brain regions for face perception.
Clarifying the anatomical organization and coding principles of the neural system for face processing within the temporal lobe.
Decoding how neurons in the brain encode facial features and identity.
Identifying that the face processing system is part of a larger map of object space.
Demonstrating that imagined and perceived objects activate the same neurons and use the same neural code.
quotes: "For an organ touted to be the most complex machine in the universe, the notion of cortical patches dedicated to processing faces seems almost ridiculously simplistic. Yet it's true, and it has been such an incredible experimental boon in many unexpected ways."
"Don't worry! You are special and you will change the world."
"I have a conviction that the brain is understandable."

name: Drew Weissman
summary: Drew Weissman is an American immunologist and physician, renowned for his collaborative work with Katalin Karikó on modified messenger RNA (mRNA) technology. Their groundbreaking discoveries enabled the development of highly effective mRNA vaccines, most notably for COVID-19. This pivotal research led to them being jointly awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, transforming vaccine development and opening new avenues for various mRNA-based therapeutics.
contributions: Discovered nucleoside base modifications that allow mRNA to avoid detection by the innate immune system.
Developed lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery techniques to protect mRNA and facilitate its entry into cells.
Pioneered the foundational technology for the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 mRNA vaccines.

Actively researches mRNA therapeutics for next-generation vaccines against various pathogens (e.g., pan-coronavirus, universal flu, herpes), gene editing, and treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases.
quotes: "I've spent my entire career working on equity — getting vaccines and therapies available to the entire world."
"My dream has been to develop something that helps people and I think I've done that."

"You have to tolerate frustration to be able to work in a lab. But when you do make a finding, even if it's a little finding, because of all of the frustration and all of the difficulty getting it, it makes it that much more important. It's really, you know, kind of an inner joy."

name: Edvard Moser
summary: Edvard Moser is a Norwegian neuroscientist and Nobel laureate, recognized for his groundbreaking work on the brain's positioning system. Alongside his then-wife May-Britt Moser, he discovered grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, which function as a coordinate system for spatial navigation. His research has significantly advanced the understanding of how the brain processes spatial location, memory, and has implications for neurological conditions like Alzheimer's disease.
contributions: Discovery of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex, providing a neural mechanism for spatial mapping
Identification of the brain's 'inner GPS' for spatial orientation and navigation
Discovery of other spatial representation cells, including head direction cells and border cells
Research into how neural microcircuits for space, time, and memory are organized
Discovery of a neural network in the lateral entorhinal cortex that expresses a person's sense of time in experiences and memories
Co-development of advanced neural recording technologies such as Neuropixels probes and 2-photon miniscopes

name: Edward Witten
summary: Edward Witten is an American theoretical physicist and a leading researcher in string theory, quantum gravity, and supersymmetric quantum field theories, whose work bridges the gap between physics and mathematics. He is renowned for applying geometrical and topological ideas to unify theories of particle physics, profoundly impacting both theoretical physics and pure mathematics. Witten was the first physicist to be awarded the Fields Medal in 1990, recognizing his significant mathematical insights in physics.
contributions: Pioneering work in string theory and M-theory, which attempts to unify fundamental forces of nature.
Significant contributions to topological quantum field theory.
Proof of the positive energy theorem in general relativity.
Development of the Seiberg–Witten equations.
Application of Chern–Simons theory to knots and 3-manifolds.
Introduced new ideas to Morse theory and supersymmetry.
quotes: "String theory is a miracle through and through."
"We know a lot of things, but what we don't know is a lot more."

"But the beauty of Einstein's equations, for example, is just as real to anyone who's experienced it as the beauty of music. We've learned in the 20th century that the equations that work have inner harmony."

name: Elaine Fuchs
summary: Elaine Fuchs is a prominent American cell biologist renowned for her groundbreaking research on mammalian skin and its stem cells. Her work has modernized dermatology by uncovering the molecular and genetic mechanisms underlying skin development, diseases, and regeneration. She is also known for pioneering reverse genetics and for her significant insights into how stem cells contribute to wound healing, inflammation, and cancer.
contributions: Pioneered reverse genetics approaches to understand protein function and its role in development and disease.
Identified and characterized keratins, the proteins forming the scaffolding of mammalian skin, and linked their mutations to human blistering skin diseases.
Developed the field of skin stem cells, elucidating their molecular mechanisms in generating hair and skin, and their roles in tissue repair.
Investigated how abnormalities in stem cell behavior contribute to inflammation and cancer susceptibility, particularly squamous cell carcinomas.
Discovered that epidermal stem cells bear epigenetic memories of stressful experiences, influencing subsequent responses to assaults.
quotes: "I think like many of the children in our world, I got interested in science just from having a butterfly net and from having a few strainers and some boots and going down to the streams and creeks and being out in the fields."

"A successful lab head mentor should not expect recognition for mentorship; rather the satisfaction must be within the joy of seeing a trainee transition to independence and over time accomplish more than what I can do."

"While I'm especially pleased that Princeton chose me amongst the women whose portraits will now adorn its halls, I'm fully aware that the message that Princeton gives here really goes much deeper and broader, and it is to honor all their woman graduates who have pursued their passion and strove to make a difference."

name: Elizabeth Blackburn
summary: Elizabeth Blackburn is an Australian-American molecular biologist and biochemist, co-recipient of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. She is renowned for her pioneering work on telomeres, the protective ends of chromosomes, and her co-discovery of the enzyme telomerase. Her research has significantly advanced the understanding of cellular aging, genetic stability, and cancer.
contributions: Discovered the molecular nature and genetic composition of telomeres.
Co-discovered the enzyme telomerase, which maintains telomere length.
Elucidated the crucial role of telomeres in protecting chromosomes during cell division.
Researched the implications of telomeres and telomerase in cellular aging and cancer.
Explored how lifestyle and psychological stress can impact telomere health and cellular aging.
quotes: Genes load the gun, and environment pulls the trigger.
Your telomeres, it turns out, are listening to you. They absorb the instructions you give them.
I didn't want to just know the names of things. I remember really wanting to know how it all worked.

name: Elon Musk
summary: Elon Musk is an entrepreneur and engineer who founded SpaceX and leads Tesla, two companies pushing the frontiers of spaceflight and sustainable energy. SpaceX pioneered reusable orbital rockets and dramatically lowered the cost of reaching space, while Tesla helped move electric vehicles and energy storage into the mainstream.
contributions: Founded SpaceX, which developed the first reusable orbital-class rockets
Leads Tesla, accelerating the global transition to electric vehicles and battery storage
Built Starlink, a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation delivering broadband worldwide

name: Emmanuelle Charpentier
summary: Emmanuelle Charpentier is a French microbiologist, geneticist, and biochemist, best known for her co-discovery of the CRISPR-Cas9 genetic scissors.
