Her groundbreaking research, which earned her a share of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, laid the foundation for genome editing. This revolutionary technology has had a profound impact on life sciences, biotechnology, and medicine, opening new possibilities for treating diseases and developing resilient crops.
contributions: Co-discovery of the CRISPR-Cas9 system, a molecular tool for gene editing
Deciphering the molecular mechanisms of the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 immune system
Discovery of tracrRNA, an RNA molecule crucial for the function of the CRISPR-Cas system
Co-founding of CRISPR Therapeutics and ERS Genomics to develop CRISPR-Cas gene editing for biomedical applications
quotes: "I haven't changed, and I won't change. The scientist that I am got me here, and that is the scientist that I want to remain."
"It's not about publishing in high-impact journals. It's about solid work."
"My wish is that this will provide a positive message to the young girls who would like to follow the path of science…"

name: Eric Cornell
summary: Eric Cornell is an American physicist who, alongside Carl Wieman, co-created the first Bose-Einstein condensate in 1995. This achievement, involving the cooling of atoms to ultracold temperatures, earned him a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics. He continues to conduct research in fundamental physics through precision measurements, including work on the electron's electric dipole moment.
contributions: Co-created the first Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) in 1995.
Developed laser and magnetic cooling techniques for achieving ultracold atomic states.
Advanced the understanding of matter in a new state at extremely low temperatures.
Conducts research in precision measurements in atomic, molecular, and optical (AMO) physics.
Contributed to efforts to measure the electric dipole moment of the electron.
quotes: “I think that writing—and writing well—is very, very important in science. The discipline of writing well forces you to think clearly.”
“Conversely, I came to realize that being good at something is hardly a reason to avoid doing it.”

name: Eric Lander
summary: Eric Lander is an American geneticist, molecular biologist, and mathematician known for his pioneering work in genomics. He was a principal leader of the international Human Genome Project and founded the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. His research focuses on understanding the human genome and applying this knowledge to discover the molecular basis of human diseases and develop new treatments.
contributions: Co-led the international Human Genome Project, contributing significantly to the sequencing and analysis of the human genome.
Co-created the first genetic map of the human genome in 1987.
Developed powerful methods for mapping genes underlying both rare and complex human diseases.
Founded and served as the first president and director of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.
Made important contributions to cancer genomics, including proposing The Cancer Genome Atlas project.
quotes: Suddenly it was clear to me that all the beautiful complexity of life had simplicity at its core.
We now know 600 different genes involved in cancer – giving rise to new drug targets.
I think it means that we'll be able to track down the actual causes of disease. Most folks don't realize we don't know the cause of asthma, of heart disease, of diabetes or hypertension.

name: Eric Rignot
summary: Eric Rignot is a distinguished glaciologist and remote sensing scientist, holding professorship at the University of California, Irvine, and a senior research scientist position at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. He is renowned for his work studying the interactions of polar ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica with global climate. His research is critical for understanding ice loss dynamics and their projected contributions to global sea level rise.
contributions: Pioneered the application of satellite radar interferometry for detailed measurements of ice sheet velocity, thickness, and discharge into the ocean.
Quantified the mass balance of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, providing comprehensive estimates of ice loss over decades.
Identified rapid and potentially irreversible grounding line retreat of West Antarctic glaciers, particularly in the Amundsen Sea sector.
Documented the accelerated rates of ice loss from polar ice sheets due to climate change.
Served as Science Lead for the NASA Operation IceBridge mission and Deputy Lead for the Ocean Melting Greenland (OMG) mission.
Contributed to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fourth Assessment Report, which was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.
quotes: Sea-level rise is probably one of the most telling stories of climate change for humans.
humanity needs to understand what's happening in the polar regions, because it can affect all of us.

name: Eric Topol
field: Cardiology, Genomics, Digital Medicine, and Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
summary: Eric Topol is an American cardiologist, scientist, and author, recognized for his pioneering work in personalized medicine, genomics, and the application of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in healthcare. He currently serves as the founder and director of the Scripps Research Translational Institute and is a professor of Molecular Medicine at Scripps Research. Topol has authored several bestselling books on the future of medicine and is one of the most cited researchers in the field.
contributions: Pioneered the development of numerous medications commonly used in medical practice, including t-PA, Plavix, Angiomax, and ReoPro.
Led the Cleveland Clinic's cardiovascular program to be ranked #1 by U.S. News & World Report for over a decade.
Founded the Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine, the first new medical school in the U.S. in 20 years at its time.
Awarded significant grants from the National Institutes of Health to lead parts of the Precision Medicine Initiative (All of Us Research Program).
His scientific focus has been on genomic and digital tools, utilizing artificial intelligence analytics to individualize medicine.
Authored bestselling books like "The Creative Destruction of Medicine," "The Patient Will See You Now," and "Deep Medicine," influencing discussions on the future of healthcare.
quotes: "The greatest opportunity offered by AI is not reducing errors or workloads, or even curing cancer: it is the opportunity to restore the precious and time-honored connection and trust—the human touch—between patients and doctors."

"Eventually, doctors will adopt AI and algorithms as their work partners. This leveling of the medical knowledge landscape will ultimately lead to a new premium: to find and train doctors who have the highest level of emotional intelligence."

name: Fabiola Gianotti
summary: Fabiola Gianotti is an Italian experimental particle physicist and the current Director-General of CERN, a role she has held since 2016 and was reappointed for a second term. She is highly recognized for her leadership as spokesperson of the ATLAS Collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider, which was crucial to the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson. Her work has significantly advanced our understanding of fundamental particles and the structure of the universe.
contributions: Led the ATLAS Collaboration at CERN, a key experiment at the Large Hadron Collider
Played a central role in the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012
First woman to be appointed Director-General of CERN and the first to serve a second full term
Contributed to detector development, software development, and data analysis for various CERN experiments, including WA70, UA2, ALEPH, and ATLAS
Involved in the pioneering work of developing a novel-geometry liquid-argon electromagnetic calorimeter for ATLAS
quotes: "When we look at the universe, what we see by eye or with our telescopes is only five percent of the universe. The rest, 95 percent is dark."
"This job is a great scientific adventure. But it's also a great human adventure."
"Science has no passport, no political party, no gender."

name: Federico Faggin
summary: Federico Faggin is an Italian-American physicist and engineer who led the design of the Intel 4004, the world's first commercial microprocessor. He pioneered the silicon-gate technology that made modern chips possible and later co-founded companies advancing microprocessor and touch technology.
contributions: Led the design of the Intel 4004, the first commercial microprocessor
Developed silicon-gate MOS technology, foundational to modern chips
Co-founded Zilog and created the Z80 microprocessor

patents.title: Object position detector with edge motion feature (touchpad)

name: Fei-Fei Li
summary: Dr. Fei-Fei Li is a computer scientist and a leading figure in artificial intelligence. Her creation of ImageNet helped ignite the deep-learning revolution, and she is a prominent advocate for human-centered, ethical AI.
contributions: Created ImageNet, the dataset that catalyzed modern deep learning
Co-directs the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI)
Champions diversity and ethics in AI through AI4ALL and policy work

name: Feng Zhang
summary: Feng Zhang is a molecular biologist and neuroscientist renowned for pioneering transformative molecular technologies. He is most recognized for adapting the CRISPR-Cas9 system for precise genome editing in human cells and for co-developing optogenetics, a method that uses light to control brain cells. His innovations have significantly advanced biomedical research and offer new avenues for treating human diseases, particularly neurological disorders.
contributions: Pioneered the use of engineered CRISPR-Cas9 systems for genome editing in human cells.
Co-developed optogenetics, a technology that uses light to control brain cells.
Extended the CRISPR toolbox by developing CRISPR-Cas12 and Cas13 systems for DNA and RNA targeting.
Developed new methods for delivering genome editing tools into human cells.
Applied CRISPR-based technologies for high-throughput genome screening and pathogen diagnosis.
quotes: "I definitely want to solve more problems and bring more solutions to the world."

"CRISPR is one of these search functions, where if you give it a piece of RNA that matches a sequence in the genome you want to target, then Cas9 will go right to that spot and allow you to start to make changes."
"Optogenetics is a technology we developed to allow us to figure out what different types of cells in the brain do."

name: Ferenc Krausz
summary: Ferenc Krausz is a Hungarian-Austrian physicist and a pioneer in attosecond science, for which he was jointly awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics. His research team successfully generated and measured the first attosecond light pulses, enabling the real-time observation of electron motion within atoms and molecules. This groundbreaking work established the field of attophysics, providing unprecedented insight into ultrafast processes in matter and opening new avenues in science, technology, and medical diagnostics.
contributions: Generated and measured the world's first attosecond light pulses, marking the birth of attophysics.
Developed experimental methods for creating attosecond pulses of light to study electron dynamics in matter.
Enabled the real-time observation of electron motion within atoms and molecules.
Pioneered ultrafast laser science, contributing to the development of high-intensity laser systems.
Explored applications of attosecond science in medical diagnostics, including early disease detection.
quotes: "I can scarcely believe this is reality and not just a dream. I feel so overwhelmed. It's truly humbling to receive such an award. But it's also a wonderful feeling to be rewarded in this way, especially after some of the setbacks along the way."
"I take the Academy's decision as a mandate for the pursuit of this very goal with utmost determination."
"We can now open the door to the world of electrons. Attosecond physics gives us the opportunity to understand mechanisms that are controlled by electrons."

name: Frances Arnold
summary: Frances Arnold is an American chemical engineer and Nobel laureate recognized for her groundbreaking work in directed evolution. She pioneered methods to engineer enzymes with new and enhanced properties, revolutionizing the creation of sustainable chemicals, biofuels, and pharmaceuticals. Her innovations harness nature's evolutionary processes to design novel biological systems.
contributions: Pioneered the development of directed evolution for enzyme engineering.
Created new enzymes for the production of biofuels and renewable chemicals.
Developed enzymes for pharmaceutical and consumer product manufacturing.
Introduced enzymes that catalyze reactions not found in nature.
quotes: "Life—the biological world—is the greatest chemist, and evolution is her design process."
"Proteins aren't designed, they're evolved."
"Curiosity fuels discovery. Never stop asking 'Why?'"

name: Frank Wilczek
summary: Frank Wilczek is an American theoretical physicist who shared the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of asymptotic freedom in the theory of the strong interaction. He has made seminal contributions to fundamental particle physics, cosmology, and condensed matter physics. Wilczek also pioneered concepts such as axions, anyons, and time crystals, and actively communicates complex scientific ideas to wider audiences.
contributions: Discovery of asymptotic freedom in the theory of the strong interaction.
Development of quantum chromodynamics (QCD).
Proposed the existence of axions, hypothetical particles that are candidates for dark matter.
Discovery and exploitation of new forms of quantum statistics (anyons).
Pioneered the concept of time crystals.
quotes: If you don't make mistakes, you're not working on hard enough problems. And that's a big mistake.
In physics, you don't have to go around making trouble for yourself – nature does it for you.
The brain rewards us for interacting with beautiful things. In this way, evolution wants to encourage us to do what is good for us.

name: Gabriela González
summary: Gabriela González is an Argentine physicist and professor of physics and astronomy at Louisiana State University. She is a prominent figure in gravitational wave physics, known for her instrumental role in the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) Scientific Collaboration. Her work was crucial to the first direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015, a landmark discovery that opened a new window to the universe.
contributions: Served as spokesperson for the LIGO Scientific Collaboration (2011-2017)
Played a key role in the first direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015
Participated in the public announcement of the gravitational wave discovery in 2016
Conducts research on data calibration and characterization for LIGO detectors
Develops experimental techniques to improve the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors
Co-authored the book "The Sounds of the Cosmos: Gravitational Waves and the Birth of Multi-Messenger Astronomy" (2023)
quotes: González believes that science will be much better off when there are as many women as men, and that this will happens when the common myths and misconceptions about physicists, which tend to segregate women from research, start to fall apart, and furthermore when people believe that physicists are simply normal people with normal lives.

name: Galileo Galilei
summary: Galileo Galilei was an Italian astronomer and physicist often called the "father of observational astronomy." His telescopic discoveries and insistence on evidence helped launch the scientific revolution.
contributions: Improved the telescope and discovered Jupiter's four largest moons
Provided key observational support for the heliocentric model
Pioneered the experimental, evidence-based method of modern science

name: Gary Ruvkun
summary: Gary Ruvkun is an American molecular biologist and geneticist, a professor at Harvard Medical School and an investigator at Massachusetts General Hospital. He is best known for his co-discovery of microRNAs (miRNAs) and their crucial role in gene regulation, which earned him the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. His research has also illuminated conserved hormonal signaling pathways that regulate aging and metabolism, primarily studied in the nematode *C. elegans*.
contributions: Co-discovery of microRNAs (miRNAs), small RNA molecules that regulate gene activity.
Elucidation of the mechanism by which *lin-4* microRNA regulates target messenger RNAs through imperfect base-pairing.
Discovery of the *let-7* microRNA and demonstrating its evolutionary conservation across animal species, including humans.
Defining an insulin-like signaling pathway that controls metabolism and longevity in *C. elegans*, with findings applicable to other animals and humans.
Pioneering research on developing methods to search for extraterrestrial genomes.
quotes: "We were just thinking that it was a really interesting finding."
"The way genetics becomes an art form is by what you decide what to look for."
"If you can generate humour, you're half way to generating discoveries."

name: Gavin Schmidt
summary: Gavin Schmidt is a British climatologist and climate modeler who serves as the Director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS). He is recognized for his significant work in developing and improving climate models, investigating climate variability, and effectively communicating climate science to the public. His research greatly contributes to understanding past, present, and future climate change.
contributions: Development and improvement of Earth System Models, notably the GISS ModelE, used for climate simulations.
Extensive research into climate variability, including its internal mechanisms and responses to external forcings.
Pioneering methods for comparing paleoclimate proxy data with the outputs of climate models.
Co-founder of the RealClimate blog, a prominent platform for critical commentary and outreach on climate science.
Contributing author to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which was recognized with the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.
Significant efforts in science communication and public outreach through numerous publications, media appearances, and a widely viewed TED Talk on climate modeling.
quotes: "While the ranking of individual years can be affected by chaotic weather patterns, the long-term trends are attributable to drivers of climate change that right now are dominated by human emissions of greenhouse gases..."
"You can get good science out of stupid questions. If someone says the world is flat, maybe in proving them wrong you can calculate the curvature of the Earth more precisely."
"If the models are as flawed as critics say you have to ask yourself, 'How come they work?'"

name: Geoffrey Hinton
summary: Geoffrey Hinton is a cognitive psychologist and computer scientist often called the "Godfather of AI." His decades of work on artificial neural networks — including backpropagation and deep learning — laid the foundations of modern artificial intelligence, earning him the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
contributions: Pioneered the backpropagation algorithm for training deep neural networks
Co-authored breakthrough work on deep networks that ignited the modern AI boom
Received the 2018 Turing Award and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics

name: George Church
summary: George Church is an American geneticist, molecular engineer, and chemist known for his pioneering contributions to personal genomics and synthetic biology. He is a Robert Winthrop Professor of Genetics at Harvard Medical School and a Professor of Health Sciences and Technology at Harvard and MIT. Church has been instrumental in developing technologies for DNA sequencing, genome engineering, and has co-founded numerous biotechnology companies, significantly impacting modern biology and medicine.
contributions: Developed the first direct genomic sequencing method and barcode-multiplexing tags (1984)
Helped initiate the Human Genome Project (1984) and the Personal Genome Project (2005)
Co-invented nanopore sequencing (1995)
Pioneered chip-based DNA libraries, genome editing, and stem cell engineering
Made his medical records and genome publicly available to researchers
Leading efforts in de-extinction, including the Woolly Mammoth Revival Project
quotes: "Every disease that's with us is caused by DNA. And every disease can be fixed by DNA."

name: George Smoot
summary: George Smoot is an American astrophysicist and cosmologist who shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics. His groundbreaking work on the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite, particularly the detection of minute temperature fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background radiation, provided crucial evidence for the Big Bang theory. This work was pivotal in establishing cosmology as a precision science.
contributions: Shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of the blackbody form and anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background radiation.
Led the team responsible for measuring small temperature variations (anisotropy) in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) using the COBE satellite.
Provided crucial observational evidence supporting the Big Bang theory of the universe.
Instrumental in advancing cosmology as a precision science.
Contributed to subsequent CMB observations through experiments like MAXIMA and the Planck satellite.
Involved in the design of the Supernova/Acceleration Probe (SNAP) to study dark energy.
quotes: "If you're religious, it's like looking at God."
"But every day I go to work I'm making a bet that the universe is simple, symmetric, and aesthetically pleasing—a universe that we humans, with our limited perspective, will someday understand."
"I think we all want to know where we came from and how we fit into the world, but some of us need to know how it all works in great detail."

name: George Whitesides
summary: George M. Whitesides is an American chemist and a professor at Harvard University, renowned for his broad and influential contributions across various scientific disciplines. He is recognized for pioneering work in molecular self-assembly, soft lithography, microfluidics, and the development of low-cost diagnostic technologies. His extensive research has significantly impacted fields from nanotechnology to the origins of life, making him one of the most cited chemists in history.
contributions: Pioneering research in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and organometallic chemistry, including the Corey–House–Posner–Whitesides reaction.
Groundbreaking work in molecular self-assembly, leading to advancements in nanoscience and surface chemistry.
Development of soft lithography and microfluidics for microfabrication and analytical devices.
Innovation in low-cost, paper-based diagnostic tools, such as the "lab on a chip," especially for healthcare in developing economies.
Contributions to soft robotics and the study of complexity, simplicity, and the origin of life.
Extensive publications (over 1,300 scientific articles) and numerous patents (over 160 issued).
quotes: "Chemists have always been in the business of taking atoms and putting them together with other atoms with precisely defined connections."
"The virtue of binary is that it's the simplest possible way of representing numbers."
"Simplicity, for reasons that are a little bit obscure, is almost not pursued, at least in the academic world."

name: Gerard 't Hooft
summary: Gerard 't Hooft is a Dutch theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate known for his fundamental contributions to the Standard Model of particle physics. He, along with Martinus J.G. Veltman, elucidated the quantum structure of electroweak interactions, for which they shared the 1999 Nobel Prize in Physics. His work, particularly in the early 1970s, provided the mathematical foundation by proving the renormalizability of gauge theories. He has also made significant advancements in areas such as quantum gravity and the holographic principle.
contributions: Proof of the renormalizability of Yang-Mills gauge theories, making them acceptable as a realistic description of particle behaviors
Development of dimensional regularization with Martinus J.G. Veltman
Fundamental contributions to the theoretical development of the Standard Model of particle physics
Pioneering the holographic principle
Major contributions to the resolution of the quark confinement problem in quantum chromodynamics
Extensive research on black holes in quantum gravity framework and fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics
quotes: "On your way towards becoming a bad theoretician, take your own immature theory, stop checking it for mistakes, don't listen to colleagues who do spot weaknesses, and start admiring your own infallible intelligence."
"Quantum mechanics as it stands would be perfect if we didn't have the quantum-gravity issue and a few other very deep fundamental problems."

name: Giorgio Parisi
summary: Giorgio Parisi is an Italian theoretical physicist who was awarded the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking contributions to the theory of complex systems. His discoveries have illuminated the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems across scales, from atomic to planetary. His work has significantly influenced not only physics but also other diverse fields like mathematics, biology, neuroscience, and machine learning.
contributions: Co-developed the QCD evolution equations for parton densities (Altarelli–Parisi or DGLAP equations)
Provided the exact solution of the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model of spin glasses
Developed the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) equation for dynamic scaling of growing interfaces
Introduced the concept of multifractals in the study of turbulence
Made groundbreaking analysis using the replica method for disordered systems
Researched the collective motion of animals, such as whirling flocks of birds
quotes: The story of Hypatia has greatly affected the collective imagination, even outside the circle of experts. She is a scientist who is killed also because a woman who was not in her place, had a public life, spoke in public and took public positions. We must never be sure that the development of science is unstoppable.
The existence of God cannot be used as any scientific hypothesis: it is something different that transcends science.
If you are confident that you can do something you will do it.

name: Gregg Semenza
summary: Gregg Semenza is an American pediatrician and Professor of Genetic Medicine at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, where he directs the vascular program at the Institute for Cell Engineering. He is renowned for his discovery of hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1), a protein vital for how cells sense and adapt to changing oxygen levels. His foundational research in oxygen homeostasis earned him a share of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, with significant implications for treating conditions like cancer and ischemic cardiovascular disease.
contributions: Discovered Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1 (HIF-1), a master regulator of cellular oxygen sensing.
Elucidated the molecular mechanisms by which cells respond to varying oxygen availability.
Identified the role of HIF-1 in regulating gene activity in response to hypoxia.
Demonstrated HIF-1's involvement in the pathophysiology of cancer and cardiovascular diseases.
Showed that HIF-1 is crucial for erythropoietin (EPO) production, a key process in red blood cell regulation.
quotes: "This is my religion: I am filled with Wonder at the outcome of 4 billion years of evolution here on our speck in the universe and Hope regarding our opportunity to improve the lives of those around us through basic science discoveries and their translation to clinical practice."
"Cancer cells invade surrounding tissue, make their way into blood vessels, and spread throughout the body. What are they searching for? My guess is oxygen."
"The freedom and the creativity, these are the really fun parts of the job that no one tells us how to do our work and as long as we are successful, we are left alone and we can do our thing."

name: Gérard Mourou
summary: Gérard Mourou is a French physicist who, along with Donna Strickland, co-invented chirped pulse amplification (CPA), a technique used to create ultrashort, high-intensity laser pulses. This groundbreaking work revolutionized the field of optics and has had significant applications in medicine, such as LASIK eye surgery, and various scientific and industrial fields. He was awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for this invention and is also known for initiating the Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) project in Europe.
contributions: Co-invented Chirped Pulse Amplification (CPA) for generating high-intensity, ultrashort laser pulses
Pioneered femtosecond ophthalmology, which led to the development of LASIK eye surgery technology
Founded the Center for Ultrafast Optical Science (CUOS) at the University of Michigan
Initiated the Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) project in Europe
Discovered that high-power laser beams in the atmosphere can create 'filaments' that act as waveguides
quotes: "Be passionate, be bold and be willing to think outside the box."
"I always believed that science should be used to unify people and I'm a strong believer in this and it's like music and everybody speaks the same language and science is the same thing."

"The passion of lights, in fact, comes from the laser. The first time I've seen the lasers, I said “Wow”, I couldn't believe, to see this light, so well behaved, this beam of light, with pure colours. That was direct captivating for me and kept me ongoing for 45 years."

name: Harold Varmus
summary: Harold Varmus is an American Nobel Prize-winning virologist and cancer researcher. He shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the cellular origin of retroviral oncogenes, fundamentally changing the understanding of cancer as a genetic disease. Beyond his research, he has held significant leadership roles, including Director of the National Institutes of Health and the National Cancer Institute, and is an outspoken advocate for open science. He continues to be active in research and scientific leadership.
contributions: Co-discovered the cellular origin of retroviral oncogenes, demonstrating that normal cellular genes can become cancer-causing genes (proto-oncogenes) through mutation.
Served as Director of the National Institutes of Health (1993-1999), overseeing substantial budget growth and establishing PubMed Central.
Served as Director of the National Cancer Institute (2010-2015), contributing to advancements in cancer research and genomics.
Co-founded the Public Library of Science (PLoS), a non-profit organization dedicated to open-access scientific publishing.
Chaired the scientific advisory committee that named the AIDS virus as Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
quotes: "Science can improve lives in ways that are elegant in design and moving in practice."
"I had learned that science is a rewarding, active process of discovery, not the passive absorption of what others had discovered."

"I begin with the premise that behavior is an incredibly important element in medicine. Peoples habits, their willingness to quit smoking, their willingness to take steps to avoid transmission of HIV, are all behavioral questions."

name: Harvey Alter
summary: Harvey Alter is an American medical researcher and Nobel laureate, recognized for his foundational contributions to the discovery of the hepatitis C virus. His extensive work has been crucial in understanding blood-borne infections and has led to the implementation of widespread blood donor screening programs. These efforts have dramatically enhanced the safety of the global blood supply, virtually eliminating transfusion-associated hepatitis.
contributions: Co-discovery of the Australia antigen, a key marker for the hepatitis B virus
Demonstrated the existence of a novel form of hepatitis, termed non-A, non-B hepatitis, transmitted through blood transfusions
Led studies that identified the hepatitis C virus (HCV) as the primary cause of non-A, non-B hepatitis
Instrumental in developing and implementing blood donor screening programs to prevent hepatitis transmission
Significantly reduced the incidence of transfusion-associated hepatitis to near zero
quotes: “There is no elevator to success — you have to take the stairs.”
“You don't always know where you're going.”

name: Hedy Lamarr
summary: Hedy Lamarr was an Austrian-American actress and inventor. During World War II she co-invented a frequency-hopping spread-spectrum system to prevent the jamming of radio-guided torpedoes — a concept that became foundational to modern Wi-Fi, GPS, and Bluetooth.
contributions: Co-invented a frequency-hopping spread-spectrum communication system
Her patent laid the groundwork for Wi-Fi, GPS, and Bluetooth
Posthumously inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame

name: Heino Falcke
summary: Heino Falcke is a German professor of radio astronomy and astroparticle physics known for his groundbreaking research on black holes. He originated the concept of the "black hole shadow" and played a leading role in the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration, which produced the first-ever image of a black hole in 2019. His work provides critical tests of Einstein's general theory of relativity in extreme gravitational environments.
contributions: Originated the concept of the "black hole shadow".
Led the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration to capture the first image of a black hole (M87*) in 2019.
Contributed to the imaging of the Sagittarius A* black hole.
Instrumental in the development of the LOFAR radio telescope.
Predicted the possibility of making measurements near the edge of a black hole and later achieved it.
Involved in the development of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).

name: Helen Quinn
summary: Helen Quinn is an Australian-born theoretical particle physicist renowned for her significant contributions to the understanding of fundamental particle interactions. Her work includes the development of the Peccei-Quinn theory, which provides a compelling explanation for the absence of strong CP violation and implies the existence of the axion, a candidate for dark matter. Beyond her theoretical research, Quinn has extensively advocated for and led initiatives in K-12 science education, shaping national standards.
contributions: Co-formulation of the Peccei-Quinn theory and the Peccei-Quinn symmetry, which offers a solution to the strong CP problem and predicts the axion particle
Pioneering contributions to the quest for a unified theory of the strong, weak, and electromagnetic interactions
Development of basic analysis methods used to search for the origin of particle-antiparticle asymmetry in nature
Co-founded and served as the first president of the Contemporary Physics Education Project (CPEP)
Chaired the National Research Council study that produced "A Framework for K-12 Science Education", which is the basis for the Next Generation Science Standards
quotes: "I want educated people. I want citizens who can look at a problem in their community and think like a scientist about the part of the problem that is science."
"The goal is not only to prepare a few students to become scientists, but to prepare all of them to become citizens who can think like scientists."
"We shouldn't simply give our students an existing model. Ask them to create their own models. It's the best way to teach them critical thinking to describe and understand the world around them."

name: Hiroshi Amano
summary: Hiroshi Amano is a Japanese electronics engineer and materials scientist known for his pioneering work in semiconductor technology. He is a co-inventor of the efficient blue light-emitting diode (LED), for which he was awarded the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics alongside Isamu Akasaki and Shuji Nakamura. His innovations have been crucial in enabling bright and energy-saving white light sources and advancing display technologies.
contributions: Co-invention of the efficient blue light-emitting diode (LED)
Developed low-temperature deposited buffer layers for the growth of group III nitride semiconductor films on sapphire substrates
Succeeded in growing p-type gallium nitride (GaN)
Fabricated the world's first p-n-junction-type GaN-based UV/blue light-emitting diode
Conducted extensive research on the growth, characterization, and device applications of group III nitride semiconductors
quotes: "Always have an image of success while conducting your research. Otherwise, you will fail."
"It was something nobody around the world had been able to do."
"I was speechless."

name: Huda Zoghbi
summary: Huda Zoghbi is a Lebanese-born American geneticist and neuroscientist, known for her groundbreaking research into devastating neurological disorders. She is a professor at Baylor College of Medicine and the founding director of the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute. Her work has been pivotal in identifying the genetic causes of conditions like Rett syndrome and spinocerebellar ataxia type 1. Her discoveries have also provided new insights into more common neurological disorders such as Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and autism.
contributions: Discovery of the MECP2 gene mutations as the cause of Rett syndrome.
Co-discovery of the ATXN1 gene responsible for spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1).
Elucidating mechanisms of protein misfolding in neurodegenerative disorders.
Identification of the Math1 (Atoh1) gene's role in neurodevelopment, impacting balance, hearing, and respiration.
Founding Director of the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.
quotes: "We call it 'the little gene that could.' It's a small gene, but it really has essential functions."
"We will never be successful and safe as a society unless we attend to all issues and all people."

name: Inez Fung
summary: Inez Fung is a Professor Emerita of Atmospheric Science at the University of California, Berkeley, and co-director of the Berkeley Institute of the Environment. Her research focuses on biosphere-atmosphere interactions, climate modeling, and biogeochemical cycles, particularly concerning carbon dioxide and other trace substances. She is recognized for her work in understanding the sources and sinks of greenhouse gases and predicting the co-evolution of atmospheric composition and climate.
contributions: Principal architect of large-scale mathematical modeling approaches and numerical models for climate change and the carbon cycle
Inferred a Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes land sink for anthropogenic CO2
Studies the sources and sinks of carbon dioxide, methane, and other climatically important trace substances
Contributed to the United Nations' Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change (IPCC) reports and shared in the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize
Developed a mathematical system using satellite data for climate treaty verification
Researched the influence of lithology and subsurface water storage ('rock moisture') on tree resilience during droughts
quotes: "It's very important for us living on Earth enjoying the biosphere, enjoying the outdoors, to know how things are changing and to understand why things are changing."
"I think nature is always smarter than me. When I think I've got it, there's another puzzle that nature presents to me."
"Trust but verify" (in the context of climate treaty verification).

name: Ingrid Daubechies
summary: Ingrid Daubechies is a Belgian-American physicist and mathematician renowned for her groundbreaking work on wavelets. Her discoveries in wavelet theory, particularly compactly supported and biorthogonal wavelets, have revolutionized image and signal processing. Her mathematical methods have been instrumental in developing modern data compression technologies and have found applications in diverse fields such as medical imaging, art restoration, and digital communication.
contributions: Developed smooth, compactly supported orthonormal wavelet bases.
Introduced biorthogonal wavelet bases, which are crucial for image compression standards like JPEG 2000.
Made fundamental discoveries in wavelet theory, enabling its application in digital signal processing.
Created sophisticated image processing techniques for art authentication and restoration.
Pioneered mathematical tools with applications in medical imaging and wireless communication.
quotes: "I don't know where ideas come from, but I do believe they come from the interaction of many things in our head."
"I hope that my work will also be instrumental in helping people see that mathematics is everywhere. Identifying patterns and applying them in a different setting is very natural, very human."
"The beauty of maths, says the influential scholar, is its power to solve problems."

name: Isaac Newton
summary: Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician and physicist whose laws of motion and universal gravitation unified the heavens and the Earth under a single set of principles. His work defined classical mechanics for centuries.
contributions: Formulated the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation
Co-invented calculus, independently of Leibniz
Authored "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica," a foundation of modern physics

name: Jack Szostak
summary: Jack W. Szostak is a Canadian-American biologist and Nobel laureate, renowned for his significant contributions to genetics, biochemistry, and molecular biology. He received the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his groundbreaking discoveries concerning how chromosomes are protected by telomeres. Currently, his research focuses on understanding the origin of life on Earth and constructing artificial cellular life in the laboratory.
contributions: Co-discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres, leading to the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Construction of the world's first yeast artificial chromosome (YAC).
Development of in vitro selection and directed evolution as tools for isolating functional RNA, DNA, and protein molecules.
Pioneering research into the origin of life through the laboratory synthesis of self-replicating systems and protocells.
quotes: "I do not know why I have always been fascinated by science or why I have been driven by the intense desire to make some original contribution. And although I have had some degree of success as a scientist, it is hard to say precisely why."
"In my lab, we're interested in the transition from chemistry to early biology on the early earth."
"We aren't smart enough to design things, we just let evolution do the hard work and then we figure out what happened."

name: James Dyson
summary: Sir James Dyson is a British inventor and industrial designer best known for reinventing everyday machines. After building thousands of prototypes, he perfected the bagless cyclonic vacuum cleaner and went on to rethink fans, hand dryers, and lighting.
contributions: Invented the first bagless cyclonic vacuum cleaner after 5,127 prototypes
Developed bladeless Air Multiplier fans and the Airblade hand dryer
Founded the James Dyson Foundation to support young engineers

name: James Hansen
summary: James Hansen is an American climatologist and adjunct professor at Columbia University, renowned for his pivotal research on global warming. He is best known for his 1988 Congressional testimony, which significantly raised public and political awareness about climate change. Hansen's work has been crucial in developing and applying global climate models to understand human-induced climate change and advocate for mitigation efforts.
contributions: Pioneering research on radiative transfer in planetary atmospheres, including Venus.
Development and refinement of global climate models to understand Earth's climate system.
Providing early long-term projections of climate change based on model simulations.
His 1988 Congressional testimony which significantly raised broad public and political awareness of global warming.
Analysis of global climate trends using observational data.
Advocacy for urgent action to mitigate the impacts of climate change.
quotes: "The greenhouse effect has been detected, and it is changing our climate now."
"Burning all the fossil fuels will destroy the planet we know, Creation, the planet of stable climate in which civilization developed."
"The greatest danger hanging over our children and grandchildren is initiation of changes that will be irreversible on any time scale that humans can imagine."

name: James P. Allison
summary: James P. Allison is an American immunologist and Nobel laureate known for his groundbreaking work in cancer immunotherapy. His research illuminated the mechanisms governing T-cell responses, leading to the pioneering of immune checkpoint blockade as a cancer treatment, which has revolutionized oncology. He shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries.
contributions: Discovered the T-cell receptor structure.
Identified CD28 as a key co-stimulatory molecule for T-cell activation.
Demonstrated that CTLA-4 inhibits T-cell activation.
Showed that blocking CTLA-4 could unleash anti-tumor immune responses and lead to tumor rejection.
Pioneered the concept and development of immune checkpoint blockade therapy for cancer.
Led to the development of ipilimumab (Yervoy), the first FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitor.
quotes: “As a kid, I wanted to be the first to know something that no one else did. I think that's true of a lot of scientists.”
"But the immune system gives you a way of getting your own T cells to attack the cancer."

name: James Peebles
summary: James Peebles is a Canadian-American theoretical cosmologist and astrophysicist renowned for his foundational work in physical cosmology. His theoretical framework, developed since the mid-1960s, forms the basis of our contemporary understanding of the universe's history, including the cosmic microwave background, dark matter, and the formation of cosmic structures. He was awarded half of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking theoretical discoveries.
contributions: Developed the theoretical framework for contemporary ideas about the universe's history.
Made major theoretical contributions to primordial nucleosynthesis.
Pioneered work on the cosmic microwave background radiation.
Made significant contributions to understanding dark matter and dark energy.
Led the theory of cosmic structure formation.
Proposed the Ostriker–Peebles criterion, relating to the stability of galactic formation.
quotes: "It's very unfortunate that one thinks of the beginning whereas in fact, we have no good theory of such a thing as the beginning."
"You should enter it for the love of the science. You should enter science because you are fascinated by it. That's what I did."
"It is an embarrassment that the dominant forms of matter in the universe remain hypothetical."

name: James Rothman
summary: James Rothman is an American biochemist and cell biologist who was awarded the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. His seminal research identified the molecular machinery regulating vesicle traffic, a critical transport system within cells. His discoveries provided a fundamental understanding of how molecules are precisely transported, delivered, and fused within cells, impacting the understanding of cellular communication and various diseases.
contributions: Discovered the molecular machinery regulating vesicle traffic, a major cellular transport system.
Identified NSF and SNAP proteins essential for membrane trafficking.
Uncovered the fundamental role of SNARE proteins in vesicle membrane fusion.
Developed a cell-free system to reconstitute vesicle budding and fusion processes.
Proposed the SNARE hypothesis, explaining how SNARE proteins mediate membrane fusion.
Clarified the GTPase-switch mechanism controlling coated vesicle budding in cells.
quotes: I had five years of failure, really, before I had the first initial sign of success.
I started taking a basic biology course, and I really loved it. I started asking research questions incessantly. I was drawn very quickly to biology.
When I was a college student at Yale, I was studying physics and mathematics and was absolutely intent on becoming a theoretical physicist.

name: Jane Goodall
summary: Dame Jane Goodall was a British primatologist whose decades of study of wild chimpanzees transformed our understanding of animal behavior and the human-animal boundary. She became one of the world's most influential conservationists.
contributions: Discovered that chimpanzees make and use tools, redefining "man the toolmaker"
Conducted the longest-running field study of wild chimpanzees, at Gombe
Founded the Jane Goodall Institute and the Roots & Shoots youth program

name: Jane Lubchenco
summary: Jane Lubchenco is a highly distinguished American environmental scientist and marine ecologist, recognized for her extensive research on intertidal communities and her impactful leadership in science policy. She served as the Administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) under President Barack Obama, where she championed sustainable fisheries and ocean health. Currently, she continues to advocate for the integration of science into public policy and address global environmental challenges, particularly those related to the ocean and climate change.
contributions: Pioneered experimental and quantitative approaches in intertidal ecology, advancing the understanding of marine community dynamics, coevolutionary interactions, and foraging tactics.

Served as Administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) from 2009-2013, focusing on restoring fisheries to sustainability, improving ocean and coastal health, and strengthening climate science.
Led the Ecological Society of America's Sustainable Biosphere Initiative, which established key research priorities in global change, biodiversity, and sustainable ecological systems.

Co-founded initiatives like the Aldo Leopold Leadership Program and the Communication Partnership for Science and the Sea (COMPASS) to enhance scientists' ability to communicate their findings to the public and policymakers.
Served as the first U.S. Science Envoy for the Ocean, conducting science diplomacy to integrate scientific knowledge with sustainable solutions for ocean health globally.
Advocated for a new narrative regarding the ocean, emphasizing that it is too central to human future to ignore, and identifying scalable solutions for ocean and climate challenges.
quotes: "The ocean is not too big to fail, nor is it too big to fix. But it is so central to our health, prosperity and well-being that it is too big to ignore."
"Now is the moment for more scientists to pivot from simply documenting the tragedy underway to also creating scalable solutions."

"A vibrant democracy requires informed citizens. Decision makers will typically consider a range of factors—values, economics, politics, and opinions of peers or family. But science should also be at the table."

name: Jean-Pierre Sauvage
summary: Jean-Pierre Sauvage is a French chemist and a Nobel laureate known for his pioneering work in the design and synthesis of molecular machines. His research has laid the groundwork for developing molecular systems capable of controlled movements, mimicking biological processes. He significantly advanced the field of supramolecular chemistry through his creation of mechanically interlocked molecular architectures.
contributions: Design and synthesis of molecular machines
First synthesis of a catenane, a molecular structure with two interlocked rings, in 1983
Development of molecular systems capable of reproducing rotation, translation, and contraction movements
Pioneering work in molecular topology, including the synthesis of catenanes and molecular knots
Contributions to the electrochemical reduction of CO2 and models of the photosynthetic reaction center
Developed the first synthesis of cryptand ligands during his doctoral thesis
quotes: "breathing a surrogate for life into molecules that were devoid of it"

"Imagination cannot be forced, but, like luck, I'm convinced that it's provoked. My readings and scientific daydreams on Saturday mornings… have played a decisive role in the synthesis of the first catenane."

name: Jeff Bezos
summary: Jeff Bezos founded Amazon, transforming it from an online bookstore into one of the world's largest technology and commerce companies and pioneering large-scale cloud computing through Amazon Web Services. In 2000 he founded the aerospace company Blue Origin to lower the cost of access to space.
contributions: Founded Amazon, reinventing global e-commerce and logistics at planetary scale
Launched Amazon Web Services, which created the modern cloud-computing industry
Founded Blue Origin to develop reusable rockets and expand human access to space

name: Jeffrey Gordon
summary: Jeffrey I. Gordon is the Dr. Robert J. Glaser Distinguished University Professor and Director of The Edison Family Center for Genome Sciences & Systems Biology at Washington University School of Medicine. He is widely recognized as the "father of human microbiome research" for his pioneering work. His research focuses on understanding how the gut microbiome impacts human health and disease, especially in the context of childhood undernutrition.
contributions: Pioneered the field of human microbiome research, establishing the gut microbiome as a microbial "organ" that affects human health and disease.
Characterized the role of the gut microbiome in health and disease, including its influence on postnatal development and susceptibility to illnesses like obesity.
Demonstrated that disrupted gut microbiome development is a contributing cause of childhood undernutrition.
Developed microbiota-directed complementary food (MDCF) formulations to repair damaged gut microbiomes in children with malnutrition.
Authored a white paper in 2005 that laid the foundation for the National Institutes of Health's Human Microbiome Project.

name: Jennifer Doudna
summary: Dr. Jennifer Doudna is an American biochemist who co-invented CRISPR-Cas9, a precise and accessible method of editing DNA. Her work has transformed genetics, medicine, and agriculture and earned her the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
contributions: Co-invented CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry)
Founded the Innovative Genomics Institute to apply gene editing for public good
Advanced understanding of RNA structure and function

name: Jensen Huang
summary: Jensen Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993 and has led it ever since as CEO. Under his direction NVIDIA invented the graphics processing unit (GPU) and later pioneered accelerated and parallel computing, which became the foundational hardware of the modern artificial-intelligence era.
contributions: Co-founded NVIDIA and led the invention of the modern GPU
Drove the creation of CUDA, opening GPUs to general-purpose scientific and AI computing
Positioned NVIDIA as the core hardware engine behind the deep-learning revolution

name: Jill Tarter
field: Astronomy, particularly the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI)
summary: Jill Tarter is an American astronomer renowned for her pioneering work in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI). She served as the former director of the Center for SETI Research and holds the Bernard M. Oliver Chair for SETI at the SETI Institute. Tarter has dedicated her career to the quest for extraterrestrial life, significantly advancing the scientific rigor and public engagement of SETI research.
contributions: Pioneering research and leadership in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI).
Co-founder of the SETI Institute in 1984.
Served as Project Scientist for NASA's High Resolution Microwave Survey (HRMS).
Directed Project Phoenix, a comprehensive search for extraterrestrial intelligence.
Played a key role in the development of the Allen Telescope Array (ATA), an observatory dedicated to SETI.
Coined the term "brown dwarf" in her 1975 PhD dissertation.
quotes: We, all of us, are what happens when a primordial mixture of hydrogen and helium evolves for so long that it begins to ask where it came from.
The story of humans is the story of ideas that shine light into dark corners.
SETI is a mirror, a mirror that can show ourselves from an extraordinary perspective and can help to trivialize the differences among us.

name: John Clauser
summary: John Clauser is an American theoretical and experimental physicist renowned for his fundamental contributions to quantum mechanics. His work, particularly experiments with entangled photons, established the violation of Bell inequalities and laid the groundwork for quantum information science. He was a recipient of the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for this groundbreaking research.
contributions: Co-developed the Clauser–Horne–Shimony–Holt (CHSH) inequality.
Conducted the first experimental test of CHSH-Bell's theorem predictions, demonstrating quantum entanglement in 1972.
Formulated the theory of Local Realism and introduced the Clauser–Horne (CH) inequality.
First to experimentally prove photons can behave as localized particles by observing sub-Poissonian statistics for light.
Proposed and patented atom interferometers for ultra-sensitive inertial and gravity sensing.
Invented the Talbot-Lau interferometer and its application in ultra-high-resolution X-ray imaging.
quotes: "I thought it was important at the time, even though everybody told me I was crazy."
"If you're not enjoying it, find something else that you are enjoying and then you can put your heart into it and really be good at it."
"In my opinion, there is no real climate crisis."

name: John Jumper
summary: John Jumper is an American chemist and computer scientist best known for his leadership in developing AlphaFold at Google DeepMind. This artificial intelligence system accurately predicts the three-dimensional structures of proteins, solving a decades-old grand challenge in biology. His groundbreaking work earned him a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, profoundly impacting structural biology and accelerating research in medicine and other fields.
contributions: Led the development of AlphaFold, an AI model that predicts protein structures to atomic accuracy
Co-developed AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 systems, which significantly enhanced AI's capability to learn from biological and chemical data
Demonstrated that protein structure prediction systems can provide accurate measures of confidence in their predictions
Developed principled machine learning methods for molecular dynamics simulations of proteins
Released over 214 million predicted protein structures through AlphaFold, greatly impacting structural biology
Awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction using AI
quotes: "I'm a big believer in interdisciplinary science. You learn so much more by talking to a diverse group of experts to learn what they're excited about and how they think about things.”
“We're closing an enormous gap, where protein sequences are discovered about 3000 times faster than protein structure. We need machine learning to close that gap,”

"Working shoulder to shoulder with experimentalists...it's a really important experience for computational scientists to do the work that causes people to do new experiments, and I couldn't think of a better place to learn it."

name: John Mather
summary: John Mather is an American astrophysicist and cosmologist, best known for his foundational work on the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite. He shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrating that the cosmic microwave background radiation has a blackbody spectrum, providing crucial evidence for the Big Bang theory. Mather also served as the Senior Project Scientist for the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) from 1995 to 2023, guiding the development of this powerful observatory.
contributions: Co-recipient of the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on cosmic microwave background radiation.
Led the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) mission, which precisely measured the cosmic microwave background.
Confirmed the Big Bang theory by showing the cosmic microwave background radiation has a blackbody spectrum.
Served as the Senior Project Scientist for the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) from 1995 to 2023.
Elevated cosmology to a precision science through the COBE project.
quotes: "I don't think it's my job or anybody's job to try to convince other people of the righteousness of my opinion. I think it's each person's job to figure out how they look at the world."
"You're an ordinary person, and nevertheless you are going to try and do something impossible."

name: John O'Keefe
summary: John O'Keefe is an American-British neuroscientist and psychologist renowned for his pioneering research on the hippocampus, a brain region critical for memory and navigation. He discovered 'place cells,' which are neurons that become active when an animal is in a specific location, forming an internal 'cognitive map' of its environment. This groundbreaking work fundamentally advanced the understanding of how the brain creates spatial memory and earned him a share of the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
contributions: Discovery of place cells in the hippocampus, which are neurons that fire when an animal is in a particular location in its environment.
Co-authored "The Hippocampus as a Cognitive Map" with Lynn Nadel, proposing the spatial theory of hippocampal function.
Discovered theta phase precession, a specific type of temporal coding in place cells related to the brain's theta rhythm.
Elucidated the role of place cells in cognitive (spatial) mapping, explaining how animals orient themselves and navigate.
His research has provided insights into neurological conditions affecting spatial memory, such as Alzheimer's disease.
quotes: I want to know how the mind works.
I am particularly interested in Alzheimer's disease and have been for some time now.
I think it's fair to say that the Nobel Prize is the highest honor any scientist or artist can achieve.

name: Juan Ignacio Cirac
summary: Juan Ignacio Cirac is a Spanish theoretical physicist recognized as a pioneer in the fields of quantum computing and quantum information theory. He is a director at the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics, where he leads the Theory Division. His foundational work includes proposals for building quantum computers and simulators, and developing advanced theoretical frameworks for quantum many-body systems. His research significantly contributes to understanding quantum phenomena and harnessing them for future information technologies.
contributions: Pioneered the field of quantum computing and quantum information theory.
Introduced, with collaborators, the first proposals of quantum computers, simulators, and repeaters with atoms.
Developed a theory of tensor networks to describe quantum many-body systems and solve problems in quantum physics.
Made seminal contributions to ion trap quantum computation, opening possibilities for experimental quantum computing.
Introduced the concept of quantum repeaters and provided security proofs for continuous variable quantum cryptography.
Researched applications of cold atoms experiments to solve problems in materials science, high-energy physics, and quantum chemistry.

name: Juan Maldacena
summary: Juan Maldacena is an Argentine theoretical physicist known for his profound contributions to string theory and quantum gravity. He is most recognized for proposing the AdS/CFT correspondence, which posits an equivalence between theories of quantum gravity and quantum field theories. This work has been crucial in advancing the understanding of black holes and has provided new tools for theoretical physics.
contributions: Proposed the Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence
Realized the holographic principle within string theory
Made significant contributions to the foundations of string theory and quantum gravity
Explained black hole radiation within the framework of string theory
Co-proposed the ER = EPR conjecture, suggesting a link between wormholes and entangled particles
quotes: "perhaps the greatest physicist of his generation... certainly the greatest theoretical physicist of his generation." - Leonard Susskind
"We need to describe space-time in a quantum mechanical way because the classical laws in which we describe space-time are not valid in certain cases."

name: Judea Pearl
summary: Judea Pearl is an Israeli-American computer scientist and philosopher, best known for championing the probabilistic approach to artificial intelligence and developing Bayesian networks. He significantly advanced the field through his creation of a mathematical framework for causal and counterfactual inference. His work has had a profound impact on understanding causality across various scientific disciplines, earning him the Turing Award.
contributions: Invention of Bayesian networks, a mathematical formalism for defining complex probability models and algorithms for inference.
Development of a mathematical framework for causal and counterfactual inference based on structural models.
Pioneering the probabilistic approach to artificial intelligence.
Authored influential books including "Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems" and "Causality: Models, Reasoning and Inference."
Introduced the concept of Null Window Alpha-Beta search and the Scout Algorithm in game-searching procedures.
quotes: "If I could sum up the message of this book in one pithy phrase, it would be that you are smarter than your data. Data do not understand causes and effects; humans do."
"You cannot answer a question that you cannot ask, and you cannot ask a question that you have no words for."
"Deep learning has instead given us machines with truly impressive abilities but no intelligence. The difference is profound and lies in the absence of a model of reality."

name: Jules Hoffmann
summary: Jules Hoffmann is a Luxembourgish-French biologist and immunologist, recognized for his groundbreaking research on innate immunity. He was a co-recipient of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries concerning the activation of innate immunity, primarily through his work with Drosophila fruit flies. His findings on the Toll signaling pathway have profoundly influenced the understanding of immune responses across diverse organisms, from insects to humans.
contributions: Discovered the crucial role of the Toll gene and its signaling pathway in activating innate immunity in Drosophila fruit flies.
Identified various antimicrobial peptides, such as Diptericin and Defensin, in insects, highlighting their significance in host defense.
Provided foundational insights that led to the subsequent discovery of Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in mammals and a broader understanding of innate immunity in humans.
Investigated the effects of the steroid hormone ecdysone on insect development and endocrinology.
Characterized the Imd pathway, another significant immune signaling pathway in insects.

name: K. Barry Sharpless
summary: K. Barry Sharpless is an American chemist and two-time Nobel laureate, renowned for his pivotal contributions to synthetic chemistry. He developed chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions, enabling the production of enantiomerically pure compounds crucial for pharmaceuticals. Sharpless also originated "click chemistry," a highly efficient and reliable modular approach to chemical synthesis that has transformed drug discovery and materials science.
contributions: Developed chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions (e.g., Sharpless epoxidation, dihydroxylation, and aminohydroxylation)
Awarded the 2001 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions
Coined the term and developed the concept of "click chemistry" for efficient molecular assembly
Discovered the copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC), a prominent click reaction
Awarded the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the development of click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry
quotes: When I started doing chemistry, I did it the way I fished – for the excitement, the discovery, the adventure, for going after the most elusive catch imaginable in uncharted seas.

The discipline, nonetheless, is exacting: everything that can be observed should be observed, even if it is only recalled as the bland background from which the intriguing bits pop out like Venus in the evening sky. The goal is always finding something new, hopefully unimagined and, better still, hitherto unimaginable.

name: Karen Uhlenbeck
summary: Karen Uhlenbeck is an American mathematician and a founder of modern geometric analysis, whose work has fundamentally impacted analysis, geometry, and mathematical physics. She is recognized for her pioneering achievements in geometric partial differential equations, gauge theory, and integrable systems. In 2019, she became the first woman to receive the prestigious Abel Prize.
contributions: Established foundational results in geometric analysis
Made pioneering achievements in geometric partial differential equations
Contributed significantly to mathematical gauge theory, including Yang-Mills theory, with impact on geometry and topology
Developed research on integrable systems
Co-authored the influential textbook "Instantons and 4-Manifolds"
Provided foundational results on minimal surfaces and harmonic maps
quotes: "I am definitely very attracted to the idea that there are a lot of different facets in mathematics and seeing the connections."
"In this class I had an 'aha' moment when I realized I could do what was in the books. I didn't have to learn it, so to speak—I could create it myself."
"It's hard to be a role model, however, because what you really need to do is show students how imperfect people can be and still succeed."

name: Karl Deisseroth
summary: Karl Deisseroth is an American psychiatrist and bioengineer recognized for pioneering groundbreaking technologies that have transformed brain research. He developed optogenetics, a method using light to precisely control genetically engineered neurons, and CLARITY, a technique for making biological tissues transparent for detailed 3D imaging. His innovations have significantly advanced the understanding of neural circuits in both healthy states and in neurological and psychiatric disorders.
contributions: Pioneering optogenetics, enabling light-based control of neural activity in living tissue
Developing CLARITY (Clear, Lipid-exchanged, Acrylamide-hybridized Rigid, Imaging-compatible, and Transparent), a method for tissue clearing and imaging
Developing hydrogel-tissue chemistry technologies, including STARmap
Elucidating the molecular structure of channelrhodopsin and discovering other light-sensitive opsins
Applying advanced genetic and optical tools to study neural circuits underlying complex behaviors and neuropsychiatric illnesses
quotes: "Only the person with borderline can travel from reality to distortion and back, speaking both tongues with dual citizenship—not quite delusional, but with an alternative framework—to help manage a hostile, unpredictable reality."
"Social interaction is one of the hardest things to do in biology."

name: Katalin Karikó
summary: Dr. Katalin Karikó is a Hungarian-American biochemist whose decades of perseverance on messenger RNA made modern mRNA vaccines possible. She shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.
contributions: Pioneered nucleoside modifications that made mRNA safe and effective as a therapeutic
Enabled the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines developed during the pandemic
Awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine

name: Katie Bouman
summary: Katie Bouman is an American engineer and computer scientist renowned for her work in computational imaging. She played a leading role in developing the CHIRP algorithm, which was crucial for the Event Horizon Telescope project to capture the first-ever image of a black hole. Her research integrates signal processing, computer vision, machine learning, and physics to advance scientific discovery through novel imaging systems. She is currently an associate professor at Caltech.
contributions: Led the development of the CHIRP algorithm for black hole imaging.
Was a key member of the Event Horizon Telescope team that captured the first image of a black hole.
Contributed significantly to verifying images and selecting parameters for filtering data from the Event Horizon Telescope.
Pioneers computational imaging by integrating algorithm and sensor design to observe previously difficult phenomena.
quotes: "We developed ways to generate synthetic data and used different algorithms and tested blindly to see if we can recover an image, we didn't want to just develop one algorithm. We wanted to develop many different algorithms that all have different assumptions built into them. If all of them recover the same general structure, then that builds your confidence."
"No one of us could've done it alone, it came together because of lots of different people from many backgrounds."

name: Kip Thorne
summary: Kip Thorne is an American theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate renowned for his foundational work in relativistic astrophysics and gravitational physics. He co-founded the LIGO project, which achieved the first direct detection of gravitational waves, confirming a major prediction of Einstein's general relativity. Thorne is also known for his efforts in popularizing science through influential books and his role as a scientific advisor for major films.
contributions: Co-recipient of the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.
Co-founded the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) Project.
Pioneering theoretical work on gravitational waves and their astrophysical sources.
Developed the 'Hoop Conjecture' theory for black hole formation.
Co-authored the classic textbook "Gravitation" (1973).
Advised on the physics of wormholes for Carl Sagan's novel "Contact" and served as scientific advisor for films like "Interstellar".
quotes: "Everything likes to live where it will age the most slowly, and gravity pulls it there."
"Gravitational waves will bring us exquisitely accurate maps of black holes - maps of their space-time."
"Closed timelike curve is the jargon for time travel. It means you go out, come back and meet yourself in the past."

name: Klaus Hasselmann
summary: Klaus Hasselmann is a German oceanographer and climate modeller, awarded the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for his seminal work in climate science. He developed groundbreaking scientific models of Earth's climate, including a stochastic model that links weather and climate, and pioneered "fingerprinting" methods to distinguish human-induced global warming from natural variability. His research has been crucial in proving the dominant role of human activities in climate change.
contributions: Developed the stochastic climate model, explaining how short-term weather variability impacts long-term climate changes.
Pioneered "fingerprinting" methods to detect and attribute human-induced climate change by separating anthropogenic signals from natural climate fluctuations.
Co-recipient of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational contributions to the physical modeling of Earth's climate.
Founded and directed the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology.
Contributed significantly to ocean wave dynamics, including the energy balance equation for wave forecasting models.
Instrumental in advancing Earth system science in Germany.
quotes: "Scientific truth will always find a way."
"We've been warning against climate change for about 50 years or so."
"I'm very happy that they direct the attention on the climate problem which is very important."

name: Klaus von Klitzing
summary: Klaus von Klitzing is a German physicist renowned for his discovery of the integer quantum Hall effect in 1980, a phenomenon where electrical resistance in a two-dimensional conductor under strong magnetic fields and low temperatures varies in precise, discrete steps. This groundbreaking work earned him the 1985 Nobel Prize in Physics. His findings led to the definition of the von Klitzing constant, which is now a fundamental standard for electrical resistance and has significantly advanced metrology and the study of low-dimensional electron systems.
contributions: Discovered the integer quantum Hall effect (1980).
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery (1985).
Established the von Klitzing constant (Rk = h/e²), a fundamental standard for electrical resistance.
Enabled highly precise measurements for fundamental constants and advanced the field of metrology.
Initiated a new scientific field focusing on low-dimensional electron systems.
quotes: "I am happy that I have so many friends all over the world who contributed to my research work, and I believe that also in the future, basic research offers the best opportunity of reaching across borders and overcoming ideological barriers."
"I discovered that physics is a very nice field to use mathematics in a very efficient way. So, I changed direction to physics."

name: Lene Hau
summary: Lene Vestergaard Hau is a Danish physicist and professor at Harvard University, renowned for her pioneering experiments in slowing and completely stopping light. Her groundbreaking work has demonstrated the conversion of light into a matter wave and back again, which has significant implications for quantum information processing and quantum computing. She is also recognized for her research into ultra-cold atoms and Bose-Einstein condensates.
contributions: Led a team that successfully slowed a pulse of light to speeds as low as 15 miles per hour.
Was the first person to completely stop a beam of light using a Bose-Einstein condensate.
Demonstrated the conversion of a light pulse into a matter copy, its storage, and subsequent revival back into light.
Pioneered the use of Bose-Einstein condensates in experiments controlling light and matter.
Conducted research on cold atoms and nanoscale systems, including interactions between cold atoms and carbon nanotubes.
quotes: Physics is about questioning, studying, probing nature. You probe, and, if you're lucky, you get strange clues.
Incidentally, think about the ramifications of storing data on light waves that can be stopped and started at the speed of light.

name: Lisa Randall
summary: Lisa Randall is an American theoretical physicist and a professor at Harvard University, known for her research into elementary particles, fundamental forces, and extra dimensions of space. Her work includes significant contributions to understanding the Standard Model, supersymmetry, and dark matter, as well as developing the influential Randall-Sundrum model. She also actively popularizes science through her acclaimed books.
contributions: Co-developed the Randall-Sundrum model, proposing warped extra dimensions of space to address the hierarchy problem concerning gravity's weakness
Researched supersymmetry, baryogenesis, and cosmological inflation
