Conducted extensive studies on dark matter, including its potential implications for the extinction of dinosaurs
Authored popular science books such as "Warped Passages" and "Dark Matter and the Dinosaurs," making complex physics accessible to a broad audience
Contributed to improving the understanding of the Standard Model of particle physics and its connections to theoretical insights
Explored ways to experimentally test and verify theoretical ideas, including research related to the Large Hadron Collider
quotes: "Science is a combination of theory and experiment and the two together are how you make progress."
"We often fail to notice things that we are not expecting."
"I'm not creating the universe. I'm creating a model of the universe, which may or may not be true."

name: Lonnie Johnson
summary: Lonnie Johnson is an American aerospace and mechanical engineer who worked on NASA missions including Galileo and Cassini. He is widely known for inventing the Super Soaker water gun and now develops advanced energy and battery technologies.
contributions: Invented the Super Soaker, one of the best-selling toys of all time
Worked as an engineer on NASA's Galileo and Cassini missions
Develops next-generation energy conversion and battery systems

patents.title: Double tank pinch trigger pump water gun (Super Soaker)

name: Louis Brus
summary: Louis Brus is an American physical chemist, recognized for his groundbreaking work on colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals, known as quantum dots. His pioneering research led to the discovery and development of these nanoparticles, whose size determines their unique properties. He was awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work, which has had a profound impact on fields such as display technology and biomedical imaging.
contributions: Co-discovery of colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals (quantum dots).
First to prove size-dependent quantum effects in particles in fluid.
Developed the theoretical framework for understanding quantum dot behavior.
Identified the relationship between semiconductor particle size and emitted light wavelength (Brus equation).
Advanced nanotechnology with applications in QLED screens, solar cells, and biomedical imaging.
quotes: "This is a collaborative effort — partly physics, partly chemistry, partly materials science."
"We are all trapped by our educational background. So, learn something new every day. This is the greatest skill we have."
"I'm just lucky, I guess, that the Nobel Prize has chosen to honor this particular area of research at this time."

name: Louis Pasteur
summary: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist renowned for his groundbreaking discoveries in vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization. His pivotal work disproved the theory of spontaneous generation and established the germ theory of disease, profoundly impacting public health and modern medicine. His research led to the development of life-saving vaccines and innovative food preservation techniques.
contributions: Developed the process of pasteurization for preserving food and beverages
Disproved the theory of spontaneous generation through experimental evidence
Established the germ theory of disease, linking microorganisms to illness
Developed the first vaccines for rabies and anthrax
Pioneered the study of molecular asymmetry, also known as chirality
Identified microorganisms as the cause of fermentation processes
quotes: "Chance favors only the prepared mind."
"Science knows no country, because knowledge belongs to humanity, and is the torch which illuminates the world."
"Let me tell you the secret that has led me to my goal: my strength lies solely in my tenacity."

name: M. Stanley Whittingham
summary: M. Stanley Whittingham is a British-American chemist and a distinguished professor known for his pioneering work in the development of lithium-ion batteries. His research on intercalation chemistry and the creation of the first rechargeable lithium metal battery laid the foundation for the widespread use of these batteries in modern electronics and electric vehicles. He was jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019 for this transformative contribution to energy storage.
contributions: Discovered intercalation electrodes and thoroughly described intercalation reactions in rechargeable batteries in the 1970s.
Invented the first rechargeable lithium metal battery (LMB), patented in 1977, which used a titanium disulfide cathode and a lithium-aluminum anode.
Pioneered the application of intercalation chemistry for energy storage materials.
Contributed significantly to the development of lithium-ion battery technology, leading to the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Founded the journal *Solid State Ionics* in 1981 and served as its editor for 20 years.
Leads ongoing research into multi-electron intercalation reactions to increase battery storage capacity.
quotes: "Use your imagination! Don't just go by the book and don't believe what you read in the literature. Really imagine the future. Come up with new ideas and pursue those. Don't let people put those ideas down. Believe in yourself and discuss your ideas with others. Don't follow what your boss tells you to do, necessarily."

"Open data is the only way to move the world forward, learning from give and take to find new ways to connect the dots and have new insights, that is what electrochemistry has done already for hundreds of years."
"The lithium is the jam in the sandwich."

name: Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz
summary: Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz is a leading Polish-British developmental biologist and a Bren Professor at the California Institute of Technology, also holding a professorship at the University of Cambridge. She is renowned for her groundbreaking research into early mammalian embryo development, cell fate determination, and the self-organization of stem cells into embryo models. Her work has significantly advanced our understanding of how life begins, with profound implications for regenerative medicine and fertility.
contributions: Uncovered that cell fate determination in early mammalian embryos is biased at a much earlier stage than previously believed, identifying responsible epigenetic and transcriptional regulatory molecules.
Developed the first in vitro culture system allowing human embryos to develop through the implantation stages up to day 14.
Pioneered the creation of the first stem cell-derived embryo models, reconstituting synthetic embryos from embryonic and extra-embryonic stem cells.
Identified crucial signaling centers for human embryo development using in vitro culture systems.
Demonstrated that aneuploid cells are eliminated by apoptosis in embryonic but not extra-embryonic tissues in mouse models of chromosome mosaicism.
Co-authored the nonfiction book "The Dance of Life: The New Science of How a Single Cell Becomes a Human Being."
quotes: "I'm particularly enchanted by the concept of plasticity."
"To be creative. To persevere. To be rebellious and dare to open up new ways of thinking about problems—in this way one discovers new things although it makes enemies on a path."

"I am thrilled and hopeful to see how our discoveries will help to advance regenerative medicine, from improving the chances of a healthy pregnancy to, perhaps, developing synthetic organs for life-saving transplantation."

name: Makoto Kobayashi
summary: Makoto Kobayashi is a Japanese physicist best known for his work on CP-violation within the Standard Model of particle physics. In collaboration with Toshihide Maskawa, he developed a theory that predicted the existence of at least three families of quarks, a prediction later confirmed experimentally. He was awarded one-fourth of the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics for this significant discovery.
contributions: Discovered the origin of broken symmetry, which predicted the existence of at least three families of quarks.
Co-developed the Kobayashi-Maskawa theory (Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix) to explain CP-violation.
Proposed that CP violation is an inherent property of the Standard Model if there are at least two additional quarks beyond the four known at the time.
Co-authored the highly cited 1973 paper "CP Violation in the Renormalizable Theory of Weak Interaction."

name: Manjul Bhargava
summary: Manjul Bhargava is a Canadian-American mathematician and a professor at Princeton University, recognized for his profound contributions to number theory. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2014 for developing innovative methods in the geometry of numbers, which he applied to count rings of small rank and to determine bounds for the average rank of elliptic curves. His research has significantly advanced the understanding of fundamental arithmetic objects.
contributions: Generalized Gauss's classical law for the composition of binary quadratic forms.
Developed powerful new methods in the geometry of numbers, including the "Bhargava cube."
Proved the 15 and 290 theorems, which address universal quadratic forms.
Introduced the Bhargava factorial, a novel generalization of the factorial function.
Established that the average rank of elliptic curves over the rational numbers is bounded (less than 1).
Revolutionized the counting of number fields of small discriminant and elliptic curves.
quotes: "When you discover things about numbers, it's very beautiful."

"As a child, I enjoyed studying Sanskrit, Sanskrit poetry and Indian classical music. I saw maths in all these things; that further inspired me to pursue mathematics. When I went to college, I took Sanskrit, a lot of music, computer science and physics, and also mathematics. To me, mathematics was the common thread in all these subjects."

name: Manu Prakash
summary: Manu Prakash is a Stanford bioengineer and pioneer of "frugal science" — building powerful scientific tools that cost almost nothing so that anyone, anywhere, can do real research. His inventions put laboratory-grade capability into the hands of communities worldwide.
contributions: Invented the Foldscope, a durable paper microscope that costs about $1
Created the Paperfuge, a hand-powered centrifuge inspired by a child's whirligig
Champion of the "frugal science" movement for ultra-low-cost research tools

name: Manu Rehani
summary: Manu Rehani is an Austin, Texas–based inventor, engineer, and advisor working at the intersection of behavioral intelligence, artificial intelligence, and dual-use technology. He describes his work as building behavioral intelligence for the AI-native renaissance, spanning cloud infrastructure, autonomous systems, and wearable technology. With two company exits and twelve patents to his name, he builds and advises across cognitive modeling and design for relevance fit.
contributions: Holds twelve patents spanning cloud storage, large language models, autonomous systems, and wearable intelligence.
Achieved two startup exits in behavioral intelligence and dual-use technology.
Works as an inventor, engineer, and advisor at the intersection of behavioral intelligence, AI, and dual-use technology.
Develops cognitive modeling and 'design for relevance fit' approaches for AI-native systems.
quotes: Behavioral intelligence for the AI-native renaissance.

patents.title: Storage system for pervasive and mobile content
Methods and systems for measuring semantics in communications
Format for displaying text analytics results
Taxonomy and application of language analysis and processing
Methods and systems for identifying, quantifying, analyzing, and optimizing the level of engagement of components within a defined ecosystem or context

name: Margaret Geller
summary: Margaret Geller is an influential American astrophysicist recognized for her pioneering research into the large-scale structure of the universe and the distribution of galaxies. Her work, including the co-discovery of the Great Wall, has significantly advanced our understanding of cosmic organization and dark matter. She is also dedicated to public science education, creating films to increase awareness of astronomy.
contributions: Pioneering maps of the nearby universe, revealing the large-scale structure of galaxies.
Co-discovery of the Great Wall, a massive superstructure of galaxies.
Studies on the relationship between galaxies and their environment.
Development of methods for measuring the distribution of matter, including dark matter, in the universe.
Co-discovery of hypervelocity stars.
Creation of award-winning educational films such as "Where the Galaxies Are" and "So Many Galaxies... So Little Time".
quotes: "When people on airplanes ask me what I do, I used to say I was a physicist, which ended the discussion. I once said I was a cosmologist, but they started asking me about makeup, and the title ‘astronomer’ gets confused with astrologer. Now I say I make maps."
"Science is driven not only by the curiosity of those who explore today but also by their confidence that others like you will succeed where they have failed."

name: Marie Curie
summary: Marie Curie was a Polish-French physicist and chemist who pioneered research on radioactivity — a term she coined. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
contributions: Pioneered the theory of radioactivity and discovered the elements polonium and radium
First person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911)
Developed mobile radiography units to treat wounded soldiers in World War I

name: Mary-Claire King
summary: Mary-Claire King is a renowned American geneticist who first identified the BRCA1 gene, establishing the hereditary link for breast and ovarian cancer. Her groundbreaking work revolutionized cancer genetics, enabling genetic screening and personalized interventions. She also pioneered the application of DNA sequencing for human rights investigations, notably in identifying victims of atrocities. Additionally, King's research revealed the close genetic relationship between humans and chimpanzees.
contributions: Identified the BRCA1 gene, demonstrating its link to inherited breast and ovarian cancer.
Pioneered the use of DNA sequencing in human rights investigations, such as identifying kidnapped children in Argentina.
Showed that humans and chimpanzees share 99% genetic identity.
Conducted extensive research into the genetic bases of complex human conditions like schizophrenia and inherited deafness.
quotes: “I think there are two keys to being creatively productive. One is not being daunted by one's fear of failure. The second is sheer perseverance.”
“I've been able to keep going and it's been enormously successful; we're saving tens of thousands of lives.”

name: May-Britt Moser
summary: May-Britt Moser is a Norwegian psychologist and neuroscientist, a co-recipient of the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her pioneering research, conducted with Edvard Moser, led to the discovery of grid cells in the brain's entorhinal cortex, which form a crucial part of the brain's positioning system. Her work has significantly advanced the understanding of spatial navigation, memory, and cognitive processes, with implications for neurological conditions like Alzheimer's disease.
contributions: Co-discovered grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, which provide an internal coordinate system for spatial navigation.
Identified other space-representing cell types in the brain, including border cells, head direction cells, speed cells, and object-vector cells.
Elucidated how different cell types in the brain cooperate to form a positioning system for spatial orientation.
Co-founded and leads several prominent research centers, including the Centre for the Biology of Memory and the Centre for Neural Computation.
Her research has contributed to new insights into cognitive processes and spatial deficits associated with neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
quotes: I had this idea that I could do anything.
We didn't care about salaries and having a nice car. We just cared about science and were really ambitious.
We need all kinds of people doing science.

name: Michael Berry
summary: Sir Michael Berry is a British theoretical physicist renowned for his foundational contributions to semiclassical physics, which bridges classical and quantum theories. He is best known for discovering the Berry phase, a geometric phase that has wide-ranging applications in quantum mechanics, optics, and condensed matter physics. His work also explores quantum chaos, connecting it to number theory and the statistics of the Riemann zeta function's zeros. Berry is celebrated for applying complex mathematical physics to explain phenomena in everyday life, from rainbows to levitating objects.
contributions: Discovered the Berry phase (geometric phase), a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics and classical optics.
Pioneered research in semiclassical physics, exploring the 'borderlands' between classical and quantum theories.
Made significant contributions to the field of quantum chaos (also known as quantum chaology).
Investigated geometrical singularities such as ray caustics and wave vortices.
Identified connections between the energy-level statistics of chaotic quantum systems and the zeros of the Riemann zeta function.
Applied abstract mathematical ideas to explain everyday phenomena, including rainbows, patterns at the bottom of swimming pools, and the levitation of frogs.
quotes: "This is unexpected recognition for six decades of obsessive scribbling."

name: Michael Faraday
summary: Michael Faraday was an English chemist and physicist who made significant contributions to the understanding of electromagnetism and electrochemistry. He is recognized for his discoveries, including electromagnetic induction, diamagnetism, and the laws of electrolysis. His foundational work paved the way for electric motor technology and the practical application of electricity. Largely self-educated, Faraday became one of the most influential scientists in history.
contributions: Discovered electromagnetic induction
Invented the first electric motor (electromagnetic rotary devices)
Established the laws of electrolysis
Discovered benzene
Discovered diamagnetism and the Faraday effect (magnetism affecting light)
Established the concept of the electromagnetic field in physics

name: Michael Houghton
summary: Sir Michael Houghton is a British-born virologist and Nobel laureate, renowned for his pivotal role in the co-discovery of the Hepatitis C virus (HCV) in 1989. This groundbreaking identification led to the rapid development of blood screening tests, dramatically reducing HCV transmission through transfusions, and facilitated the creation of highly effective antiviral treatments. He continues to contribute to virology research, including vaccine development for HCV and other viral diseases, as a professor at the University of Alberta.
contributions: Co-discovery of the Hepatitis C virus (HCV) in 1989.
Co-discovery of the Hepatitis D genome in 1986.
Developed diagnostic reagents and blood screening tests for HCV, virtually eliminating transfusion-related infections.
His work led to the development of antiviral therapies capable of curing Hepatitis C in most patients.
Developed an effective vaccine for the SARS-CoV-1 virus in 2004.
Leading efforts in developing an HCV vaccine and working on vaccines and therapeutics for diseases like COVID-19.

name: Michael Levin
summary: Michael Levin is the Vannevar Bush Distinguished Professor of Biology at Tufts University, where he directs the Allen Discovery Center and co-directs the Institute for Computationally Designed Organisms. His interdisciplinary research investigates how bioelectrical communication networks guide multicellular organisms during development, regeneration, and cancer suppression. Levin's work has advanced the understanding of morphogenesis and the concept of collective cellular intelligence, leading to novel approaches in regenerative medicine and synthetic biology.
contributions: Co-discovery of xenobots, novel living robots engineered from frog skin cells.
Pioneering the study of developmental bioelectricity, focusing on how cells use electrical signals to coordinate large-scale anatomical patterning.
Developed tools to read and manipulate the bioelectric code, enabling control over growth, form, and regeneration in various model organisms.
Demonstrated bioelectric approaches to suppress cancer and repair birth defects.
Identified the first genetic pathway determining the left-right asymmetry of body organs.
quotes: "We don't want to try to tell every cell and every gene what to do," Levin said. "We're not looking to teach cells how to grow a leg; we're looking to convince them that that's what they should do."
"Bioelectricity is the cognitive glue holding our cells together."
"I believe that I'm going to see this in my lifetime."

name: Michael Levitt
summary: Michael Levitt is a Nobel Prize-winning biophysicist and a professor of structural biology at Stanford University. He was awarded the 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his pioneering work, along with Martin Karplus and Arieh Warshel, on the development of multiscale models for complex chemical systems. His research has been instrumental in popularizing the use of computer modeling to understand the molecular structures and dynamics of biological molecules like proteins and DNA.
contributions: Developed multiscale models for complex chemical systems, combining classical and quantum mechanics
Pioneered molecular dynamics simulations of DNA and proteins
Developed the first computerized model of an enzyme reaction
Made significant contributions to the understanding of protein folding
Helped popularize the use of computer modeling in biology

name: Michael Mann
summary: Michael Mann is an American climatologist and geophysicist, currently a Presidential Distinguished Professor at the University of Pennsylvania. He is renowned for his significant contributions to the scientific understanding of historic climate change. His work, most notably the "hockey stick graph," illustrates the unprecedented nature of modern, human-caused global warming. Mann also actively engages in public communication regarding climate science and its policy implications.
contributions: Co-created the "hockey stick graph," a reconstruction of Northern Hemisphere temperatures over the past millennium, demonstrating recent anomalous warming.
Pioneered techniques for synthesizing patterns in past climate data using paleoclimate proxy records like tree rings and ice cores.
Served as a Lead Author for the "Observed Climate Variability and Change" chapter of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Third Scientific Assessment Report.
Contributed to understanding the impact of climate change on extreme weather events such as heat waves, droughts, wildfires, and floods.
Co-founded RealClimate.org, an award-winning climate science website.
Authored numerous books on climate change science, impacts, and policy, including "The New Climate War" and "Our Fragile Moment."
quotes: Climate change is a crisis, but a solvable crisis.
The greatest threat to meaningful climate action today is no longer denial, but despair and doomism, premised on the flawed notion that it is too late to do anything.

name: Michel Mayor
summary: Michel Mayor is a Swiss astrophysicist and professor emeritus at the University of Geneva, renowned for his groundbreaking work in exoplanet research. He was a co-recipient of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet found orbiting a sun-like star. His innovations in observational instrumentation significantly advanced the field of exoplanet detection and characterization.
contributions: Co-discovery of 51 Pegasi b in 1995, the first exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star, with Didier Queloz.
Pioneering the development of high-precision spectrographs such as ELODIE, CORALIE, and HARPS for radial velocity measurements.
Leading extensive observational surveys that contributed to the discovery of hundreds of exoplanets, including several 'super-Earths.'
Contributions to research in stellar kinematics, galactic structure, and the dynamics of globular clusters.
quotes: "If we are talking about exoplanets, things should be clear: We will not migrate there."
"We must take care of our planet. It is very beautiful and still absolutely livable."
"Curiosity is the most important point to be a scientist."

name: Morten Meldal
summary: Morten Meldal is a Danish chemist and Nobel laureate, recognized for his significant contributions to the field of organic chemistry. He is a professor at the University of Copenhagen and is best known for independently developing the copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction. This efficient and versatile "click chemistry" reaction has profoundly impacted fields such as materials science, pharmaceutical development, and chemical biology.
contributions: Co-development of the copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction, a cornerstone of click chemistry.
Pioneering advances in solid-phase synthesis and combinatorial chemistry, particularly for peptides.
Development of technological techniques and instruments for peptide synthesis, including PEG-based resins.
Contributions to bioconjugation methods for linking biomolecules.
Research into carbohydrate chemistry, polymer chemistry, and the design of artificial receptors and enzymes.
quotes: "Whatever honour you get, the most interesting is still what goes on in the fume hood."
"My philosophy is that you cannot make any new discoveries behind the office desk. You make them in a fume hood."
"The complexity in organic chemistry is reflected in the chemistry of life… we are only scratching the surface of what we know in organic chemistry."

name: Moungi Bawendi
summary: Moungi Bawendi is an American-Tunisian-French chemist and the Lester Wolfe Professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2023 for his pivotal work in revolutionizing the chemical production of high-quality quantum dots. His advancements in synthesizing stable and uniform quantum dots have significantly impacted nanotechnology, enabling their widespread use in diverse applications.
contributions: Revolutionized the chemical production of high-quality quantum dots.
Developed standardized and scalable methods for synthesizing stable and uniform quantum dots.
Conducted pioneering research into the fundamental properties of quantum dots.
Demonstrated diverse applications of quantum dots, including in displays, LEDs, solar cells, and biomedical imaging.
Co-recipient of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery and development of quantum dots.
quotes: "The Packard Fellowship was instrumental in getting my career started."
"I think that what is extremely important is to stay curious."
"Persevere," and don't let setbacks "destroy you."

name: Natalie Batalha
summary: Natalie Batalha is a professor of Astronomy and Astrophysics at UC Santa Cruz, renowned for her pivotal leadership in NASA's Kepler Mission. She played a crucial role in the discovery and characterization of thousands of exoplanets, including the first confirmed rocky planet outside our solar system, Kepler 10b. Her work has significantly advanced the search for planetary habitability and life beyond Earth, and she continues to contribute to exoplanet research with the James Webb Space Telescope.
contributions: Served as the Science Team Lead, Mission Scientist, and Project Scientist for NASA's Kepler Mission, leading the effort to identify exoplanets.
Led the analysis that resulted in the discovery of Kepler 10b, the first confirmed rocky planet outside the Solar System.
Contributed to the discovery of over 2,700 confirmed exoplanets and thousands of additional candidates from Kepler data.
Responsible for the selection of more than 150,000 stars monitored by the Kepler telescope.
Co-leads NASA's Nexus for Exoplanet Systems Science (NExSS), an initiative to advance the search for life on exoplanets.
Involved in the first unequivocal detection of carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere using the James Webb Space Telescope.
quotes: "I was moved that the universe could be described in numbers."
"You can't have curiosity about the natural world without feeling a sense of wonder."
"You see the expanse of the cosmos, and you realize how small we are and how connected we are, and that what's good for you has to be good for me."

name: Neil Shubin
summary: Neil Shubin is an American paleontologist, evolutionary biologist, and science communicator known for his work on the evolutionary origins of anatomical features in animals. He is a professor at the University of Chicago and the Provost of the Field Museum of Natural History. His research integrates paleontology, developmental genetics, and comparative morphology to understand major transitions in vertebrate history.
contributions: Co-discovery of Tiktaalik roseae, a 375-million-year-old fossil fish considered a key transitional form between fish and land animals.
Research on the evolution of new organs, particularly limbs, using expeditionary paleontology and developmental biology.
Authored popular science books, including the best-selling "Your Inner Fish" (2008), which was adapted into an Emmy Award-winning PBS series.
Identified the role of the Sonic hedgehog gene in limb development, showing its importance across various limbed animals.
Elected president of the National Academy of Sciences, with his term beginning July 1, 2026.
quotes: "We were not designed rationally, but are products of a convoluted history."
"We were staring at the origin of a piece of our own bodies inside this 375-million-year-old fish. We had a fish with a wrist."

name: Neil deGrasse Tyson
summary: Neil deGrasse Tyson is an American astrophysicist and one of the world's most prominent science communicators. As director of the Hayden Planetarium and host of Cosmos and StarTalk, he has brought astronomy and the wonder of the universe to millions.
contributions: Director of the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History
Host of Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey and the StarTalk podcast
Best-selling author popularizing astrophysics for the public

name: Niels Bohr
summary: Niels Bohr was a Danish theoretical physicist who made foundational contributions to understanding atomic structure and quantum theory. He is renowned for developing the Bohr model of the atom, which proposed that electrons revolve in stable orbits with discrete energy levels. His work significantly advanced the field of quantum mechanics, earning him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922.
contributions: Developed the Bohr model of the atom, incorporating quantum theory to explain atomic structure
Made foundational contributions to quantum theory and atomic structure, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922
Introduced the concept of complementarity, suggesting that particles can be analyzed as both waves and particles
Proposed the compound nucleus theory in 1936, explaining neutron capture by the nucleus
Advocated for peaceful applications of atomic energy and openness between nations regarding nuclear weapons
quotes: "Everything we call real is made up of things that cannot be regarded as real. If quantum mechanics hasn't profoundly shocked you, you haven't understood it yet."
"Never express yourself more clearly than you can think."
"An expert is a man who has made all the mistakes which can be made, in a very narrow field."

name: Nikola Tesla
summary: Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor and electrical engineer whose work on alternating-current (AC) power systems became the backbone of the modern electrical grid. His prolific imagination spanned wireless power, radio, and rotating magnetic fields.
contributions: Designed the modern alternating-current (AC) electricity supply system
Invented the induction motor and the Tesla coil
Pioneered early work in wireless transmission of energy and radio

name: Nima Arkani-Hamed
summary: Nima Arkani-Hamed is an Iranian-American-Canadian theoretical physicist specializing in high-energy physics, quantum field theory, string theory, cosmology, and collider physics. He is a permanent faculty member at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, and a leading researcher in fundamental physics. His work explores profound questions concerning the nature of space-time, gravity, and the universe's structure, aiming to reconcile the Standard Model with new physical principles.
contributions: Proposed the paradigm of large extra dimensions to explain the weakness of gravity
Developed "Little Higgs" theories
Introduced the concept of split supersymmetry
Conducted research on dark matter
Explored new mathematical structures in gauge theory scattering amplitudes, including the amplituhedron
Proposed new physical theories testable at the Large Hadron Collider
quotes: "We're machines for turning caffeine into physics."
"Things that seem incredibly different can really be manifestations of the same underlying phenomena."
"The Universe is inevitable. The Universe is impossible."

name: Omar Yaghi
summary: Omar Yaghi is a chemist renowned for developing metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and pioneering reticular chemistry, a field focused on constructing extended structures from molecular building blocks. His work has led to the creation of new materials with extremely high surface areas, offering solutions for clean energy applications such as hydrogen and methane storage, carbon capture, and water harvesting from desert air. Yaghi was awarded the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his groundbreaking contributions in this area.
contributions: Pioneered reticular chemistry, a new branch of chemistry dedicated to assembling molecular building blocks into open, crystalline frameworks.
Developed Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOFs), highly porous materials used for gas storage, carbon capture, and water harvesting.
Created Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs), another class of porous crystalline solids with applications in separations, storage, and catalysis.
Invented Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks (ZIFs), a subclass of MOFs useful in energy-intensive industrial separation processes.
Led efforts to apply reticular materials in clean energy technologies, including hydrogen and methane storage.
Developed materials and methods for capturing carbon dioxide and harvesting water from desert air.
quotes: "I think science is the greatest equalising force in the world, because anyone – regardless of their background, regardless of their gender, regardless of their academic standing, regardless of their economic standing in society – can go into a lab and potentially make a discovery, and that discovery can change the world."

"Our development of metal–organic frameworks, or MOFs, began with a simple but bold idea: that we could design materials with atomic precision, forming strong purposeful bonds that unlock remarkable functions."
"I feel like I've gone from scarcity to abundance through science. That's really the beauty of a scientific endeavor and dedicating oneself to science."

name: Pablo Jarillo-Herrero
summary: Pablo Jarillo-Herrero is a Spanish experimental condensed matter physicist and a professor at MIT. He is widely recognized for his groundbreaking work in "twistronics," particularly his 2018 discovery of correlated insulator states and superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. His research has significantly advanced the understanding and manipulation of quantum electronic properties in two-dimensional materials.
contributions: Experimentally discovered correlated insulator states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene.
Discovered superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene.
Pioneered the field of "twistronics," which involves controlling material properties by rotating layers of two-dimensional materials.
Demonstrated the ability to tune bilayer graphene between an insulator, a conductor, and a superconductor by applying specific voltages.
Contributed to research on two-dimensional crystalline magnets and topological insulators.
quotes: "The magic angle is like a philosopher's stone, but in reverse: it allows us to turn graphene into any other type of material."

name: Pardis Sabeti
field: Computational Biology, Evolutionary Genetics, and Infectious Disease
summary: Pardis Sabeti is an Iranian-American computational biologist, medical geneticist, and evolutionary geneticist, holding professorships at Harvard University and the Broad Institute. She is recognized for pioneering genomic and analytical methods to study evolutionary adaptation in humans and pathogens. Her work has been crucial in developing real-time genomic sequencing technologies for detecting and tracking deadly infectious diseases like Ebola, Lassa, Zika, and SARS-CoV-2, significantly impacting global health and pandemic preparedness.
contributions: Developed algorithms and molecular tools to characterize the human genome and identify regions under natural selection.
Initiated technologies for detecting, tracking, and countering deadly pathogens, including Ebola, Zika, Lassa, and SARS-CoV-2.
Co-founded the African Center of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Disease (ACEGID) to enhance pathogen surveillance and education in Africa.
Pioneered real-time genetic sequencing during infectious disease outbreaks to track viral evolution and spread.
Created transformative methods for gene delivery of new biomedicines to specific tissues.
Co-created Operation Outbreak, an outbreak prevention and preparedness curriculum and Bluetooth-based outbreak simulation.
quotes: “Life is a marathon. A lot of the people that are most successful aren't the best in the class. They're the ones who are endlessly curious.”
“Always do the thing that keeps you up at night, wakes you up in the morning, and then just keeps you fascinated.”

name: Paul Nurse
summary: Sir Paul Nurse is an English geneticist and cell biologist, best known for his groundbreaking work on the molecular mechanisms controlling the eukaryotic cell cycle. His discoveries, particularly of the cdc2 gene and cyclin-dependent kinases, earned him a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. His research has significantly advanced the understanding of cell reproduction, growth, and its implications for diseases like cancer.
contributions: Identified the cdc2 gene in fission yeast, which regulates cell cycle progression.
Discovered that the cdc2 gene encodes a protein kinase crucial for cell division.
Isolated the human homologous gene, Cdk1, demonstrating its conserved role in human cell cycle control.
Co-awarded the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries of key protein molecules controlling cell division.
Held significant leadership roles, including President of the Royal Society and Director of the Francis Crick Institute, advocating for science.
quotes: I felt strongly that since the pursuit of good science was so difficult it was essential that the problem being studied was an important one to justify the effort expanded.”
It has been a privilege to pursue knowledge for its own sake and to see how it might help mankind in more practical ways.”
How scientists go about their job: and it's a process, it's a question of asking questions, respecting observation, respecting experiment, having tentative explanations and then testing them....

name: Peter Agre
summary: Peter Agre is an American physician and molecular biologist who shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his discovery of aquaporins, specialized water channels in cell membranes. His work provided crucial insight into how living organisms transport water molecules, impacting the understanding of kidney function and other physiological processes. He has also significantly contributed to malaria research and engaged in international science diplomacy.
contributions: Discovery of aquaporin water channels in cell membranes.
Elucidated the mechanism of rapid water transport across cell membranes.
Pioneering research on the Rhesus (Rh) blood group antigen.
Identified spectrin deficiency as a cause of hereditary spherocytosis.
Directed the Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute.
Fostered international scientific collaboration through science diplomacy.
quotes: Well, all life forms are dependent upon water.
It is a remarkable honor to receive a Nobel Prize, because it not only recognizes discoveries, but also their usefulness to the advancement of fundamental science.
The need for general scientific understanding by the public has never been larger, and the penalty for scientific illiteracy never harsher.

name: Peter Diamandis
summary: Dr. Peter Diamandis is an entrepreneur and futurist who founded the XPRIZE Foundation, which uses large incentive prizes to drive breakthroughs in space, health, and the environment. He also co-founded Singularity University to educate leaders on exponential technologies.
contributions: Founded the XPRIZE Foundation, pioneering incentivized competition for grand challenges
Co-founded Singularity University and Human Longevity, Inc.
Author of "Abundance" and "Bold," charting how technology can solve humanity's biggest problems

name: Peter Ratcliffe
summary: Sir Peter J. Ratcliffe is a British physician-scientist who was awarded the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, shared with William Kaelin Jr. and Gregg L. Semenza. His groundbreaking research illuminated the fundamental mechanisms by which cells sense and adapt to changing oxygen levels, a process known as hypoxia. This work has significantly advanced the understanding of how oxygen availability impacts cellular metabolism and physiological functions, offering new avenues for treating diseases like anemia, cancer, and heart disease.
contributions: Discovered how cells sense and adapt to oxygen availability (hypoxia).
Elucidated the molecular mechanisms underlying oxygen sensing and signaling pathways.
Demonstrated that oxygen-sensing mechanisms operate across virtually all animal cells, not solely in kidney-related erythropoietin production.
Identified the role of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and its regulation by prolyl hydroxylation and the VHL protein in cellular oxygen sensing.
Revealed that cellular responses to oxygen availability affect critical processes such as energy metabolism, angiogenesis, and cell survival and differentiation.

name: Peter Scholze
summary: Peter Scholze is a German mathematician renowned for his foundational contributions to arithmetic geometry. He introduced groundbreaking concepts such as perfectoid spaces and prismatic cohomology, which have provided new tools to bridge different areas of mathematics and solve long-standing problems in number theory and algebraic geometry. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2018 for his transformative work in the field.
contributions: Introduced the theory of perfectoid spaces, revolutionizing arithmetic algebraic geometry over p-adic fields.
Developed prismatic cohomology, a new cohomology theory unifying singular, de Rham, ℓ-adic, and crystalline cohomologies.
Contributed significantly to condensed mathematics, a program for rebuilding the foundations of topology and algebraic methods.
Provided a solution to a special case of the weight-monodromy conjecture using perfectoid spaces.
Advanced the geometrization of the local Langlands conjectures.
quotes: What I care most about are definitions. For one thing, humans describe mathematics through language, and, as always, we need sharp words in order to articulate our ideas clearly.

name: Peter Zoller
summary: Peter Zoller is an Austrian theoretical physicist renowned for his pioneering work in quantum computing, quantum simulation, and quantum communication. His research has been instrumental in translating theoretical concepts of quantum information into experimental settings and establishing quantum optical systems as leading platforms for quantum technologies. He has made significant contributions to atomic physics, many-body physics, and quantum information science.
contributions: Co-proposed the first experimentally realistic and comprehensive proposal for a universal quantum computer, the "Cirac–Zoller trapped-ion quantum computer" (1995).
Pioneered theoretical research in quantum computing, quantum simulation, and quantum communication.
Proposed using ultracold atoms in optical lattices as an analog quantum simulator for Hubbard models to investigate solid-state physics.
Made foundational contributions to open quantum systems and quantum noise in quantum optics.
Co-founded Alpine Quantum Technologies (AQT), a quantum computing hardware company (2018).

name: Philip Kim
summary: Philip Kim is a prominent condensed matter physicist renowned for his pioneering research on low-dimensional materials such as graphene and carbon nanotubes. His work has advanced the understanding of their unique electrical, thermal, and quantum properties. He currently holds a professorship in Physics and Applied Physics at Harvard University, contributing significantly to the field of quantum materials research.
contributions: Pioneering research and exploration of low-dimensional materials, including graphene and carbon nanotubes.
Developed methods for isolating graphene using atomic force microscopy (AFM) techniques, facilitating its study.
Co-discovery of quantum effects in graphene under strong magnetic fields, providing evidence of massless fermions.
Demonstrated the quantum Hall effect in single-layer graphene.
Contributed to the understanding of electrical and heat flow in carbon nanotubes and their application in nanotweezers.
Showed that nanostructuring graphene into nanoribbons can create a band gap, essential for semiconductor applications.
quotes: I owe Philip a great deal for this, and many people heard me saying – before and after the Nobel Prize – that I would be honored to share it with him.” (Andre Geim, 2010 Nobel Prize lecture)
I am sure there are many more surprises waiting to be discovered.”

name: Phillip Sharp
summary: Phillip A. Sharp is an American geneticist and molecular biologist who shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the co-discovery of RNA splicing. This landmark finding revealed that genes in eukaryotes are not continuous and contain non-coding regions called introns, fundamentally changing the understanding of gene structure and expression. He is an Institute Professor at MIT and has been instrumental in the development of the biotechnology industry, co-founding companies like Biogen.
contributions: Co-discovered RNA splicing, demonstrating that genes in eukaryotes are discontinuous and contain introns.
Revealed that the splicing of messenger RNA (mRNA) to delete introns can occur in different ways, yielding different proteins from the same DNA sequence.
Advanced the understanding of gene expression relevant to cancer and the mechanisms of RNA splicing.
Co-founded significant biotechnology companies, including Biogen and Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, contributing to new drug therapies.
Continues research on small RNAs and non-coding RNAs, investigating their roles in gene regulation, angiogenesis, and cellular stress.
quotes: What we were able to discover was that in human cells and in many other cells of higher-order organisms, the genes come in discontinuous segments.
The genome is actually just the beginning of biology. It is going to set us on a whole new plane or rate of discovery that will make it fascinating for decades to come.

name: Pierre Agostini
summary: Pierre Agostini is a French experimental physicist and an Emeritus Professor at The Ohio State University. He is renowned for his groundbreaking work in strong-field laser physics and attosecond science. He was jointly awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics for his experimental methods that generate attosecond pulses of light, which are crucial for studying electron dynamics in matter.
contributions: Observation of above-threshold ionization (ATI) in 1979
Invention of the RABBITT (reconstruction of attosecond beating by interference of two-photon transitions) technique for characterizing attosecond light pulses
Production and investigation of the first train of attosecond light pulses, each lasting 250 attoseconds, in 2001
Pioneering the field of attosecond science and strong-field laser physics
Developed experimental methods for generating attosecond pulses of light to study electron dynamics in matter

name: Radia Perlman
summary: Radia Perlman is an American computer scientist often called the "Mother of the Internet." Her invention of the Spanning Tree Protocol made it possible to build large, reliable networks, shaping the foundations of how modern data networks operate.
contributions: Invented the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) underpinning modern Ethernet networks
Made major contributions to network routing and security
Author of influential textbooks on network protocols

patents.title: Reliable broadcast of information in a wide area network (Spanning Tree Protocol)
Method and apparatus for preventing spanning tree loops during traffic overload conditions

name: Rainer Weiss
summary: Rainer Weiss is a German-American physicist renowned for his foundational work in gravitational physics and astrophysics. He is a co-founder of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) project and is credited with inventing the laser interferometric technique crucial for detecting gravitational waves. His pioneering research also includes measurements of the cosmic microwave background radiation and contributions to the COBE satellite. In 2017, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his pivotal role in the direct observation of gravitational waves.
contributions: Invented the laser interferometric technique, which is fundamental to the operation of LIGO.
Co-founded the NSF LIGO (gravitational-wave detection) project.
Made pioneering measurements of the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background radiation.
Served as a co-founder and science advisor for the NASA Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite.
Awarded the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves.
Developed the concept behind LIGO as an exercise for a general relativity course in 1967.
quotes: "For reasons probably related to the popular vision of Albert Einstein and, also, the threat posed by black holes in comic books and science fiction, our gravitational wave discoveries have had an amazing public impact."
"What was done is measure directly, with exquisitely sensitive instruments, gravitational waves predicted about 100 years ago by Albert Einstein."
"A gravitational wave is a very slight stretching in one dimension."

name: Randy Schekman
field: Cell Biology, Biochemistry, and Molecular Biology
summary: Randy Schekman is an American cell biologist and biochemist who shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries concerning the machinery regulating vesicle traffic, a major transport system in our cells. His research, primarily using yeast, identified key genes and proteins involved in cellular secretion and transport, providing fundamental insights into how cells organize and deliver molecules. This work is crucial for understanding diseases related to transport malfunctions, and he is also an advocate for open-access science publishing.
contributions: Discovered genetic mechanisms regulating vesicle traffic in cells.
Identified *sec* mutants and proteins essential for cellular secretion and transport.
Developed genetic and biochemical approaches to study eukaryotic membrane traffic.
Elucidated mechanisms of vesicle budding and protein transport from the endoplasmic reticulum.
Researched unconventional secretion of extracellular vesicles and their role in Parkinson's Disease.
Advocated for open-access science publishing.
quotes: Just as Wall Street needs to break the hold of the bonus culture, which drives risk-taking that is rational for individuals but damaging to the financial system, so science must break the tyranny of the luxury journals. The result will be better research that better serves science and society.
I got into science because I thought that, with inspiration and hard work, I could figure out how life works.

name: Rashid Sunyaev
summary: Rashid Sunyaev is a Russian-German astrophysicist renowned for his theoretical contributions to physical cosmology and high-energy astrophysics. He is best known for co-proposing the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, which describes cosmic microwave background distortions by galaxy clusters, and developing the Shakura-Sunyaev model for accretion onto black holes. His work has significantly advanced our understanding of the early universe and X-ray astronomy.
contributions: Co-proposed the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, describing distortions in the cosmic microwave background caused by galaxy clusters.
Developed the Shakura-Sunyaev model, which describes the accretion of matter onto a black hole from a disk.
Predicted baryon acoustic oscillations in the early universe, observable as brightness fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background.
Led X-ray observatory missions, including Kvant and Granat, which made the first X-ray observations of a supernova.
Made fundamental contributions to understanding cosmic X-ray sources and the formation of the cosmic microwave background radiation.
quotes: "A great moment for me was when I saw the paper by a radio astronomer from Chicago, John Carlstrom, together with his colleagues, reporting the results of Berkeley-Illinois-Maryland Association interferometer observations of the effect in the direction of clusters at different redshifts from z=0.17 up to z=0.888."

"But obviously, it was impossible to even dream in 1969, when I first started to write about the effect, that today the South Pole Telescope, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope and the Planck spacecraft would discover more than a thousand previously unknown clusters of galaxies on the blank sky."

name: Reinhard Genzel
summary: Reinhard Genzel is a German astrophysicist, co-director of the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, and an emeritus professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He was awarded the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with Andrea Ghez and Roger Penrose, for his groundbreaking work on the discovery of a supermassive compact object at the center of our galaxy. His research focuses on infrared and submillimetre astronomy, developing sensitive instruments to study active galaxies and the evolution of massive black holes.
contributions: Co-discovery of a supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, at the center of the Milky Way Galaxy.
Pioneering observations of the motions of stars at the Galactic center using infrared and submillimetre astronomy.
Development of advanced ground- and space-based instruments, including adaptive optics and interferometry, for high-resolution astronomical observations.
Provided strong evidence for the existence and mass of the supermassive black hole by measuring stellar velocities and orbits.
Conducted research into the formation and evolution of galaxies, particularly focusing on active galaxies and their central regions.
Demonstrated the gravitational redshift on a star orbiting the galactic center, consistent with Einstein's theory of General Relativity.
quotes: "Completely unexpected and, wow, I'm on cloud 17."
"We can sense the motions of stars which are orbiting the black hole with exquisite precision."
"In my life, I've learned not to be interested in — and not to ask questions about — things that I know there are no answers to."

name: Richard Alley
summary: Richard Alley is an American geologist and Evan Pugh Professor of Geosciences at Pennsylvania State University, known for his pioneering research on Earth's cryosphere. His work primarily focuses on the relationships between ice sheets, abrupt climate change, and sea level rise, often utilizing ice core data from Greenland and Antarctica. Alley is also recognized for his significant contributions to science communication, translating complex climate science for broader audiences and policymakers.
contributions: Revolutionized understanding of abrupt climate change, demonstrating that the last Ice Age ended rapidly, within a few years.
Conducted extensive research using polar ice cores to reconstruct past climate and predict future changes in climate and sea level.
Identified key processes governing the flow and stability of ice sheets and glaciers, particularly in Antarctica and Greenland.
Authored over 300 refereed scientific papers and the influential popular science book "The Two-Mile Time Machine".
Served as a lead author and contributor to the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reports.
Hosted the PBS television series "Earth: The Operator's Manual" and its companion book, enhancing public understanding of climate and energy.
quotes: "The more the climate is forced to change, the more likely it is to hit some unforeseen threshold that can trigger quite fast, surprising and perhaps unpleasant changes."
"We would be much better off if we could just plan ahead using the science we have on climate change."
"You might think of the climate as a drunk, when left alone, it sits; when forced to move, it staggers."

name: Richard Roberts
summary: Sir Richard J. Roberts is a British biochemist and molecular biologist, jointly awarded the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He is renowned for his discovery of introns in eukaryotic DNA and the mechanism of gene splicing, which revolutionized the understanding of gene structure and expression. His work has significantly impacted eukaryotic biology, the interpretation of the human genome, and various fields including cancer research. He currently serves as the Chief Scientific Officer at New England Biolabs, continuing research in enzyme discovery and bioinformatics.
contributions: Discovery of introns in eukaryotic DNA
Discovery of the mechanism of gene splicing
Pioneering work in DNA sequencing
Isolation and characterization of numerous restriction enzymes
Development of early computer programs for DNA analysis
Advocacy for the safety and use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs)
quotes: "The significance stems from the fact that it completely changed our view of what constituted a gene in eukaryotes."

"It had repercussions throughout eukaryotic biology and was of crucial importance for interpreting the human genome sequence, for example. It meant that all higher organisms had an extra degree of complexity in the way in which they used the information encoded in their DNA."
"Even today we are still learning more about how split genes are processed and finding additional complexities in the regulation of the information present in these split genes."

name: Richard Schrock
summary: Richard R. Schrock is an American chemist and Nobel laureate, recognized for his pivotal contributions to the development of the olefin metathesis reaction in organic synthesis. His pioneering work in creating efficient metal-compound catalysts for metathesis has significantly advanced the production of pharmaceuticals, plastics, and other materials, and has enabled more environmentally friendly chemical processes.
contributions: Developed the metathesis method in organic synthesis.
Discovered alpha hydrogen abstraction reactions leading to alkylidene and alkylidyne complexes.
Designed and synthesized highly active molybdenum and tungsten alkylidene catalysts for olefin metathesis.
Elucidated the structure and mechanism of olefin metathesis catalysts.
Pioneered work in ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP).
Demonstrated the catalytic reduction of dinitrogen to ammonia under mild conditions.
quotes: "I think I've done something important."
"It's not my catalyst, it's nature's."
"Everything is chemistry."

name: Rob Knight
summary: Rob Knight is a pioneering computational microbiologist and professor at the University of California, San Diego. He is recognized for developing innovative laboratory and computational methods to characterize the microbiomes of humans, animals, and the environment. His research has significantly advanced our understanding of the role microbes play in health and ecosystems, and he co-founded major global initiatives like the Earth Microbiome Project.
contributions: Developed laboratory and computational techniques for characterizing microbiomes.
Co-founded the Earth Microbiome Project.
Co-founded the American Gut Project.
Developed essential software tools for high-throughput microbiome science, including QIIME and UniFrac.
Linked microbiomes to a range of health conditions, such as obesity and inflammatory bowel disease, and various environmental processes.
Authored popular science books, including "Follow Your Gut: The Enormous Impact of Tiny Microbes," to increase public understanding of microbiomes.

name: Robert Horvitz
summary: H. Robert Horvitz is an American biologist and Nobel laureate recognized for his groundbreaking research on the genetic regulation of organ development and programmed cell death (apoptosis). Using the nematode C. elegans as a model, he identified key genes controlling cell death, demonstrating their fundamental importance in animal biology and their relevance to human diseases like cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. He is currently a Professor of Biology at MIT and an Investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.
contributions: Shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning the genetic regulation of organ development and programmed cell death.
Identified the "death genes" ced-3 and ced-4 in C. elegans, which are essential for programmed cell death.
Discovered that the gene ced-9 protects against cell death by interacting with ced-3 and ced-4.
Demonstrated that human genes exist that are counterparts to the C. elegans cell death genes, showing the evolutionary conservation of these mechanisms.
Pioneered the use of C. elegans to analyze the genetic control of animal development and behavior, including signal transduction and neural development.
Contributed to the identification of the first gene causing familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

name: Robert Kirshner
summary: Robert P. Kirshner is an American astronomer and Clowes Research Professor of Science emeritus at Harvard University, currently serving as Executive Director of the Thirty Meter International Observatory. He is renowned for his fundamental contributions to understanding supernovae and their role in cosmology, including the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe. His research has significantly advanced the understanding of dark energy and the large-scale structure of the cosmos.
contributions: Co-discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe, indicating the existence of dark energy, as part of the High-Z Supernova Search Team.
Extensive research on supernovae, particularly Type Ia, for measuring cosmic distances and understanding stellar explosions.
Led significant studies of Supernova 1987A, the brightest supernova since 1604.
Co-discovery of the Boötes Void, a vast, nearly empty region of space.
Participation in large-scale galaxy redshift surveys, such as the Las Campanas Redshift Survey.
quotes: "Although the universe is under no obligation to make sense, students in pursuit of a Ph. D. are."
"Science is not a vast encyclopedia, it is a thin flame of reason burning across ample reservoirs of ignorance."

name: Robert Langer
summary: Robert Langer is an American biomedical and chemical engineer, inventor, and entrepreneur. He is an Institute Professor at MIT, renowned for his pioneering work in controlled drug delivery systems and tissue engineering. His research has led to groundbreaking innovations, including numerous FDA-approved products, and he is one of the most cited engineers in history.
contributions: Pioneered controlled drug delivery systems, enabling precise release of medication for various treatments, including cancer therapy.
Co-founded the field of tissue engineering, developing biodegradable polymer scaffolds for growing new tissues and organs like skin, cartilage, and engineered spinal tissue.
Developed methods for encapsulating macromolecules, including mRNA, in nanoparticles for targeted delivery, enabling cellular production of proteins for disease protection and treatment.
Invented drug release systems operated by remote control and implantable 'pharmacy on a chip' devices.
Co-founded over 40 biotechnology companies, including Moderna, to translate academic research into practical medical products.
quotes: I think if you really believe in what you're trying to do, “no” is not going to stop you.
Dream big dreams, dreams that can change the world, and don't give up on them.
In life the thing that's defining is not how good your answers are but it's how good your questions are.

name: Robert Laughlin
summary: Robert B. Laughlin is an American theoretical physicist who, with Daniel C. Tsui and Horst Störmer, was awarded the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physics. He received the prize for his explanation of the fractional quantum Hall effect, theorizing that electrons in powerful magnetic fields can form a quantum fluid with fractionally charged excitations. Laughlin is currently a professor of physics at Stanford University, where his research includes high-temperature superconductivity and correlated-electron phenomenology.
contributions: Provided a theoretical explanation for the fractional quantum Hall effect.
Developed the Laughlin wavefunction, a mathematical model describing electron behavior in exotic states of matter.
Proposed the concept of a quantum fluid with fractionally charged excitations.
Contributed to theoretical models of high-temperature superconductivity.
Researched correlated-electron phenomenology and proposed orbital antiferromagnetism in Mott insulators.
quotes: "The questions worth asking, in other words, come not from other people but from nature, and are for the most part delicate things easily drowned out by the noise of everyday life."
"Real understanding of a thing comes from taking it apart oneself, not reading about it in a book or hearing about it in a classroom."

"The reason we believe in relativity today is not because we had a great transition in our beliefs about what should be so. We believe in relativity because we have no choice. It's true — measured to be true."

name: Robert Lefkowitz
summary: Robert J. Lefkowitz is an American physician and biochemist renowned for his groundbreaking discoveries concerning G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). His research has illuminated how cells receive and respond to signals, revolutionizing the understanding of cell communication and significantly impacting drug development. He was awarded the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.
contributions: Demonstrated the existence of cell-surface receptors and developed methods to track them using radioactive labeling.
Pioneered research on the structure and function of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a large family of cell signal-receiving molecules.
Cloned the gene for the beta-adrenergic receptor, revealing its seven-pass transmembrane structure and establishing it as the first member of a new protein family.
Discovered and characterized G protein-coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) and beta-arrestins, which are crucial for regulating GPCR activity and mediating cellular signaling.
His work forms the basic science foundation for approximately half of all modern prescription drugs, including treatments for hypertension, asthma, and heart conditions.
quotes: "Science is 99 percent failure, and that's an optimistic view."
"There are four keys to success in research: the first is focus, the second is focus, the third is focus, and the fourth you have to figure out for yourself."
"Try to see humor in everyday situations… Both humor and scientific curiosity involve looking at a situation and seeing relationships that other people might not see."

name: Robert Weinberg
summary: Robert Weinberg is a prominent American biologist renowned for his foundational contributions to cancer research. He is best known for identifying the first human oncogene (Ras) and the first tumor suppressor gene (Rb), which fundamentally changed the understanding of cancer's genetic basis. His work, including co-authoring "The Hallmarks of Cancer," has provided a critical framework for comprehending cancer cell behavior and has influenced the development of targeted cancer therapies.
contributions: Discovered the first human oncogene, Ras, demonstrating that cancer could arise from mutated cellular genes.
Isolated the first known tumor suppressor gene, Rb (retinoblastoma gene), highlighting genes that prevent cancer.
Co-authored the seminal paper "The Hallmarks of Cancer" (2000, updated 2011), outlining the biological capabilities acquired by cancer cells.
Achieved the first experimental transformation of normal human cells into neoplastic cells.
Investigated the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) program, showing its role in metastasis and in creating cancer stem cells.
quotes: "Most people have a series of goals in life. I just take one step after another."
"I'm not a person who's planned out his course in life. I just stumble from one steppingstone to the next."
"Indeed, many of the good ideas in my lab did not come from my brain, but from the brain of the young people whom I was fortunate enough to recruit."

name: Roderick MacKinnon
summary: Roderick MacKinnon is an American biophysicist and Nobel laureate, recognized for his seminal contributions to understanding ion channels. As a professor at Rockefeller University, he pioneered the use of X-ray crystallography to determine the atomic structures of these crucial membrane proteins. His groundbreaking work illuminated how ion channels selectively regulate the flow of ions across cell membranes, which is fundamental to nerve impulses and various other biological functions. This research earned him the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
contributions: Determined the three-dimensional molecular structure of a potassium channel using X-ray crystallography
Elucidated the precise mechanism by which potassium channels achieve ion selectivity, differentiating potassium from other ions like sodium
Revealed fundamental aspects of electrical signaling in living organisms by studying ion channel operation
Described how voltage-dependent ion channels regulate their pores and how ligand binding, including Ca2⁺, PIP2, and G proteins, modulates their activity
Developed the membrane dome model to explain the mechanosensory function of Piezo ion channels
Showed how dysfunctions in ion channels are associated with a range of neurological and cardiovascular disorders
quotes: "We used mutagenesis for nearly 10 years to study how the potassium channel works without getting the answer we needed."

name: Roger Kornberg
summary: Roger D. Kornberg is an American biochemist and professor of structural biology at Stanford University School of Medicine. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2006 for his groundbreaking studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription, detailing how genetic information from DNA is copied to RNA. His research has provided crucial insights into this fundamental process for life and its implications for various diseases, including cancer.
contributions: Discovered the nucleosome, the basic unit of chromosome packaging in eukaryotic cells.
Elucidated the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription, explaining how genetic information from DNA is copied to RNA.
Determined the three-dimensional structure of RNA polymerase II and its associated proteins using X-ray crystallography.
Identified the Mediator complex, a key component in gene regulation and transcription machinery in eukaryotes.
Discovered the "flip-flop" and lateral diffusion of phospholipids in bilayer membranes.
Developed a faithful transcription system from baker's yeast to study the process.
quotes: "Science was a part of dinner conversation and an activity in the afternoons and on weekends. Both my parents had fine scientific minds and taught by example how to approach questions and problems in a logical, dispassionate way. Scientific reasoning became second nature."
"The one thing I look for is chemistry."

name: Roger Penrose
summary: Sir Roger Penrose is a British mathematician and mathematical physicist renowned for his groundbreaking contributions to general relativity and cosmology. He was awarded half of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery that black hole formation is a robust prediction of the general theory of relativity. His work has profoundly shaped our understanding of the universe, from the nature of space-time to the mysteries of consciousness.
contributions: Developed, with Stephen Hawking, the Penrose–Hawking singularity theorems, demonstrating the inevitability of singularities within black holes and the Big Bang.
Introduced twistor theory, a new mathematical framework for uniting relativity and quantum theory.
Discovered Penrose tiling, aperiodic tilings that exhibit fivefold rotational symmetry and later observed in quasicrystals.
Developed Penrose diagrams, a method for mapping the regions of space-time surrounding a black hole.
Proposed the cosmic censorship hypothesis, suggesting that singularities are 'hidden' from external observers.
quotes: Intelligence cannot be present without understanding. No computer has any awareness of what it does.

We have a closed circle of consistency here: the laws of physics produce complex systems, and these complex systems lead to consciousness, which then produces mathematics, which can then encode in a succinct and inspiring way the very underlying laws of physics that gave rise to it.

name: Rudolf Jaenisch
summary: Rudolf Jaenisch is a pioneering German-American biologist, a founding member of the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, and a professor of biology at MIT. He is renowned for his groundbreaking work in transgenic science, epigenetic regulation of gene expression, and stem cell biology, which has profoundly influenced regenerative medicine. His research has provided crucial insights into genetic diseases, cancer, and neurological disorders, particularly through the development and application of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells.
contributions: Developed the first transgenic animals by integrating foreign DNA into early mouse embryos, a foundational step for disease modeling.
Pioneered research into epigenetic mechanisms and their role in gene expression, mammalian development, and disease.
Made significant advancements in understanding embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, including their creation from adult cells.
Demonstrated the therapeutic potential of iPS cells by correcting genetic defects and treating diseases like sickle-cell anemia and Parkinson's disease in mouse models.
Established the critical role of DNA methylation in survival and its causal relationship with certain types of cancer.
Publicly advocated against human reproductive cloning, citing high failure rates and unacceptable risks to developing individuals.
quotes: Cloning is the most unbiased test of epigenetics.
Given the failure rate, it would be dangerous and irresponsible to attempt human cloning. The risks to the fetus and the developing child are unacceptable.

name: Salim Ismail
summary: Salim Ismail is a technology strategist, speaker, and serial entrepreneur. As founding executive director of Singularity University and author of "Exponential Organizations," he studies how organizations can scale rapidly by leveraging accelerating technologies.
contributions: Founding executive director of Singularity University
Lead author of "Exponential Organizations," a framework for technology-driven scaling
Founder of OpenExO, a global transformation platform

name: Sandra Faber
summary: Sandra Faber is a distinguished American astrophysicist and Professor Emerita at the University of California, Santa Cruz, renowned for her groundbreaking research on the evolution of galaxies. Her work has significantly advanced our understanding of galaxy formation, the role of dark matter, and the large-scale structure of the universe. She has also been instrumental in the development of major astronomical instruments, shaping modern observational astronomy.
contributions: Co-discovery of the Faber-Jackson relation, linking the brightness of elliptical galaxies to the speed of stars within them
Pioneering work in developing the 'cold dark matter' theory of galaxy formation and evolution
Co-discovery of the 'Great Attractor,' a gravitational anomaly influencing galaxy movement
Instrumental role in the design and development of the Keck telescopes
Key contributions to the Hubble Space Telescope, including diagnosing and helping to repair its flawed optics and developing its Wide Field Planetary Camera
Led the development of the DEIMOS spectrograph for the Keck II telescope
quotes: I'd really like people to understand that fantastic groundwork has been laid — a cosmic experiment has been running for 14 billion years, and it has gotten to an interesting point. How incredibly tragic it would be if we foolishly pulled our own plug.

name: Sara Seager
summary: Sara Seager is an astrophysicist and planetary scientist at MIT and a leading figure in the search for planets beyond our solar system. Her theoretical work on exoplanet atmospheres and biosignature gases helped define how scientists detect and characterize distant worlds.
contributions: Developed foundational theory for analyzing exoplanet atmospheres and biosignatures
Pioneered methods to characterize the composition of planets orbiting distant stars
Named a MacArthur Fellow for advancing the search for life beyond Earth

name: Sarah Gilbert
summary: Sarah Gilbert is an English vaccinologist and Professor of Vaccinology at the University of Oxford, and co-founder of Vaccitech. She is renowned for her pivotal role in the rapid co-development of the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Her research focuses on creating viral vectored vaccines to combat influenza and a range of emerging viral pathogens, significantly contributing to global health and pandemic preparedness.
contributions: Co-developed the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine.
Led the development and testing of a universal flu vaccine.
Specializes in the development of vaccines against influenza and emerging viral pathogens.
Conducts research on viral vectored vaccines designed to induce strong T and B cell immune responses.
Contributed to vaccine development for diseases such as Nipah virus, MERS, and Lassa virus.
Co-founded the biotechnology company Vaccitech.
quotes: I have worked in the development of vaccines against infectious pathogens for many years and in the last 2 years have been able to draw on all that I have learned in order to respond to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. I have been so fortunate to work with a very talented and dedicated team who made it possible to develop a vaccine in less time than anyone thought possible.

name: Sau Lan Wu
summary: Sau Lan Wu is an Enrico Fermi Distinguished Professor of Physics and a Vilas Professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.
