She is a renowned particle physicist recognized for her pivotal contributions to three major discoveries: the charm quark, the gluon, and the Higgs boson. Her work has significantly shaped the understanding and development of the Standard Model of particle physics.
contributions: Contributed to the discovery of the J/psi particle in 1974, providing experimental evidence for the charm quark.
Played a leading role in the discovery of the gluon in 1979 through three-jet events in the TASSO experiment.
Played a leading role, with her Wisconsin group, in the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 at CERN's ATLAS experiment.
Contributed to the observation of Higgs boson production in association with a top quark pair, confirming its coupling to top quarks.
Actively involved in the search for dark matter at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
Mentored over 60 PhD students, fostering new generations of physicists.

name: Saul Perlmutter
summary: Saul Perlmutter is an American astrophysicist and professor of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, where he leads the Supernova Cosmology Project. He is renowned for his co-discovery, with two other scientists, that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. This groundbreaking finding provided evidence for the existence of dark energy, a mysterious force driving this acceleration, and earned him a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
contributions: Co-discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe
Provided evidence for the existence of dark energy
Led the international Supernova Cosmology Project
Pioneered methods for using Type Ia supernovae as 'standard candles' to measure cosmic distances
Co-recipient of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics
quotes: "If you're puzzled by what dark energy is, you're in good company."
"As a scientist, you feel a sense of team spirit for your country but you also have a sense of team spirit for the international community."
"There are still so many questions to answer. When you look at any part of the universe, you have to feel humbled."

name: Sean Carroll
field: Theoretical Physics, Cosmology, Philosophy of Science
summary: Sean Carroll is an American theoretical physicist and science communicator known for his contributions to quantum mechanics, cosmology, and general relativity. He is currently the Homewood Professor of Natural Philosophy at Johns Hopkins University, where his research extends to the philosophy of science. Carroll is also a prolific author and podcast host, actively engaged in popularizing complex scientific ideas for a broader audience.
contributions: Significant contributions to theoretical cosmology, including models of dark energy and spacetime symmetries.
Research on the foundations of quantum mechanics, exploring topics like the origin of probability and the emergence of space and time.
Work in statistical mechanics, focusing on entropy, the arrow of time, and the dynamics of complexity.
Authored multiple popular science books and a graduate-level textbook on general relativity.
Hosts the 'Mindscape' podcast, disseminating scientific and philosophical ideas to the public.
quotes: The world is not magic — and that's the most magical thing about it.
We are part of the universe that has developed a remarkable ability: We can hold an image of the world in our minds.
At heart, science is the quest for awesome - the literal awe that you feel when you understand something profound for the first time.

name: Serge Haroche
summary: Serge Haroche is a French physicist who was awarded the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with David J. Wineland, for his pioneering work in cavity quantum electrodynamics. He developed groundbreaking experimental methods to measure and manipulate individual quantum systems, such as photons, without destroying their quantum state. His research has significantly advanced the understanding of fundamental quantum physics. Haroche's work has also laid foundations for quantum information science. [1, 4, 5, 6, 12]
contributions: Devised ground-breaking experimental methods that enable the measuring and manipulation of individual quantum systems, specifically photons. [1, 4, 6, 12]
Pioneered the field of cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED), studying the interaction between single atoms and a few photons in a high-Q cavity. [2, 3, 12, 15]
Demonstrated the direct monitoring of the decoherence of mesoscopic superpositions of states, also known as Schrödinger cat states. [1, 12, 14]
Achieved quantum non-demolition (QND) detection of single photons, allowing their detection without absorption or loss. [2, 12, 15]
Demonstrated elementary steps of quantum information procedures, including the generation of atom-atom and atom-photon entanglement and the operation of quantum logic gates. [12, 14]
quotes: "Most technological advances in our life now come from serendipitous discoveries. That is a contraction of rocket technology and computer technology and atomic clock technology." [10, 11]

"It is important to fund young researchers who want to do curiosity-driven research. Curiosity-driven research is a part of life. Some people are curious. They want to learn more about nature and society should help that. It's like art: you can learn more and bring more beauty." [13]

name: Sheldon Glashow
summary: Sheldon Glashow is an American theoretical physicist who shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for his fundamental contributions to the electroweak theory, which unifies the weak and electromagnetic forces. His work significantly advanced the Standard Model of particle physics, explaining how elementary particles interact. He is currently an emeritus professor at Harvard University and a Metcalf Professor of Mathematics and Physics at Boston University.
contributions: Co-developed the electroweak theory, unifying the weak and electromagnetic interactions.
Predicted the existence of the charm quark.
Proposed the SU(2) × U(1) symmetry structure, foundational to the electroweak theory.
Predicted the weak neutral current, later experimentally confirmed.
Co-proposed the first Grand Unified Theory (GUT) in 1973.
quotes: "Tapestries are made by many artisans working together. The contributions of separate workers cannot be discerned in the completed work, and the loose and false threads have been covered over. So it is in our picture of particle physics."
"We called the new [fourth] quark the 'charmed quark' because we were pleased, and fascinated by the symmetry it brought to the subnuclear world."
"True, the Standard Model does explain a very great deal. Nevertheless it is not yet a proper theory, principally because it does not satisfy the physicists naive faith in elegance and simplicity."

name: Shimon Sakaguchi
summary: Shimon Sakaguchi is a Japanese immunologist renowned for his discovery of regulatory T cells (Tregs). His research illuminated how the immune system maintains self-tolerance and prevents autoimmune diseases by regulating immune responses. His work has significantly impacted the understanding and treatment of autoimmune disorders, cancer, and organ transplantation.
contributions: Discovered regulatory T cells (Tregs) in 1995
Described the crucial role of Tregs in maintaining immune self-tolerance and homeostasis
Elucidated the pathogenesis of autoimmune disorders as abnormal Treg cell function
Demonstrated that increasing Treg cells can prevent and treat autoimmune diseases
Showed that Tregs suppress anti-tumor immunity, leading to applications in cancer immunotherapy
Identified the gene responsible for the development of regulatory T cells
quotes: "I thought that if this paradoxical phenomenon of the immune response was resolved, a universal principle behind autoimmune disease would be revealed."
"What I always tell young people is that 'everything takes time.'"
"I believe this will encourage immunologists and physicians to apply the Tregs to treat various immunological diseases.”

name: Shinya Yamanaka
summary: Shinya Yamanaka is a Japanese Nobel Prize-winning stem cell researcher renowned for his discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells). This breakthrough demonstrated that mature adult cells could be reprogrammed into an embryonic-like pluripotent state, revolutionizing regenerative medicine by offering an alternative to human embryonic stem cells. His work has profound implications for understanding disease, developing new drugs, and creating cell-based therapies.
contributions: Generated induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells from adult mouse fibroblasts in 2006.
Identified four key transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc) essential for reprogramming somatic cells into iPS cells.
Successfully derived human iPS cells from adult fibroblasts in 2007.
Awarded the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery that mature cells can be converted to stem cells.
Provided a method for obtaining pluripotent stem cells without the controversial use of human embryos.
quotes: My goals over the decade include to develop new drugs to treat intractable diseases by using iPS cell technology and to conduct clinical trials using it.
I thought, we can't keep destroying embryos for our research. There must be another way.

I started my career as a surgeon 25 years ago. But it turned out that I am not talented as a surgeon, so I decided to change my career. But I still feel that I am a doctor. So my goal, all my life, is to bring this stem-cell technology to the bedside.

name: Shuji Nakamura
summary: Shuji Nakamura is a Japanese-born American materials scientist and electronics engineer, renowned for his work in optoelectronics. He was awarded the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for his invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes (LEDs). His groundbreaking research has enabled bright, energy-saving white light sources and the development of blue laser diodes used in technologies like Blu-ray.
contributions: Invented the first commercial high-brightness blue light-emitting diode (LED) in 1993.
Developed the method for producing strongly p-type gallium nitride (GaN), a crucial breakthrough for blue LEDs.
Enabled the creation of white LEDs by combining blue LEDs with yellow phosphor.
Developed the first group-III nitride-based violet laser diodes in 1995.
Pioneered the use of gallium nitride (GaN) as a semiconductor material for optoelectronics.
quotes: "Don't give up, even when others call you a fool. Stay true to your innovative ideas."
"I was very curious about nature because nature is so beautiful in Oku (Japan). Asking questions about nature is how I became interested in science."
"The LED light bulb is more than ten times the efficiency of regular incandescent lighting, so it can save the world hundreds of billions of dollars in electricity costs."

name: Stanislas Dehaene
summary: Stanislas Dehaene is a prominent French cognitive neuroscientist known for his research into the neural underpinnings of human cognition, including numerical abilities, reading, and consciousness. He directs the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging unit at NeuroSpin and holds the Chair of Experimental Cognitive Psychology at the Collège de France. His work utilizes advanced brain imaging techniques to explore how the human brain develops complex capacities through a combination of innate predispositions and learning.
contributions: Pioneered the study of numerical cognition, identifying specific brain regions in the parietal lobe responsible for the 'number sense' and related disorders like dyscalculia.
Discovered and analyzed the visual word form area (VWFA), a crucial region in the left occipitotemporal cortex that specializes in invariant recognition of written words during reading acquisition.
Developed computational models of consciousness, based on the Global Neuronal Workspace theory, and conducted brain imaging experiments on conscious and subliminal processing.
Proposed the 'neuronal recycling theory,' which posits that cultural inventions like reading and arithmetic are acquired by repurposing existing, evolutionarily older primate brain circuits.
quotes: The moral here is that nature and nurture should not be opposed. Pure learning, in the absence of any innate constraints, simply does not exist.”
Education is the main accelerator of our brain.”

Amazingly, most teachers receive little or no professional training in the science of learning. My feeling is that we should urgently change this state of affairs, because we now possess considerable scientific knowledge about the brain's learning algorithms and the pedagogies that are the most efficient.”

name: Stephen Elledge
summary: Stephen J. Elledge is an American geneticist renowned for his foundational discoveries in cell cycle regulation and the DNA damage response (DDR). His pioneering research has significantly advanced the understanding of how cells maintain genomic stability and respond to DNA damage, providing crucial insights into cancer development and potential therapeutic strategies. He currently serves as the Gregor Mendel Professor of Genetics and of Medicine at Harvard Medical School.
contributions: Discovery of the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway, a key signal transduction pathway that senses and responds to DNA damage.
Elucidation of genetic controls for cell-cycle regulation, including the identification and characterization of cell-cycle checkpoint proteins like p21 and cdk2.
Discovery of the F-box protein structural motif and its central role in ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation.
Development of novel genetic technologies and cloning tools, such as the phasmid vector, to expedite the study of cellular protein interactions.
Development of VirScan, a platform that can detect viral infections in patients from a small blood sample.
quotes: "I had a negative attitude about biology, because in high school it had seemed to be mostly about dissecting frogs and looking at plants and learning their weird names."
"Once I realized that biology was molecular, I got interested. I realized all the things that you could do with it."

"This prize is not just a recognition of my lab, but also a celebration of science itself. It is important for our society to promote the culture of science and celebrate its values: the values of reasoning, openness, tolerance, and respect for evidence. The Breakthrough Prize is promoting the values of science and helping drive home the importance of science to the entire world."

name: Stephen Hawking
summary: Stephen Hawking was an English theoretical physicist and cosmologist who significantly advanced our understanding of black holes and the origins of the universe. Despite a debilitating illness, he made groundbreaking contributions to science and popularized complex theoretical physics through his best-selling books.
contributions: Collaborated on gravitational singularity theorems with Roger Penrose.
Theoretically predicted that black holes emit radiation, now known as Hawking radiation.
Developed a theory of cosmology uniting general relativity and quantum mechanics.
Pioneered the study of primordial black holes.
Authored popular science books, including "A Brief History of Time".
quotes: "One, remember to look up at the stars and not down at your feet. Two, never give up work. Work gives you meaning and purpose and life is empty without it. Three, if you are lucky enough to find love, remember it is there and don't throw it away."
"Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change."
"Life would be tragic if it weren't funny."

name: Steven Chu
summary: Steven Chu is an American physicist and Nobel laureate who shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work in cooling and trapping atoms with laser light. He is also recognized for his significant contributions to biophysics, his tenure as the 12th U.S. Secretary of Energy, and his advocacy for sustainable energy and climate change solutions. He currently holds professorships at Stanford University in physics, molecular and cellular physiology, and energy science and engineering.
contributions: Developed methods for laser cooling and trapping atoms, for which he received the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Pioneered the use of optical tweezers to manipulate and study individual DNA molecules and other biomolecules.
Introduced atom interferometry based on optical pulses of light.
Demonstrated the magneto-optic trap (MOT).
Served as the 12th U.S. Secretary of Energy (2009-2013), initiating programs like ARPA-E and Energy Innovation Hubs.
Devoted a significant portion of his career to finding solutions for energy and climate challenges, advocating for renewable energy and efficiency.
quotes: “As the saying goes, the Stone Age did not end because we ran out of stones; we transitioned to better solutions. The same opportunity lies before us with energy efficiency and clean energy.”
“Science is not a partisan issue. It is the pursuit of truth and understanding.”

“While we cannot accurately predict the course of climate change in the coming decades, the risks we run if we don't change our course are enormous. Prudent risk management does not equate uncertainty with inaction.”

name: Stuart Russell
summary: Stuart Russell is a prominent British computer scientist and a professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He is recognized for his foundational contributions to artificial intelligence and for co-authoring "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach," a leading textbook in the field. Russell is also a vocal advocate for ensuring that AI systems are beneficial to humanity and has been active in the movement to ban autonomous weapons.
contributions: Co-authored the seminal textbook "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach"
Made foundational contributions to machine learning, probabilistic reasoning, knowledge representation, and planning
Defined and studied the concept of bounded optimality
Developed Bayesian logic and the NETVISA global seismic monitoring algorithm for nuclear test verification
Founded the Center for Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) at UC Berkeley
Active participant in the international campaign to ban lethal autonomous weapons systems
quotes: "Intelligent robots don't need to be conscious to turn against us."
"Perhaps the most important thing we can do is to design AI systems that are, to the extent possible, provably safe and beneficial for humans."
"What AI could do is essentially be a power tool that magnifies human intelligence and gives us the ability to move our civilization forward."

name: Subir Sachdev
summary: Subir Sachdev is the Herchel Smith Professor of Physics at Harvard University, renowned for his theoretical condensed matter physics research. He has significantly advanced the understanding of quantum entanglement in natural systems, quantum phase transitions, and their implications for high-temperature superconductors and strange metals. His work includes the development of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and has uncovered remarkable connections between quantum entanglement in laboratory materials and astrophysical black holes.
contributions: Developed the theory of quantum criticality, elucidating its implications for experimental observations on materials.
Pioneered the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, a solvable model of complex quantum entanglement in metals.
Established connections between quantum entanglement in certain laboratory materials and the quantum entanglement in black holes.
Made extensive contributions to the theory of high-temperature superconductors and strange metals.
Advanced the understanding of quantum spin liquids and emergent gauge theories.

name: Susan Solomon
summary: Susan Solomon is a distinguished American atmospheric chemist, renowned for her pivotal work in explaining the formation of the Antarctic ozone hole. She led critical expeditions to Antarctica in the 1980s, providing the first direct evidence that human-made chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were responsible for ozone depletion. Her foundational research has significantly influenced international environmental policies, most notably the Montreal Protocol, and she has made substantial contributions to our understanding of global climate change.
contributions: Pioneered the theory linking polar stratospheric clouds and chlorofluorocarbons to the Antarctic ozone hole.
Led expeditions to Antarctica that gathered the first chemical measurements confirming CFCs as the cause of ozone depletion.
Showed that volcanic activity can accelerate the destruction of the ozone layer by CFCs.
Played a key leadership role as co-chair of Working Group I for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) Fourth Assessment Report.
Demonstrated that changes in stratospheric composition due to ozone depletion also affected Antarctic surface climate.
Her work provided the scientific basis for the UN Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to regulate ozone-depleting substances.
quotes: "We have a beautiful planet, and I feel very privileged to have the chance to work as a public servant in helping the public understand that planet."
"It's really important that scientists interact with politicians as much as we can".
"Let's not give up now – we're right on the cusp of success".

name: Svante Pääbo
summary: Svante Pääbo is a Swedish geneticist and Nobel Laureate, widely recognized as one of the founders of paleogenetics. He is celebrated for pioneering methods to extract and analyze ancient DNA from extinct organisms, significantly advancing our understanding of human evolution. His groundbreaking work includes sequencing the Neanderthal genome and discovering the Denisovans, revealing complex interbreeding events with early modern humans.
contributions: Co-founding the scientific discipline of paleogenetics.
Developing pioneering techniques for extracting and sequencing ancient DNA from archaeological and paleontological remains.
Achieving the first sequencing of the Neanderthal genome.
Discovering the Denisovans, a previously unknown hominin group, through ancient DNA analysis.
Demonstrating that gene flow occurred between Neanderthals and Homo sapiens, contributing Neanderthal DNA to present-day non-African populations.
Identifying genetic differences between modern humans and extinct hominins that may underlie human-specific traits, such as those related to cognitive and language abilities.
quotes: The dirty little secret of genomics is that we still know next to nothing about how a genome translates into the particularities of a living and breathing individual.”
From a genomic perspective, we are all Africans.”
Neanderthals are not totally extinct. In some of us they live on, a little bit."

name: Takaaki Kajita
summary: Takaaki Kajita is a Japanese physicist best known for his groundbreaking discovery of neutrino oscillations, which demonstrated that neutrinos possess mass. This pivotal finding, for which he shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics, significantly expanded the Standard Model of particle physics. His extensive research at the Kamiokande and Super-Kamiokande detectors has profoundly influenced elementary particle physics and astrophysics.
contributions: Discovered neutrino oscillations, demonstrating that neutrinos have mass.
Led atmospheric neutrino studies at the Super-Kamiokande experiment, confirming the deficit of atmospheric muon neutrinos.
Contributed to the Kamiokande-II experiment, including the detection of neutrinos from Supernova 1987A.
Currently conducts research on gravitational waves and the KAGRA detector.
quotes: I want to thank the neutrinos, of course. And since neutrinos are created by cosmic rays, I want to thank them, too.

name: Tasuku Honjo
summary: Tasuku Honjo is a Japanese physician-scientist and immunologist who was awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. He is renowned for his identification of programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), a pivotal discovery that paved the way for the development of effective cancer immunotherapies. His groundbreaking work has significantly transformed the landscape of cancer treatment and research.
contributions: Identified programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) in 1992, which functions as a brake on T-cells and is crucial for cancer immunotherapy.
Discovered activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), an enzyme essential for class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes.
Elucidated the basic conceptual framework and molecular mechanism of immunoglobulin class switch recombination.
Molecularly identified key immune-regulatory cytokines, including IL-4 and IL-5.
Demonstrated that PD-1 inhibition enhances anti-tumor responses, leading to the development of PD-1 blockade cancer therapies.
Contributed to developmental biology by identifying RBP-J as a Notch signaling target.
quotes: "Questioning assumptions is the foundation of scientific progress."
"Discoveries are often born out of failure, so don't be discouraged by setbacks."
"My motto is 'research what you want to know.'"

name: Terence Tao
summary: Terence Tao is an Australian-American mathematician, often referred to as the "Mozart of Math," who is a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2006 for his wide-ranging and profound contributions to various areas of mathematics. Tao is known for his exceptional breadth and depth of knowledge, making significant breakthroughs across numerous mathematical disciplines.
contributions: Co-proof of the Green–Tao theorem, demonstrating the existence of arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of prime numbers.
Significant advancements in partial differential equations, including crucial existence theorems for nonlinear Schrödinger equations.
Resolution of the Erdős discrepancy problem, utilizing entropy estimates within analytic number theory.
Made progress on the Collatz conjecture.
Extensive studies and progress in the field of random matrices.
Groundbreaking work in harmonic analysis, combinatorics, and additive number theory.
quotes: Talent is important, but how one develops and nurtures it is even more so.
Mathematics is not just about solving problems, it is about understanding structures and patterns.
I work in a number of areas, but I don't view them as being disconnected; I tend to view mathematics as a unified subject.

name: Theodor Hänsch
summary: Theodor W. Hänsch is a German physicist and Nobel laureate recognized for his foundational work in laser-based precision spectroscopy. He shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions, particularly the development of the optical frequency comb technique, which allows for exceptionally precise measurements of light frequencies. His research has significantly advanced atomic physics, enabling rigorous testing of fundamental physical theories and constants. Hänsch remains an active researcher, continuing to explore new applications for frequency combs and the quantum physics of ultracold atoms.
contributions: Development of laser-based precision spectroscopy
Invention of the optical frequency comb technique
Pioneered the first narrowband tunable dye laser
Proposed the first method for laser cooling of atomic gases
Conducted precision spectroscopy of the hydrogen atom, providing accurate values for the Rydberg constant and Lamb shift
Realized the first two- and three-dimensional atomic lattices bound by light
quotes: "I think in a way much of my work has revolved around tools, around inventions, gadgets, partly because I really enjoy playing with gadgets."
"I'm still driven by my inventive spirit. I follow my instincts and do experiments without knowing exactly where they will lead."

name: Thomas Südhof
summary: Thomas Südhof is a German-American neuroscientist recognized for his groundbreaking work on synaptic transmission, the process by which nerve cells communicate in the brain. His discoveries have illuminated the molecular mechanisms underlying the precise and rapid signaling at synapses, which is crucial for brain function. This research has significantly advanced the understanding of neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's, schizophrenia, and autism.
contributions: Awarded the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning the machinery regulating vesicle traffic, a major transport system in cells.
Identified key molecular components and mechanisms essential for chemical signaling between neurons.
Elucidated how synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitters through fusion with neuronal membranes.
Discovered synaptotagmin proteins that sense calcium and mediate neurotransmitter release.
Identified neurexins and neuroligins, proteins crucial for synapse formation and specification, and linked their mutations to disorders like autism and schizophrenia.
quotes: "What we have done is to try to understand better how one cell sends out the information to the next cell at the synapse and ideally also how it processes that information. Our major contribution, I believe, was in figuring out the fundamental molecular processes that govern this ability of a nerve cell in all brains, in all cells, in all animals."

"A common theme in science is we do science best when we don't have an application in mind because it limits our imagination and creativity. But, in the end, we feel most rewarded when what we discover, out of a quest for knowledge, leads actually to an application."

name: Tim Berners-Lee
summary: Sir Tim Berners-Lee is a British computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web in 1989. He created the first web browser and server and chose to make the underlying technology free and open to all.
contributions: Invented the World Wide Web, including HTTP, HTML, and the URL
Built the first web browser and web server
Founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) to keep the web open

name: Tim Hunt
summary: Sir Richard Timothy "Tim" Hunt is a British biochemist and molecular physiologist, recognized for his groundbreaking work on cell cycle regulation. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of protein molecules that control cell division. His pivotal discovery of cyclins, proteins essential for the progression through the cell cycle, profoundly advanced the understanding of fundamental biological processes and their implications for conditions like cancer.
contributions: Discovered cyclins, proteins that regulate the progression through the cell cycle.
Shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries of key regulators of the cell cycle.
Demonstrated the importance of periodic cyclin degradation as a cell cycle regulatory mechanism.
Contributed to understanding cancer-cell development through his cell cycle research.
Co-authored influential books on the cell cycle, including "The Cell Cycle: An Introduction".

name: Titia de Lange
summary: Titia de Lange is a distinguished Dutch molecular and cell biologist renowned for her foundational research on telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. Her work has been crucial in understanding how telomeres maintain genome integrity, prevent DNA damage responses, and play a significant role in cellular aging and cancer development. She is currently the Director of the Anderson Center for Cancer Research and Leon Hess Professor at Rockefeller University.
contributions: Isolated and identified the sequence of human telomeres.
Discovered the six-subunit protein complex, named shelterin, that specifically binds to and protects telomeres.
Demonstrated how shelterin represses DNA damage response pathways at chromosome ends.
Identified the t-loop structure of telomeres, revealing how chromosome ends are hidden from DNA repair mechanisms.
Elucidated the dual role of telomeres in tumor suppression by telomere shortening and the induction of genome instability in cancer.
quotes: "That was where I first saw how science is really done. … It was a very vibrant, competitive, international lab. It was a lot of fun, so that made me stay in science."
"At the time, women were expected to be homemakers; at best women pursued professions as a hobby."
"I am grateful that evolution generated telomeres, the most fascinating and rewarding subject I can imagine."

name: Tony Hunter
summary: Tony Hunter is a British-American biologist and cancer researcher known for his seminal discovery of protein tyrosine phosphorylation. His work, beginning in the late 1970s, revealed a fundamental cellular regulatory mechanism and its critical role in cancer development. This breakthrough has profoundly influenced the understanding of cell growth control and led to the development of numerous targeted cancer therapies.
contributions: Discovered protein tyrosine phosphorylation as a fundamental mechanism for transmembrane-signal transduction.
Demonstrated that dysregulation of tyrosine phosphorylation by activated oncogenic protein tyrosine kinases is pivotal in malignant cell transformation.
Identified the oncogene Src as a tyrosine kinase.
Pioneered research that led to the development of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), including the leukemia drug Gleevec.
Developed anti-phosphotyrosine antibodies, a powerful tool for studying cancer signals.
Continues to research new therapeutic targets for cancers, including disrupting signaling molecules like LIF in pancreatic cancer.
quotes: "The study of tumor viruses and their oncogenes really led to a revolution in our understanding of cancer."
"I discovered tyrosine phosphorylation as a cancer mechanism while carrying out studies with a simple chicken tumor virus, hoping our findings would give us clues as to how human cancer develops."

name: Uğur Şahin
summary: Uğur Şahin is a German medical researcher, oncologist, and immunologist, best known as the co-founder and CEO of BioNTech. He pioneered breakthroughs in messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) medicines, leading to the development of the world's first mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccine. His extensive work also focuses on developing individualized cancer immunotherapies.
contributions: Co-founding BioNTech in 2008 to develop active immunotherapies for cancer and infectious diseases.
Leading the development of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine, the first mRNA-based vaccine approved against COVID-19.
Pioneering mRNA-based individualized cancer immunotherapies.
Co-inventing more than 500 filed patent applications and patents in life science and biotechnology.
Co-founding Ganymed Pharmaceuticals in 2001, focusing on cancer therapies.
quotes: "To all of you who are out there – we are very grateful for what you do. You are our heroes… please don't lose faith and continue. There is an end to this."

name: Veerabhadran Ramanathan
summary: Veerabhadran Ramanathan is an Indian-American atmospheric scientist and Professor Emeritus at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California, San Diego. He is renowned for his groundbreaking discoveries in climate science, particularly identifying the significant greenhouse effect of non-CO2 gases like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and black carbon. His research has profoundly influenced our understanding of global warming and contributed to the formation of international policies to mitigate climate change and air pollution. He also champions climate literacy and solutions.
contributions: Discovered the significant greenhouse effect of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) in 1975, establishing that non-CO2 gases are major contributors to planetary warming.
Co-developed the first version of the U.S. community climate model in the 1980s.
Led a NASA study that demonstrated clouds have a large global cooling effect.
Discovered and characterized "Atmospheric Brown Clouds" (ABCs) over South Asia, highlighting the crucial role of black carbon as a greenhouse compound.
Pioneered the concept of mitigating Short-Lived Climate Pollutants (SLCPs), such as black carbon, methane, ozone, and HFCs, to significantly slow near-term global warming.
Founded Project Surya, an initiative focused on reducing black carbon and other climate-warming emissions from solid biomass cooking in South Asia and Africa, while improving public health.
quotes: "The effect of greenhouse gases on global warming is, in my opinion, the most important environmental issue facing the world today."
"I discovered there that science, and religion can work together to address the climate crisis. Faith leaders have access to people in a way that scientists do not."

name: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan
summary: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan is a British-American structural biologist known for his groundbreaking work on the atomic structure and function of ribosomes. He shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his research, which elucidated how these cellular machines synthesize proteins. His discoveries have significantly advanced the understanding of fundamental biological processes and have important implications for the development of new antibiotics.
contributions: Determined the atomic structure of the 30S ribosomal subunit.
Elucidated the complete molecular structure of the ribosome and its complexes with antibiotics.
Provided structural insights into the mechanism of protein biosynthesis fidelity.
Contributed to understanding chromatin organization, including the structure and role of linker histones.
Pioneered the use of X-ray crystallography and neutron scattering in structural biology.
quotes: "Don't be afraid to take risks and challenge established ideas. That's how progress is made."
"You don't have to be a genius to do science; you just have to be curious and persistent."
"Science is curiosity, testing and experimenting."

name: Victor Ambros
summary: Victor Ambros is an American developmental biologist and molecular geneticist, best known for his co-discovery of microRNA (miRNA) with Gary Ruvkun. Their groundbreaking research identified a novel class of short, non-coding RNA molecules crucial for regulating gene expression and animal development. This fundamental discovery significantly advanced the understanding of cell function and mechanisms underlying gene activity, earning them the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
contributions: Co-discovery of lin-4, the first known microRNA, in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
Identification of microRNA as a novel class of small RNA molecules that regulate gene expression.
Elucidation of microRNA's critical role in post-transcriptional gene regulation and developmental timing.
Co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of microRNA.
quotes: We see it as a, in a way, as a celebration not really of the particular scientist in this case, but of the way of doing science, you know.

name: Victoria Kaspi
summary: Victoria Kaspi is a Canadian astrophysicist and a professor at McGill University, renowned for her pioneering research on neutron stars, pulsars, and magnetars. She has significantly advanced our understanding of these extreme celestial objects and their role in the universe. Her work also includes leading discoveries in the field of Fast Radio Bursts, exploring some of the most puzzling phenomena in modern astrophysics.
contributions: Pioneering studies of neutron stars, pulsars, and magnetars, shedding light on their properties and behavior.
Discovery of the fastest spinning pulsar known, PSR J1748-2446ad.
Conducted precise tests of Einstein's theory of gravity (general relativity) using observations of binary pulsars.
Led the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) Fast Radio Burst (FRB) project, dramatically expanding the known population of FRBs.
Observed the first "anti-glitch" (a sudden spin-down event) in a magnetar, providing new constraints on the internal structure of neutron stars.
quotes: "Something, somewhere in the cosmos, is producing a huge burst of radio waves, and we don't know what…."
"It is a truly golden age in radio astronomy."
"There are some days when I can't believe they pay me to do it."

name: Wendy Freedman
summary: Wendy Freedman is a Canadian-American observational cosmologist and astrophysicist, currently a University Professor at the University of Chicago. She is renowned for leading the Hubble Space Telescope Key Project, which provided precise measurements of the universe's expansion rate (the Hubble Constant). Her work has significantly refined our understanding of the universe's scale, age, and evolution, laying the foundation for modern precision cosmology.
contributions: Led the Hubble Space Telescope Key Project to accurately measure the universe's expansion rate and age.
Established precision measurements of the Hubble constant, resolving a long-standing debate about the age and size of the universe.
Refined the cosmic distance ladder using Cepheid variable stars and supernovae as cosmic distance markers.
Chaired the board of directors for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) project, a next-generation ground-based observatory.
Researches dark energy and its role in the accelerating expansion of the universe.
Investigates whether discrepancies in Hubble Constant measurements indicate new physics beyond the standard cosmological model.
quotes: "The Hubble constant, which measures the expansion rate, together with the total energy density of the Universe, sets the size of the observable Universe, its age, and its radius of curvature."

"We are at an interesting juncture in cosmology. With new methods and technology, the accuracy in measurement of the Hubble constant has vastly improved, but a recent tension has arisen that is either signaling new physics or as-yet unrecognized uncertainties."

"When I started out in this field, there was a big debate at the time about how old the universe was and the debate was, is the universe 10 billion years old or is it 20 billion years old? ... And so I'm I'm known for resolving this debate, making a measurement of the universe, which is about thirteen point seven billion years between the values of 10 and 20 billion years that people have been arguing about before that time."

name: William Kaelin
summary: William G. Kaelin Jr. is an American Nobel laureate physician-scientist renowned for his seminal discoveries on how cells sense and adapt to changing oxygen availability. His research, particularly on tumor suppressor genes like VHL, has profoundly influenced the understanding of cancer metabolism and oxygen biology. He currently serves as a professor of medicine at Harvard University and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, with his work leading to new therapeutic strategies for various diseases, including cancer and anemia.
contributions: Co-discovery of the molecular mechanisms by which cells sense and adapt to oxygen levels, which earned him the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Elucidating how the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor protein regulates the stability of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs).
Identifying the critical roles of mutations in tumor suppressor genes, including retinoblastoma, VHL, and p53, in cancer development.
Paving the way for the development of VEGF-inhibiting drugs for kidney cancer and HIF-targeting therapies for anemia and other cancers.
Discovering the mechanism by which thalidomide-like drugs lead to 'molecular glue degraders' effective against multiple myeloma.
quotes: "If your goal in science is simply to get prizes and to get recognition, you may be doing it for the wrong reason, and you'll probably, frankly, wind up being a miserable person, because there's certainly some luck involved in winning prizes."
"What young trainees have to understand is that, at least for those of us who love science, getting to do science is a prize in and of itself."

"I discovered I enjoyed science so much I would do it even if I wasn't getting paid. In fact, there are many times I feel guilty I'm getting paid to do this because it feels like I'm playing rather than working."

name: William Phillips
summary: William Daniel Phillips is an American physicist who was awarded the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking work in developing methods to cool and trap atoms using laser light. His research at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) led to the creation of ultracold atomic systems, which are crucial for advancing technologies such as atomic clocks and quantum computing. Phillips's innovations have significantly deepened the understanding of fundamental quantum phenomena and have enabled high-precision measurements. He is currently a Research Fellow at NIST and a Professor of Physics at the University of Maryland, College Park's Joint Quantum Institute.
contributions: Developed methods to cool and trap atoms with laser light, earning him a share of the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Invented the "Zeeman slower," a device using lasers and a magnetic field to decelerate and cool an atomic beam.
Demonstrated the first device capable of trapping electrically neutral atoms using a magnetic trap.
Discovered sub-Doppler cooling, achieving atomic temperatures significantly lower than previously predicted theoretical limits.
Founded NIST's laser cooling and trapping group, developing techniques used globally for cold-atom experiments.
His work contributed to the development of atomic fountain clocks, which are primary standards for world timekeeping, and aided in the first observation of the Bose-Einstein condensate.
quotes: "By the time I was five years old, I was completely fascinated by science."
"It seems like I've been interested in physics as long as I can remember."

name: Wolfgang Ketterle
summary: Wolfgang Ketterle is a German-born physicist and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), known for his pioneering research in ultracold atomic matter. He was a co-recipient of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics for the achievement of Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) in dilute gases of alkali atoms and for early fundamental studies of their properties. His work involves trapping and cooling atoms to temperatures near absolute zero, expanding the understanding of quantum physics.
contributions: Co-recipient of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics for achieving Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) in dilute gases of alkali atoms.
Created the first gaseous Bose-Einstein condensate from sodium atoms.
Realized the first "atom laser."
Demonstrated interference between two colliding Bose-Einstein condensates.
Conducted fundamental studies of ultracold atomic matter, including molecular Bose condensates and fermionic condensates.

name: Yann LeCun
summary: Yann LeCun is a French-American computer scientist renowned as a pioneer in deep learning and one of the "Godfathers of AI". He is primarily recognized for his foundational work on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which have significantly advanced computer vision, image recognition, and various real-world AI applications. His research has been instrumental in enabling machines to learn directly from data.
contributions: Pioneering work and development of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
Designed the LeNet-5 network, widely used for handwritten character recognition
Proposed an early version of the backpropagation algorithm for neural networks
Co-created the DjVu image compression technology
Co-developed the Lush programming language
Developed the "Optimal Brain Damage" regularization method for neural networks
quotes: "AI is going to bring a new renaissance for humanity, a new form of enlightenment, if you want, because AI is going to amplify everybody's intelligence."
"Before we reach human-level AI, we will have to reach cat-level AI and dog-level AI."
"A system trained on language alone will never approximate human intelligence, even if trained from now until the heat death of the universe."

name: Yoshua Bengio
summary: Yoshua Bengio is a Canadian computer scientist and a pioneering figure in artificial neural networks and deep learning. He is a professor at the Université de Montréal and the founder and scientific director of Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute. Bengio co-received the 2018 A.M. Turing Award, often called the "Nobel Prize of Computing," for his foundational work on deep learning. He is also a leading voice in the responsible development of AI, chairing the International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI.
contributions: Pioneering work in artificial neural networks and deep learning.
Co-recipient of the 2018 A.M. Turing Award for foundational contributions to deep learning.
Developed the neural probabilistic language model, addressing the "curse of dimensionality" in natural language processing.
Made significant contributions to generative models, including the principles behind Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
Founded and leads Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, a major deep learning research center.
Actively involved in AI safety research and policy, chairing the International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI.
quotes: "Since we don't really know how fast technological advances in AI or elsewhere (e.g., biotechnology) will come, it's best to get on with the task of better regulating these kinds of powerful tools right away."

"People demanding that AIs have rights [are making] a huge mistake. Frontier AI models already show signs of self-preservation in experimental settings today, and eventually giving them rights would mean we're not allowed to shut them down."
"The thing I'm more worried about, in a foreseeable future, is not computers taking over the world. I'm more worried about misuse of AI."

name: Özlem Türeci
summary: Özlem Türeci is a German physician, immunologist, and entrepreneur known for her pioneering work in cancer immunotherapy and mRNA technology. As co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of BioNTech, she played a pivotal role in developing the first mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccine. Her research focuses on identifying tumor-specific molecules and translating scientific insights into novel therapies for cancer, infectious diseases, and autoimmune disorders.
contributions: Co-founded Ganymed Pharmaceuticals (2001) to develop monoclonal antibodies for cancer treatment.
Co-founded BioNTech (2008) to advance individualized mRNA-based immunotherapies for cancer.
Led the clinical development of the BNT162b2, the first mRNA-based vaccine approved for COVID-19.
Contributed significantly to the identification and characterization of tumor-specific molecules for personalized therapeutic approaches.
Advanced mRNA technology for a broad range of applications, including vaccines for infectious diseases and treatments for autoimmune conditions.
quotes: “For as long as I can remember, I've been interested in medicine and the human immune system. Understanding how these mechanisms work and finding ways to use these insights for the benefit of people or humanity – this is what my work is all about.”

“Let us not wait for a baptism of fire for all the high-potential technologies, the powerful scientific concepts, that already – today – can contribute to the well-being of humanity, the preservation of this planet, and other global challenges of our time.”
